resources.title: Water and Hydrogen Bonding: Study Guide (Biology 1.1)
resources.description: Learn how water's polarity and hydrogen bonds lead to cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat, evaporative cooling, floating ice and solvent power, and why these matter to living things.
prerequisites: Atoms, electrons and covalent bonds
Basic idea of temperature and energy (joules)
learningObjectives: Explain why the O–H bonds in water are polar and why water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Link cohesion, adhesion and surface tension to water transport in plants
Use q = mcΔT to show how water's high specific heat buffers temperature
Explain evaporative cooling, floating ice and water's solvent properties in terms of hydrogen bonding
Identify variables and controls in an experiment on water movement, and separate correlation from causation
resources.calculatorNote: Specific heat capacity of liquid water: 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Other specific heats are given where they are used
keyPoints: Oxygen pulls shared electrons harder than hydrogen, so each O–H bond is polar: O is partly negative (δ⁻), each H is partly positive (δ⁺).
A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a δ⁺ hydrogen of one molecule and a δ⁻ atom (here O) of another. Each one is weak; millions together are strong.
Hydrogen bonds explain cohesion, adhesion and surface tension, a high specific heat, a high heat of vaporization, floating ice and water's power as a solvent.
Energy for warming: q = mcΔT, with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ for water. Large c means small temperature change for a given energy.

faqs.question: Is a hydrogen bond a real chemical bond?
faqs.answer: It is an attraction between molecules (or between parts of one large molecule), not a shared pair of electrons. It is much weaker than the covalent O–H bond inside a water molecule, which is why water can boil without its molecules falling apart.

faqs.question: Do hydrogen bonds only matter for water?
faqs.answer: No. Hydrogen bonds also hold the two strands of DNA together and help proteins fold into their shapes. Water is simply the most important example in this topic.

resources.title: Elements of Life: Study Guide (Biology 1.2)
resources.description: Learn which elements build carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, where sulfur, phosphorus and nitrogen sit in them, and how organisms take these atoms from their surroundings.
prerequisites: Atoms, elements and chemical formulas
Covalent bonds and the polarity of water (Topic 1.1)
learningObjectives: Explain why organisms must take in atoms and molecules from their surroundings to build new biological molecules
State which elements make up carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids
Describe where sulfur, phosphorus and nitrogen are found in proteins, phospholipids and nucleic acids
Use a formula, a table of elements or tracer data to decide which class a biological molecule belongs to
Calculate the percentage by mass of an element in a biological molecule
resources.calculatorNote: Atomic masses: H 1.01, C 12.01, N 14.01, O 16.00, P 30.97, S 32.06. Keep full values until the last step; give percentages to 3 significant figures
keyPoints: Living things cannot make atoms. They take atoms and molecules from their surroundings and rearrange them into new biological molecules.
Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are the most common elements in all four classes of large biological molecule.
Sulfur marks proteins (in two amino acids). Phosphorus marks nucleic acids and phospholipids (in phosphate groups). Nitrogen is in nucleic acids (in the bases) and in proteins (in every amino acid).
Because each class has its own set of elements, a radioactive sulfur or phosphorus label can show which molecules a cell is building.

faqs.question: Do carbohydrates ever contain nitrogen?
faqs.answer: Most carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. A few modified sugars carry a nitrogen-containing group; chitin, in insect skeletons and fungal cell walls, is one example. For this topic, treat carbohydrates as C, H and O.

faqs.question: Why do I need to know which elements are in which molecule?
faqs.answer: It tells you what an organism must take in from its environment, explains why a shortage of nitrate or phosphate slows growth, and lets you interpret experiments that follow labelled atoms into particular molecules.

resources.title: Introduction to Macromolecules: Study Guide (Biology 1.3)
resources.description: Learn how cells build polymers from monomers by dehydration synthesis and break them apart by hydrolysis, where the water goes, and how to count bonds, water molecules and mass.
prerequisites: Covalent bonds and the elements that make up biological molecules (Topic 1.2)
The structure of a water molecule (Topic 1.1)
learningObjectives: Describe how dehydration synthesis joins two monomers with a covalent bond and releases the equivalent of one water molecule
Describe how hydrolysis uses water to break the bond between monomers, with H going to one monomer and –OH to the other
Link polymerization to repeated dehydration synthesis, and digestion to repeated hydrolysis
Count the bonds and water molecules involved in building or breaking a polymer, and use them to find its mass
Describe what a diagram of these reactions shows, including the direction of the reaction and where each atom goes
resources.calculatorNote: Molar masses used in this guide: glucose 180.2 g mol⁻¹ and water 18.0 g mol⁻¹. Give masses to 1 decimal place, matching the data
keyPoints: Large biological molecules (polymers) are chains of smaller repeating units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds.
Dehydration synthesis joins two monomers: one loses H, the other loses –OH, and together these leave as one water molecule.
Hydrolysis breaks the bond by adding water: H goes to one monomer and –OH to the other.
A straight or branched chain of n monomers has n − 1 bonds, so building it releases n − 1 water molecules and breaking it fully uses n − 1.

faqs.question: Is dehydration synthesis the same as a condensation reaction?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both names describe joining two molecules with the loss of a small molecule, here water. Many textbooks use the word condensation.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the exact structures of sugars, amino acids or nucleotides?
faqs.answer: No. The course does not assess the detailed molecular structures of specific polymers, amino acids or nucleotides. You need to describe the reactions and read diagrams of them, which is why this guide uses simple blocks.

resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Carbohydrates: Study Guide (Biology 1.4)
resources.description: Learn how monosaccharides join by covalent bonds into disaccharides and linear or branched polysaccharides, and how starch, glycogen and cellulose fit their roles.
prerequisites: Dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis (Topic 1.3)
Hydrogen bonds and polar molecules (Topic 1.1)
learningObjectives: Identify monosaccharides as the monomers of complex carbohydrates and give examples of each
Describe how monosaccharides are joined by covalent bonds, with the loss of water, to form disaccharides and polysaccharides
Tell linear and branched polysaccharides apart and explain how each shape suits its job
Compare starch, glycogen and cellulose by where they are found, their shape and their function
Count monomers, linkages and water molecules in a carbohydrate chain, and use a simple model to reason about branching
resources.calculatorNote: Atomic masses used: C = 12.011, H = 1.008, O = 15.999. Molar masses are given to 1 decimal place
keyPoints: Monosaccharides (simple sugars such as glucose) are the monomers. Polysaccharides (complex carbohydrates) are the polymers built from them.
Each link between two sugars is a covalent bond made by dehydration synthesis (one water out) and broken by hydrolysis (one water in).
Polysaccharides can be linear or branched. Shape fits function: branched glycogen releases glucose fast; linear cellulose packs into strong fibres.
Starch stores energy in plants, glycogen stores energy in animals, and cellulose builds plant cell walls. All three are made of glucose.

faqs.question: If starch and cellulose are both made of glucose, why can't humans digest cellulose?
faqs.answer: The glucose units in cellulose are joined in a different way from those in starch. Human digestive enzymes fit the links in starch but not the links in cellulose. Animals such as cows rely on microbes in their gut that make the enzymes needed.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the structure of starch or cellulose?
faqs.answer: No. The detailed molecular structure of specific carbohydrate polymers is outside the scope of the exam. You need to know the monomer, that monomers are joined by covalent bonds, whether a polymer is linear or branched, and what it does.

resources.title: Lipids: Study Guide (Biology 1.5)
resources.description: Learn how fatty acids, fats, phospholipids and steroids are built, why saturated and unsaturated fats behave differently, and how lipid structure explains energy storage, insulation and membranes.
prerequisites: Polar and nonpolar molecules, and why nonpolar substances are hydrophobic (Topic 1.1)
Dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis (Topic 1.3)
learningObjectives: Explain why most lipids are nonpolar and hydrophobic, and how their parts are put together
Tell saturated and unsaturated fatty acids apart and link the number of double bonds to kinks, packing and whether a fat is solid or liquid
Describe the jobs of fats, phospholipids, steroids and cholesterol in living things
Explain why phospholipids arrange themselves into a bilayer in water
Predict what happens to a cell or organism when the lipids it makes or contains are changed
resources.calculatorNote: Energy released by complete respiration: fat about 37 kJ g⁻¹; carbohydrate about 17 kJ g⁻¹. Give answers to 2 or 3 significant figures
keyPoints: Lipids are mostly carbon and hydrogen joined by nonpolar C–H bonds, so most lipids are hydrophobic. They are not polymers of repeating monomers.
A saturated fatty acid has only C–C single bonds and a straight tail. An unsaturated one has at least one C=C double bond, which kinks the tail.
More double bonds mean more kinks, looser packing and a fat that is more liquid at room temperature.
Fats store energy (about twice as much per gram as carbohydrate) and can insulate. Phospholipids form membrane bilayers. Steroids act as hormones. Cholesterol stabilises animal cell membranes.
Structure explains function: change the lipid and you change what it can do.

faqs.question: Are lipids polymers?
faqs.answer: No. Fats are made by joining fatty acids to glycerol by dehydration synthesis, but there is no long chain of repeating monomers as in starch, proteins or DNA. Lipids are grouped together because they are hydrophobic, not because they share one type of monomer.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the exact structure of cholesterol or a particular fatty acid?
faqs.answer: No. The detailed molecular structure of specific lipids is outside the scope of this course. You do need to recognise the general shapes: glycerol with fatty acid tails, a phospholipid's polar head and nonpolar tails, and the four joined rings of a steroid.

keyPoints: Nucleotide = five-carbon sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base. The order of bases carries the information.
5′ end = free phosphate; 3′ end = free –OH. New nucleotides join the 3′ end, so strands grow 5′ → 3′.
DNA: antiparallel double helix, A–T and C–G by hydrogen bonds. RNA: ribose, uracil, usually single-stranded.

resources.title: Nucleic Acids: Study Guide (Biology 1.6)
resources.description: Learn how nucleotides build DNA and RNA, what the 5′ and 3′ ends mean, why the DNA double helix is antiparallel, how bases pair, and how DNA and RNA differ in structure.
prerequisites: Monomers, polymers, dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis
Covalent bonds and hydrogen bonds
learningObjectives: Name the three parts of a nucleotide and say which sugar and which bases belong to DNA and to RNA
Label the 5′ and 3′ ends of a nucleic acid strand and explain why a new nucleotide can only join at the 3′ end
Describe DNA as two antiparallel strands held together by hydrogen bonds between A–T and C–G pairs
Write a complementary DNA or RNA sequence with both ends labelled correctly
Use base-pairing rules to calculate base percentages and to decide whether a sample is single- or double-stranded
Compare DNA and RNA by sugar, bases and number of strands, using a diagram as evidence
resources.calculatorNote: Only simple arithmetic is needed: percentages that add up to 100% and counts of bonds
keyPoints: DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.
The information is the order of the bases. The sugar–phosphate backbone is the same all along the strand.
Every strand has a 5′ end (phosphate) and a 3′ end (–OH). New nucleotides are joined by covalent bonds to the 3′ end only.
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. A pairs with T and C pairs with G by hydrogen bonds; in RNA, A pairs with U.
DNA has deoxyribose, thymine and (usually) two strands. RNA has ribose, uracil and (usually) one strand.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the chemical structure of each base?
faqs.answer: No. For this course you need the parts of a nucleotide, the 5′ and 3′ ends, the pairing rules and the DNA–RNA differences. The detailed molecular structure of individual nucleotides is outside the scope of the exam.

faqs.question: What do 5′ and 3′ actually mean?
faqs.answer: They are numbers of carbon atoms in the sugar. The phosphate is attached to carbon 5′ and the –OH group that the next nucleotide links to is on carbon 3′. The prime (′) shows that the number belongs to the sugar, not the base.

Peptide bond: carboxyl of one amino acid + amine of the next, one water released. A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds.
Sequence → folding → shape → function. Secondary structure is held by backbone hydrogen bonds; tertiary structure by R-group interactions.

resources.title: Proteins: Study Guide (Biology 1.7)
resources.description: Learn how amino acids join by peptide bonds, how R groups and hydrogen bonds build the four levels of protein structure, and how a change in sequence can change shape and function.
prerequisites: Dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis of polymers (Topic 1.3)
Polarity, hydrogen bonds and why nonpolar substances are hydrophobic (Topic 1.1)
learningObjectives: Describe the general structure of an amino acid and sort R groups into nonpolar, polar and ionic
Explain how a peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the next
Distinguish primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure by what holds each level together
Count peptide bonds and water molecules for one or more chains and use them to find a protein's mass
Predict and justify how changing one amino acid could change a protein's shape and function
resources.calculatorNote: Mass of a water molecule: 18 Da. Mean amino acid masses are given where they are used. Round to the precision of the data
keyPoints: A protein is one or more linear chains of amino acids joined by covalent peptide bonds. Each bond forms between a carboxyl group and the next amine group, and releases one water molecule.
Every amino acid has the same core (central carbon, H, amine group, carboxyl group) plus a variable R group that is nonpolar, polar or ionic.
Primary structure is the sequence. Secondary structure (α-helices, β-pleated sheets) comes from hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms.
Tertiary structure comes from R-group interactions: hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic interactions and disulfide bridges. Quaternary structure is two or more chains fitting together.
The sequence decides the shape, and the shape decides the function. One changed amino acid can be enough to change both.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn the structures of all the amino acids?
faqs.answer: No. You need the general structure that every amino acid shares and the three types of R group. The course framework places the detailed structures of individual amino acids outside the exam.

faqs.question: Does every protein have quaternary structure?
faqs.answer: No. Only proteins made of two or more polypeptide chains have quaternary structure. A protein made of a single chain has three levels of structure.

resources.title: Cell Structure and Function: Study Guide (Biology 2.1)
resources.description: Learn how ribosomes, the endomembrane system, mitochondria, chloroplasts, lysosomes and vacuoles each contribute to how a cell works, and how to make a claim from organelle data.
prerequisites: Proteins are chains of amino acids whose shape depends on their sequence (Topic 1.7)

learningObjectives: Describe what ribosomes are made of, what they do and why their presence in every cell points to common ancestry
Trace a protein made for export through the rough ER, Golgi complex, vesicles and plasma membrane
Contrast rough and smooth ER, and explain the roles of the Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles

keyPoints: Ribosomes are made of rRNA and protein, have no membrane and are found in every living cell. They build proteins by reading mRNA.
The endomembrane system (nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles, vesicles and plasma membrane) works as one route that modifies, packages and moves proteins, lipids and polysaccharides.
Rough ER carries ribosomes and makes proteins for export or membranes. Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. The Golgi finishes, modifies and sorts products.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts each have two membranes. The folded inner membrane of a mitochondrion gives more surface for making ATP.
Lysosomes digest material with hydrolytic enzymes and help in programmed cell death. A plant cell's large central vacuole keeps the cell firm (turgid).

faqs.question: Do prokaryotic cells have organelles?
faqs.answer: They have ribosomes, which are not surrounded by a membrane, but they have no membrane-bound organelles such as an ER, Golgi or mitochondria. Topic 2.10 looks at how compartments may have arisen.

faqs.question: Is the plasma membrane part of the endomembrane system?
faqs.answer: Yes. Vesicles from the Golgi fuse with it, adding membrane and releasing their contents. That is why it is counted with the internal membranes, even though it is on the outside of the cell.

prerequisites: Membrane-bound organelles and why compartments help a eukaryotic cell (Topic 2.9)

learningObjectives: Describe the specialized internal regions of a prokaryotic cell and how they differ from membrane-bound organelles

keyPoints: Prokaryotes usually have no membrane-bound organelles, but their insides are not uniform: DNA sits in a nucleoid region, ribosomes make proteins, and the plasma membrane and a few internal structures carry out special jobs.
Eukaryotic cells keep many internal membranes that divide the cell into specialized compartments.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living prokaryotes that were taken inside another cell and stayed. This is endosymbiosis.
The evidence: two membranes, their own small circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes, division by splitting, and DNA sequences most like those of particular groups of bacteria.

faqs.question: If mitochondria were once bacteria, why can't they live on their own today?
faqs.answer: Over a very long time most of their genes moved to the host cell's nucleus or were lost. Human mitochondrial DNA now codes for only 13 proteins, so a mitochondrion depends on hundreds of proteins made by the rest of the cell.

faqs.question: Did the nucleus also come from endosymbiosis?
faqs.answer: The endosymbiosis evidence in this topic applies to mitochondria and chloroplasts. A common hypothesis is that the nuclear envelope and ER formed from folds of the plasma membrane, but you are not expected to know the details.

resources.title: Cell Size: Study Guide (Biology 2.2)
resources.description: Learn why surface area-to-volume ratio limits cell size, how to calculate it for cubes, spheres, cylinders and boxes, and how folds, shape and body size affect exchange and heat loss.
prerequisites: Subcellular structures, including the plasma membrane and folded mitochondrial membranes (Topic 2.1)
Area and volume formulas for simple shapes; working with powers
learningObjectives: Calculate surface area, volume and surface area-to-volume ratio for cubes, spheres, rectangular solids and cylinders
Explain why a cell's exchange with its surroundings depends on surface area but its needs depend on volume
Explain how small size, flattened or long shapes and membrane folds such as microvilli raise the ratio

resources.calculatorNote: Use the π key, not 3.14. Keep full calculator values until the last step. Ratios have units of µm⁻¹ when lengths are in µm
keyPoints: Materials enter and leave a cell through its surface, but every part of its volume uses them. So the surface area-to-volume ratio (SA/V) controls how well a cell can keep up.
As a cell grows, volume rises faster than surface area, so SA/V falls. For a cube SA/V = 6/s; for a sphere SA/V = 3/r.
Cells stay small, take flat or long shapes, or fold their membranes (microvilli, root hairs, cristae) to keep exchange fast enough.
Larger organisms have a lower SA/V, so they exchange heat with the environment more slowly in proportion to their mass. Smaller organisms usually have a higher metabolic rate per unit body mass.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise the area and volume formulas?
faqs.answer: The course provides the formulas for spheres, cubes, rectangular solids and cylinders on its equation sheet. You still need to know which one to use, how to substitute and how to interpret the answer.

faqs.question: Does a bigger cell have less surface area?
faqs.answer: No. A bigger cell has more surface area in total. It has less surface area for each unit of volume, which is what matters for keeping up with its needs.

prerequisites: Phospholipid structure: a polar head and two nonpolar fatty acid tails (Topic 1.5)

learningObjectives: Explain why phospholipids in a membrane point their heads towards the watery fluids on both sides and their tails towards each other
Predict which parts of a membrane protein are hydrophobic and which are hydrophilic from where they sit in the membrane

keyPoints: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: polar heads face the watery fluid inside and outside the cell, and nonpolar fatty acid tails face each other in the middle.
Membrane proteins sit where their R groups are comfortable: hydrophobic R groups touch the fatty acid tails; hydrophilic R groups face the cytosol, the outside fluid or a water-filled pore.
The fluid mosaic model: a mosaic of phospholipids, proteins, cholesterol (in vertebrate animals), glycoproteins and glycolipids, all able to drift sideways within the membrane.

Each component helps keep the internal environment of the cell steady: lipids form the barrier, proteins move and detect substances, cholesterol steadies the membrane, carbohydrate chains help cells recognise each other.

faqs.question: Is the plasma membrane solid like a wall?
faqs.answer: No. It behaves more like a thin oily film. Phospholipids and many proteins drift sideways within their own layer all the time. That is the 'fluid' in the fluid mosaic model.

faqs.question: Why are the carbohydrate chains only drawn on the outside?
faqs.answer: In the plasma membrane, the sugar chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids face the outside of the cell. That is where they meet other cells and signal molecules, which is their job.

resources.description: Learn why the hydrophobic interior of a membrane lets some molecules through and blocks others, how cell walls protect cells from bursting, and how to test a hypothesis with error bars.
prerequisites: Phospholipid bilayer structure and the fluid mosaic model (Topic 2.3)
Polar, nonpolar and charged molecules; hydration shells around ions (Topic 1.1)
Mean and standard deviation
learningObjectives: Explain how the hydrophobic interior of a membrane makes it selectively permeable
Predict whether a substance crosses the bilayer freely, in small amounts or only through proteins, from its size, polarity and charge

resources.calculatorNote: Standard error SE = s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the number of values. Error bars of mean ± 2 SE show roughly a 95% confidence interval
keyPoints: A membrane is selectively permeable because its interior is hydrophobic: the fatty acid tails block ions and polar molecules.
Small nonpolar molecules (N₂, O₂, CO₂) cross freely. Small polar, uncharged molecules (H₂O, NH₃) cross in small amounts. Ions and large polar molecules need channel or transport proteins.
Cell walls in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants give shape, block some substances and stop the cell bursting when water rushes in (osmotic lysis).
To evaluate a hypothesis, state a null hypothesis of no difference. If the mean ± 2 SE error bars do not overlap, reject it; if they overlap, fail to reject it.

faqs.question: If water is polar, how does it cross the membrane at all?
faqs.answer: Water molecules are very small and have no overall charge, so a few slip through the bilayer. The amount is small. Many cells also have channel proteins for water, which you will meet later in this unit.

faqs.question: Is the cell wall selectively permeable like the membrane?
faqs.answer: Not in the same way. A cell wall is a porous layer that lets water, gases and most small molecules through but holds back some larger ones. The plasma membrane underneath does the fine selecting.

resources.title: Membrane Transport: Study Guide (Biology 2.5)
resources.description: Learn how selective permeability creates concentration gradients, how passive and active transport differ, and how cells move large substances by endocytosis and exocytosis.
prerequisites: Phospholipid bilayer and the fluid mosaic model (Topic 2.3)
Which substances can cross the bilayer on their own and which need proteins (Topic 2.4)
ATP as the cell's immediate energy source (basic idea)
learningObjectives: Explain how a selectively permeable membrane lets a cell build and keep concentration gradients
Describe passive transport as net movement down a concentration gradient with no direct metabolic energy
Describe active transport as movement that needs a direct input of energy and can move substances from low to high concentration
Describe how endocytosis and exocytosis move large substances, or large amounts of material, into and out of cells, and why they need energy

Evaluate a transport experiment and propose a better investigation
resources.calculatorNote: No constants are needed. Concentrations are in mmol L⁻¹; round to the precision of the data
keyPoints: Because the membrane lets some substances through and blocks others, a cell can keep different concentrations inside and outside. These differences are concentration gradients.
Passive transport is net movement from high to low concentration. It needs no direct input of metabolic energy (no ATP).
Active transport needs a direct input of energy, usually from ATP, and a membrane protein. It can move a substance from low to high concentration.
Endocytosis (into the cell) and exocytosis (out of the cell) move large molecules, particles or large amounts of material inside vesicles. Both need energy.
Evidence for active transport: the substance builds up above its outside concentration, and the build-up stops when ATP production is blocked.

faqs.question: Is osmosis passive or active transport?
faqs.answer: Passive. Water moves down its own gradient without the cell spending ATP. You study osmosis and water potential in Topic 2.7.

faqs.question: Does active transport always move substances against their gradient?
faqs.answer: No. The defining feature is the direct input of energy. Moving a substance from low to high concentration is the most common reason a cell uses it, but it is not part of the definition.

resources.title: Facilitated Diffusion: Study Guide (Biology 2.6)
resources.description: Learn why ions and large polar molecules need channel or carrier proteins to cross a membrane, how ion movement polarizes membranes, and how aquaporins move large amounts of water.
prerequisites: The hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer (Topics 2.3 and 2.4)
Passive and active transport and concentration gradients (Topic 2.5)
learningObjectives: Explain how the size, polarity and charge of a molecule decide whether it needs a protein to cross the membrane
Compare channel proteins and carrier proteins and explain why both give passive transport
Explain why ions such as Na⁺ and K⁺ need channel proteins, and how their movement can polarize a membrane

resources.calculatorNote: No constants are needed. Round to the precision of the data
keyPoints: Facilitated diffusion is passive transport through a membrane protein: down the concentration gradient, with no energy input from the cell.
Ions (such as Na⁺ and K⁺) and large polar molecules (such as glucose) cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the bilayer, so they need channel or carrier proteins.
Channel proteins form a hydrophilic pore; carrier proteins bind a specific molecule and change shape. Both are specific.
When ions move through channels they carry charge, so the membrane can become polarized: one side more negative than the other.
Aquaporins are water channels that move large amounts of water quickly. Because each protein can only work so fast, the rate of facilitated diffusion levels off at high concentration.

faqs.question: If a protein is involved, why is facilitated diffusion not active transport?
faqs.answer: Because the cell supplies no energy and the substance only moves down its gradient. The protein provides a route, not a push. Active transport needs a direct energy input and can move substances from low to high concentration.

faqs.question: Can water cross a membrane without aquaporins?
faqs.answer: Yes. Water is small and uncharged, so some crosses the bilayer directly (Topic 2.4), but it is polar, so this is slow. Aquaporins let much more water cross much faster.

Cell walls prevent bursting; contractile vacuoles and central vacuoles are osmoregulatory structures.

resources.title: Tonicity and Osmoregulation: Study Guide (Biology 2.7)
resources.description: Learn how tonicity and water potential predict the direction of osmosis, how to calculate solute potential, and how cells and organisms control their water balance.
prerequisites: Diffusion, selective permeability and aquaporins (Topics 2.4–2.6)
Moles and molar concentration (mol L⁻¹)
learningObjectives: Use the terms hypotonic, hypertonic and isotonic correctly, always comparing one solution with another
Predict the direction of net water movement from solute concentrations or from water potentials

resources.calculatorNote: Pressure constant R = 0.0831 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Temperature in kelvin = °C + 273. Water potentials in bars, to 2 or 3 significant figures
keyPoints: Tonicity compares two solutions. Water moves by osmosis from the hypotonic side (fewer solute particles) to the hypertonic side (more solute particles). Isotonic means no net movement.
Water moves from higher water potential to lower water potential. Ψ = Ψp + Ψs, where Ψp is pressure potential and Ψs is solute potential.
Solute potential is never positive: Ψs = −iCRT, with R = 0.0831 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T in kelvin. Pure water in an open container has Ψ = 0.
A cell wall lets plant cells become turgid without bursting; animal cells and wall-less protists must control water balance in other ways, such as a contractile vacuole.
Osmoregulation keeps internal water and solute levels within limits, which cells need for growth and homeostasis.

faqs.question: Is water potential the same as water concentration?
faqs.answer: Not quite. Water potential is a measure of the tendency of water to move, and it includes pressure as well as solutes. Two solutions with the same solute concentration can have different water potentials if one is under pressure, as in a turgid plant cell.

faqs.question: Why is the ionization constant 2 for sodium chloride?
faqs.answer: Each NaCl unit separates into two particles in water, Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Solute potential depends on the number of dissolved particles, so NaCl lowers water potential about twice as much as the same molar concentration of sucrose, which does not ionize (i = 1).

resources.title: Mechanisms of Transport: Study Guide (Biology 2.8)
resources.description: Learn how cells use membrane proteins and ATP to move ions against their gradients, how the sodium–potassium pump works, and how pumps build electrochemical gradients and membrane potential.
prerequisites: Passive transport, facilitated diffusion and channel proteins (Topics 2.5–2.6)
ATP as the cell's energy carrier and proteins changing shape (Topic 1.7)
learningObjectives: Compare simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport by energy use, direction and the proteins involved
Explain why active transport needs membrane proteins and a direct input of metabolic energy such as ATP
Describe the steps of the sodium–potassium pump cycle and its 3 Na⁺ : 2 K⁺ : 1 ATP ratio
Explain what an electrochemical gradient is and how the pump helps maintain the membrane potential
Use pump stoichiometry to calculate ion movement and ATP use

resources.calculatorNote: Sodium–potassium pump: 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in for each ATP hydrolysed. Large numbers in standard form, to 2 or 3 significant figures
keyPoints: Active transport moves substances using a direct input of metabolic energy, usually ATP. It often moves ions against their concentration gradient, from low to high concentration.
Active transport always needs a membrane protein (a pump). The pump is specific and changes shape as it works.
The sodium–potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in for every ATP. This keeps Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside.

An electrochemical gradient combines a concentration difference and a charge difference. The pump moves one net positive charge out per cycle, helping keep the inside of the cell negative (the membrane potential).
Stop the ATP supply and the pumps stop: gradients run down as ions leak back by passive transport.

faqs.question: Does active transport always move substances against their gradient?
faqs.answer: Not always, but often. What defines active transport is the direct use of metabolic energy by a membrane protein. In some cases this energy is used to move a substance from low to high concentration, which passive transport can never do.

faqs.question: Why does the cell spend so much ATP on pumping ions?
faqs.answer: The gradients the pumps build are a store of energy and information. Cells use them to control volume, to send nerve signals, and to drive the uptake of other substances. Many cells spend a large share of their ATP on the sodium–potassium pump alone.

prerequisites: The main organelles and what each one does (Topic 2.1)

learningObjectives: Describe the membrane-bound structures of a eukaryotic cell and the process each one keeps separate

keyPoints: Membranes and membrane-bound organelles divide a eukaryotic cell into compartments. Each compartment holds its own set of enzymes and runs its own reactions.
Compartments keep competing reactions apart. Building and breaking down can happen at the same time in different places, and each compartment can keep its own conditions, such as pH.

Folded internal membranes give a large surface area in a small volume. Many reactions, such as ATP synthesis in mitochondria, happen on proteins embedded in membranes, so more membrane means more of these reactions.
Damage to a compartment has predictable effects: its reactions slow down, and enzymes or substances can end up where they do harm.

faqs.question: How is this topic different from Topic 2.1?
faqs.answer: Topic 2.1 asks what each organelle does. This topic asks why it helps to do that job inside a separate, membrane-bounded space, and why so many membranes are folded.

faqs.question: Do prokaryotes have compartments too?
faqs.answer: Prokaryotes usually lack membrane-bound organelles, but they do have specialized internal regions. Topic 2.10 compares the two kinds of cell and explains where mitochondria and chloroplasts came from.

resources.title: Enzymes: Study Guide (Biology 3.1)
resources.description: Learn how enzymes speed up reactions by lowering activation energy, why a substrate must match the active site in shape and charge, and how to measure and compare reaction rates.
prerequisites: Protein structure: R groups and the tertiary fold that gives a protein its shape (Topic 1.7)
Hydrogen bonds and ionic attractions between charged groups (Topics 1.1 and 1.7)
learningObjectives: Explain that enzymes are protein catalysts that speed up reactions in cells by lowering the activation energy
Read an energy profile and show that an enzyme changes the activation energy but not the overall free energy change
Explain why a substrate must be compatible with the active site in both shape and charge, using the enzyme–substrate complex model
Calculate a reaction rate from product–time data and explain why the rate falls as substrate is used up
Identify the independent and dependent variables in an enzyme experiment and justify negative and positive controls
resources.calculatorNote: No constants are needed. Rates are change in amount divided by time; keep the units of the data and round to 2 or 3 significant figures
keyPoints: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts. They make reactions in cells happen far faster by lowering the activation energy.
An enzyme does not change the free energy change (ΔG) of a reaction, does not supply energy and is not used up. It is released unchanged and used again.
A substrate binds only if its shape and its charges fit the active site. Substrate plus enzyme forms an enzyme–substrate complex, which then releases the products.
Because a cell controls which enzymes it makes and when they are active, enzymes regulate which reactions happen and how fast.
Rate = change in amount of product (or substrate) ÷ time. The initial rate is measured at the start, before substrate runs low.

faqs.question: Are all enzymes proteins?
faqs.answer: For this course, yes: enzymes are treated as protein catalysts. As background, a few RNA molecules (ribozymes) can also catalyse reactions, for example in the ribosome, but these are not what exam questions on enzymes are about.

faqs.question: Why do enzyme names often end in -ase?
faqs.answer: It is a naming habit, not a rule. Many names describe the substrate or the reaction: lactase acts on lactose, and amylase acts on starch. Some older names, such as pepsin, do not follow the pattern.

resources.title: Environmental Impacts on Enzyme Function: Study Guide (Biology 3.2)
resources.description: Learn how temperature, pH, chemicals, substrate and product concentrations and inhibitors change enzyme activity, and when denaturation can be reversed.
prerequisites: Enzymes, activation energy and the enzyme–substrate complex (Topic 3.1)
Hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and the levels of protein structure (Topic 1.7)
learningObjectives: Explain how temperature and pH outside an enzyme's optimal range change its shape by disrupting hydrogen bonds and other interactions
Explain why heating increases reaction rate up to the optimum, and why rate falls above it
Distinguish reversible changes in activity from permanent denaturation, using evidence from an experiment
Explain how the relative concentrations of substrate and product affect how efficiently an enzyme reaction proceeds

keyPoints: An enzyme works only while its active site keeps the right shape and charge. Anything that disrupts the hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions holding the fold can lower or stop its activity.
Raising the temperature speeds molecules up and increases collisions, so the rate rises until the optimum. Above the optimum, the enzyme denatures and the rate falls.
pH outside the optimum changes the charges on R groups, which disrupts the fold and the charge pattern of the active site.
Denaturation stops catalysis. Sometimes it is reversible and the enzyme regains activity when normal conditions return; often, after strong heating, it is not.

The relative amounts of substrate and product set how efficiently a reaction runs. Competitive inhibitors block the active site; noncompetitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and change the active site's shape.

faqs.question: Does cold denature enzymes?
faqs.answer: Usually not. At low temperatures molecules move slowly, so collisions are less frequent and the rate is low, but the enzyme's shape is normally kept. When the temperature rises again, activity returns.

faqs.question: Are inhibitors always harmful?
faqs.answer: No. Cells use inhibitors to control their own pathways, and many medicines work by inhibiting a particular enzyme in a pathogen or in the body.

resources.title: Cellular Energy: Study Guide (Biology 3.3)
resources.description: Learn why every cell needs a steady energy input, how life stays ordered within the laws of thermodynamics, how ATP couples reactions, why pathways run in steps and what shared pathways say about ancestry.
prerequisites: Enzymes lower activation energy and work best within a range of conditions (Topics 3.1 and 3.2)

learningObjectives: Explain why all living systems need a continuous input of energy to stay alive and ordered

keyPoints: Every living system needs a constant energy input. Energy coming in must be greater than energy lost, or order breaks down and the organism dies.
Life obeys thermodynamics: energy is converted, never created, and each conversion releases some heat, which raises the disorder of the surroundings.
Cells couple energy-releasing reactions to energy-requiring ones, most often through ATP → ADP + Pᵢ.
Energy pathways run in many small steps; the product of one step is the reactant of the next, so energy is released in controlled amounts.
Glycolysis and ATP synthesis driven by a membrane gradient appear in all three domains, which supports common ancestry.

faqs.question: Do I need the Gibbs free energy equation for this topic?
faqs.answer: No. You need to understand energy release, energy input and coupling in words and with simple energy values. The free energy equation itself is outside the course.

faqs.question: If organisms are so ordered, do they break the second law of thermodynamics?
faqs.answer: No. An organism becomes more ordered only by releasing heat and simple waste molecules into its surroundings. The total disorder of the organism plus its surroundings still increases.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn the steps of the Calvin cycle?
faqs.answer: No. You need to know where it happens, what goes in (CO₂, ATP, NADPH) and what comes out (carbohydrate, ADP, Pᵢ, NADP⁺). The individual steps, the molecules' structures and the enzyme names are outside the course. The one enzyme you must know is ATP synthase.

faqs.question: Where does the oxygen released by plants come from?
faqs.answer: From water. When water is split to replace the electrons lost from photosystem II, its oxygen atoms are released as O₂. The oxygen atoms in CO₂ end up in the sugar and in water.

keyPoints: Glycolysis (cytosol) → pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle (matrix) → ETC and ATP synthase (inner membrane).
O₂ is used only at the end of the ETC, as the final electron acceptor.
High H⁺ in the intermembrane space, higher pH in the matrix; protons flow back through ATP synthase.

resources.title: Cellular Respiration: Study Guide (Biology 3.5)
resources.description: How cells release energy from glucose: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, chemiosmosis and ATP synthase, uncoupling and heat, and fermentation without oxygen.
prerequisites: ATP, ADP and energy coupling in cells
Enzymes as catalysts, and how temperature affects them

learningObjectives: Describe where glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain happen, and what goes in and comes out of each
Explain how electron carriers (NADH and FADH₂) link the early stages to the electron transport chain, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor
Explain how the electron transport chain builds a proton gradient that ATP synthase uses to make ATP (chemiosmosis)

Construct a correctly labelled graph from respiration data and use it to compare rates
resources.calculatorNote: Rates are found from the gradient of a graph or from total change ÷ time. Model values used here: about 30 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration, 2 ATP per glucose in fermentation
keyPoints: Cellular respiration releases energy from food molecules to make ATP. It happens in plants, animals, fungi and microbes, not only in animals.
Glycolysis (cytosol) splits glucose into 2 pyruvate and makes a little ATP and NADH. The Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) releases CO₂ and loads more electrons onto NAD⁺ and FAD.
NADH and FADH₂ hand electrons to the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and becomes water.
Electron flow pumps protons into the intermembrane space. Protons flowing back through ATP synthase drive ATP synthesis: oxidative phosphorylation by chemiosmosis.
Without oxygen, fermentation recycles NADH back to NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep making its 2 ATP per glucose, producing lactic acid or ethanol.

faqs.question: Do plants respire, or do they only photosynthesise?
faqs.answer: Plants do both. Their cells have mitochondria and respire all the time, day and night. In bright light, photosynthesis is usually faster than respiration, so a leaf takes in CO₂ overall; in the dark it only gives out CO₂.

faqs.question: How many ATP does one glucose make?
faqs.answer: Glycolysis plus fermentation gives 2 ATP. Full aerobic respiration gives many more: modern estimates are about 30–32, while older books say 36–38. You will not be asked to memorise an exact figure; questions give the value they want you to use.

faqs.question: Is anaerobic respiration the same as fermentation?
faqs.answer: No. Some prokaryotes respire without oxygen by using another final electron acceptor, such as nitrate or sulfate, in an electron transport chain. Fermentation uses no electron transport chain at all; it only regenerates NAD⁺ for glycolysis.

resources.title: Cell Communication: Study Guide (Biology 4.1)
resources.description: How cells talk to each other: direct contact through junctions and surface molecules, local signalling over short distances, and hormones that travel long distances to distant target cells.
prerequisites: Plasma membrane structure and the idea of a membrane protein (Unit 2)
Diffusion of molecules from high to low concentration
learningObjectives: Describe the two broad ways cells communicate: by touching and by sending chemical signals across a distance

keyPoints: Cells communicate in two broad ways: by direct contact with another cell, or by releasing a chemical signal that reaches other cells across a distance.
Direct contact can join two cells' cytoplasm (gap junctions in animals, plasmodesmata in plants) or bring surface molecules together, as when immune cells touch.
Local regulators act on cells close to the cell that releases them: neurotransmitters, morphogens in an embryo and the signals of quorum sensing in bacteria.
Hormones such as insulin, growth hormone, thyroid hormones, testosterone and estrogen travel in the blood to target cells far away.
A signal reaches many cells, but only cells with a matching receptor respond. Receptors, not delivery, decide which cells are targets.

faqs.question: Is a nerve impulse long-distance or short-distance signalling?
faqs.answer: The electrical impulse travels along the neuron, which can be long. The chemical signal, the neurotransmitter, only crosses the narrow gap to the next cell, so neurotransmitter signalling counts as short-distance (local) communication.

faqs.question: Do single-celled organisms communicate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many bacteria release signal molecules and sense how much of them is around. This quorum sensing lets a population switch genes on together once it is dense enough.

resources.title: Introduction to Signal Transduction: Study Guide (Biology 4.2)
resources.description: How a cell turns a signal into a response: ligands and receptors, G protein-coupled receptors, ligand-gated channels, intracellular receptors, phosphorylation cascades, cAMP and amplification.
prerequisites: Ways cells communicate and the idea of a target cell (Topic 4.1)
Membrane structure and which molecules cross a phospholipid bilayer (Unit 2)
Protein shape and function; ATP as an energy carrier (Units 1 and 3)
learningObjectives: Describe the three stages of cell signalling (reception, transduction, response) and the job of each
Explain how a receptor's ligand-binding domain recognises a specific ligand, and predict where the receptor sits from the type of ligand
Describe how G protein-coupled receptors, ligand-gated ion channels and intracellular receptors pass on a signal
Explain how kinases, phosphatases and second messengers such as cAMP relay and amplify a signal
Calculate the amplification in a model cascade and interpret experiments that locate a receptor or test a second messenger
resources.calculatorNote: Amplification is found by multiplying the factor at each step of the cascade. All values in the worked examples are model values
keyPoints: Signal transduction links reception of a signal to a response inside the cell, in three stages: reception, transduction and response.

A ligand binds the ligand-binding domain of a specific receptor. Water-soluble ligands, such as peptides, use receptors on the cell surface; small nonpolar ligands, such as steroids, cross the membrane and bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
Binding changes the receptor's shape, including its intracellular domain, which starts transduction.
Kinases add phosphate groups to proteins, switching their activity; a chain of kinases is a phosphorylation cascade. Second messengers such as cAMP relay the signal and amplify it.
Responses include cell growth, secretion of molecules and changes in gene expression. Ligand-gated channels respond by opening or closing.

faqs.question: Is the second messenger the same as the hormone?
faqs.answer: No. The hormone (the first messenger) usually stays outside the cell, bound to the receptor. The second messenger, such as cAMP, is a small molecule made inside the cell in response, which carries the message on.

faqs.question: Does phosphorylation always switch a protein on?
faqs.answer: No. Adding a phosphate group changes a protein's shape. For some proteins that switches them on; for others it switches them off. Either way, phosphorylation acts as a switch.

resources.description: What a signalling pathway can make a cell do, from fast enzyme changes to new gene expression, new phenotypes and apoptosis, and how mutations, drugs and toxins switch pathways on or off.
prerequisites: The parts of a signal transduction pathway: ligand, receptor, relay proteins, second messengers and protein kinases
How a protein's shape depends on its amino acid sequence
Genes code for proteins; transcription factors control which genes are expressed
learningObjectives: Describe the kinds of response a signalling pathway can produce: changed activity of existing proteins, changed gene expression, a new phenotype or apoptosis

keyPoints: A signalling pathway can change the activity of proteins the cell already has (fast), or change which genes are expressed (slower). Either can alter the cell's phenotype, and some pathways trigger apoptosis, programmed cell death.
Bacteria use quorum sensing: each cell releases a signal molecule, and only when the population is dense enough does the signal reach the level that switches on new genes.
A mutation in any part of the pathway can change everything downstream. A part that cannot be switched on blocks the response; a part stuck in the 'on' state gives a response with no signal.
Chemicals can mimic a signal, block a receptor or act on any later step, so they can activate or inhibit the pathway.
To find where a fault lies, ask: which steps still work, and does adding a later step back restore the response?

faqs.question: Is this topic the same as Topic 4.2?
faqs.answer: Topic 4.2 names the parts of a pathway (ligand, receptor, second messenger, kinases). Topic 4.3 asks what the pathway does to the cell, and what happens when any part of it changes. You use the parts from 4.2 to argue about the effects in 4.3.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise every illustrative example?
faqs.answer: No. You need to understand the principles well enough to apply them to an example you have never seen. Examples such as quorum sensing or a cancer-causing mutation are there to make the principles concrete.

resources.title: Feedback: Study Guide (Biology 4.4)
resources.description: How negative feedback returns a variable to its set point and positive feedback amplifies a change, with blood glucose, childbirth, lactation and fruit ripening, and how to predict what happens when a loop breaks.
prerequisites: Signals, receptors and cellular responses
Enzymes and how inhibitors change their activity
learningObjectives: Describe the parts of a feedback loop and the idea of a set point
Explain how negative feedback reduces the original change and returns a system to its set point, at molecular, cellular and organism level
Explain how positive feedback amplifies a change and moves a system further from its starting point, and what ends the loop
Use blood glucose regulation by insulin and glucagon as a model of negative feedback
Predict the effects of disrupting any part of a feedback loop, using data where given
resources.calculatorNote: Blood glucose is given in mg dL⁻¹ (divide by 18 for mmol L⁻¹). All data sets on this page are fictional models
keyPoints: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions close to a set point. Feedback is what happens when the response to a change acts back on the change itself.
Negative feedback reduces the original change and returns the variable towards the set point. It is the usual way the body stays stable.
Positive feedback increases the original change, pushing the variable further from where it started. It drives events that must finish quickly, and an outside event ends it.
Blood glucose: a rise triggers insulin, which lowers glucose; a fall triggers glucagon, which raises glucose. Both are negative feedback.
To predict the effect of a disruption, find the broken link and follow the loop: what can no longer happen, and what does the variable do?

faqs.question: Is positive feedback good and negative feedback bad?
faqs.answer: No. The words describe direction, not value. Negative feedback opposes a change; positive feedback reinforces it. Both are normal and useful in the right place.

faqs.question: Is the set point a single fixed number?
faqs.answer: It is a target value, and the real value moves up and down a little around it all the time. That is why homeostasis is called dynamic. Some set points also change, for example body temperature rises during a fever.

resources.title: Cell Cycle: Study Guide (Biology 4.5)
resources.description: The stages of the eukaryotic cell cycle: G1, S and G2 of interphase, G0, the four steps of mitosis and cytokinesis, with mitotic index and DNA-content calculations.
prerequisites: DNA structure and the idea that DNA is copied before a cell divides
Cell structures: nucleus, nuclear envelope, cytoskeleton, plasma membrane and cell wall
learningObjectives: Describe what the cell does in G1, S and G2, and what it means for a cell to be in G0
Explain how DNA replication in S phase produces sister chromatids joined at a centromere
Describe the events of prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, and how cytokinesis differs in animal and plant cells
Explain how mitosis passes a complete, identical set of chromosomes to each daughter cell, and its roles in growth, repair and asexual reproduction
Track chromosome number, chromatid number and DNA content through one cell cycle
Calculate a mitotic index and estimate the time spent in each stage from cell counts
resources.calculatorNote: Mitotic index = (cells in mitosis ÷ total cells counted) × 100. Time in a stage ≈ (cells in that stage ÷ total cells) × length of the whole cycle
keyPoints: The cell cycle is interphase (G1, S, G2), then mitosis, then cytokinesis. Most of a dividing cell's life is spent in interphase.
G1: the cell grows and copies organelles. S: DNA replicates, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. G2: the cell makes proteins and ATP and prepares to divide.

Mitosis has four steps: prophase (chromosomes condense, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes line up at the equator), anaphase (sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles), telophase (nuclear envelopes re-form).
Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm: a cleavage furrow in animal cells, a cell plate in plant cells. The two daughter cells are genetically identical to each other and to the parent.
Cells that stop dividing enter G0. Many can re-enter the cycle when they receive the right signals.

faqs.question: Is mitosis the same thing as cell division?
faqs.answer: Not quite. Mitosis is the division of the nucleus, so each new nucleus gets a full set of chromosomes. Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm. Cell division needs both.

faqs.question: Does the number of chromosomes double in S phase?
faqs.answer: No. The amount of DNA doubles, but each chromosome is now made of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere, so the chromosome count stays the same. The count doubles only briefly in anaphase, when the sister chromatids separate.

faqs.question: Why do bacteria not appear in this topic?
faqs.answer: The cell cycle with interphase and mitosis is how eukaryotic cells divide. Prokaryotes have no nucleus and divide by a simpler process called binary fission.

resources.title: Regulation of Cell Cycle: Study Guide (Biology 4.6)
resources.description: How checkpoints and cyclin-CDK interactions control the cell cycle, and how disruptions can lead to cancer or to apoptosis (programmed cell death), with data-based predictions.
prerequisites: The stages of the cell cycle: G1, S, G2, mitosis and cytokinesis, and the G0 state
Protein kinases and phosphorylation in cell signalling
learningObjectives: Describe what the G1, G2 and M checkpoints check, and what can happen to a cell that does not pass
Explain how cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) interact to move a cell from one stage to the next
Read a graph of cyclin concentration and CDK activity, and predict the effect of changing either
Describe apoptosis and explain its roles in removing damaged or unneeded cells

resources.calculatorNote: Calculations use rates (change ÷ time), percentages and percentage change from fictional data. Concentrations are in arbitrary units (au)
keyPoints: Checkpoints are internal controls that stop the cycle until conditions are right: G1 (is the cell ready, and should it divide?), G2 (is the DNA fully and correctly copied?) and M (is every chromosome attached to the spindle?).
Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are enzymes that are present all the time but active only when bound to a cyclin. Cyclin levels rise and fall, so CDK activity rises and falls.
An active cyclin-CDK complex phosphorylates target proteins, which drives the cell past a checkpoint. Breaking down the cyclin switches the CDK off.
Apoptosis is programmed cell death: an orderly self-destruction that removes damaged or unneeded cells.
When the controls fail, cells can divide without restraint and with damaged DNA. This can lead to cancer.

faqs.question: Do I need to know which cyclin pairs with which CDK?
faqs.answer: No. Specific cyclin-CDK pairs, and specific growth factors, are beyond the scope of the course. You need the general idea: cyclin levels change, CDKs need cyclin to be active, and active complexes push the cycle forward.

faqs.question: Is apoptosis harmful?
faqs.answer: Usually it is protective. It removes cells with DNA damage that cannot be repaired, and it shapes organs during development. Problems arise when there is too little apoptosis (damaged cells survive) or too much (healthy tissue is lost).

faqs.question: Is cancer caused by a single mutation?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most cancers develop after several mutations build up in the same cell line, each one weakening a different control on division or cell death.

resources.title: Meiosis: Study Guide (Biology 5.1)
resources.description: How meiosis turns one diploid cell into four haploid cells: homologous chromosomes, the stages of meiosis I and II, counting chromosomes and DNA, and how meiosis compares with mitosis.
prerequisites: Chromosomes, chromatids and the centromere
The cell cycle: DNA replication in S phase, and the stages of mitosis
learningObjectives: Explain why sexually reproducing diploid organisms need meiosis to make haploid gametes
Describe what happens to chromosomes in each stage of meiosis I and meiosis II
Track the number of cells, chromosomes, chromatids and DNA content through meiosis
Identify whether a dividing cell is in mitosis, meiosis I or meiosis II from its chromosomes
Compare the processes and outcomes of mitosis and meiosis
resources.calculatorNote: Only counting and halving or doubling are needed. Count chromosomes by counting centromeres
keyPoints: Meiosis makes haploid (n) cells from a diploid (2n) cell. In animals these cells become gametes, so fertilization restores the diploid number.
DNA is copied once (in S phase before meiosis), but the cell divides twice. That is why chromosome number halves.
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes: it is the division that halves the chromosome number. Sister chromatids stay joined.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, much like mitosis. The result is four haploid cells, each chromosome with a single chromatid.
Mitosis and meiosis both use a spindle to move chromosomes, but mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells while meiosis gives four haploid cells that differ genetically.

faqs.question: Is a cell at the end of meiosis I haploid, even though its chromosomes still have two chromatids?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ploidy depends on the number of chromosome sets, not on chromatids. After meiosis I each cell has one member of each homologous pair, so it is haploid. Each chromosome is still duplicated until anaphase II.

faqs.question: Does DNA replicate again between meiosis I and meiosis II?
faqs.answer: No. There is no S phase between the two divisions. Meiosis II simply separates the sister chromatids that were made in the single S phase before meiosis I.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn how meiosis fits into the life cycles of plants, fungi and animals?
faqs.answer: Not in detail. The course expects you to know what happens in meiosis and why it produces haploid cells; the details of different organisms' sexual life cycles are outside the exam's scope.

resources.title: Meiosis and Genetic Diversity: Study Guide (Biology 5.2)
resources.description: How meiosis and fertilization create genetic variation: crossing over, independent assortment of homologous pairs, random fertilization, and what nondisjunction does to chromosome number.
prerequisites: The stages of meiosis I and meiosis II
Homologous chromosomes, sister chromatids, haploid and diploid
learningObjectives: Explain how correct separation of homologues and sister chromatids gives each gamete one set of chromosomes with a mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes
Explain how crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I produces recombinant chromatids
Calculate the number of chromosome combinations produced by independent assortment and by random fertilization
Predict the chromosome numbers of gametes and zygotes after nondisjunction in meiosis I or meiosis II
Pose a testable question about meiosis or genetic variation from an observation or data
resources.calculatorNote: Use powers of 2 (2ⁿ) for independent assortment. Large results are given to 2 or 3 significant figures
keyPoints: When meiosis works correctly, every gamete gets exactly one chromosome from each homologous pair: a haploid set that mixes maternal and paternal chromosomes.
Crossing over: in prophase I, non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair swap matching segments, making chromatids with new combinations of alleles.
Independent assortment: each homologous pair lines up at metaphase I independently of the others, giving 2ⁿ chromosome combinations (over 8 million for humans, n = 23).
Random fertilization multiplies the variation again: any one of a huge number of eggs can meet any one of a huge number of sperm.
Nondisjunction is a failure of separation. Gametes end up with n + 1 or n − 1 chromosomes, and the zygote is no longer correctly diploid.

faqs.question: Does crossing over create new alleles?
faqs.answer: No. It creates new combinations of alleles that already exist on the two homologues. New alleles come from mutation.

faqs.question: Why does nondisjunction in meiosis I affect all four gametes, but in meiosis II only two?
faqs.answer: In meiosis I, a whole homologous pair goes to one cell, so both cells from the first division are wrong, and so are all four products. In meiosis II, the error happens in only one of the two cells, so the other cell still makes two normal gametes.

faqs.question: Do I need to know the life cycles of ferns, mosses or other organisms?
faqs.answer: No. The course states that the details of sexual life cycles in different plants and animals are beyond the scope of the exam. Focus on what happens to chromosomes in meiosis and fertilization.

resources.title: Mendelian Genetics: Study Guide (Biology 5.3)
resources.description: How alleles segregate and assort independently, how to use Punnett squares, the sum and product rules, test crosses and pedigrees, and how to run a chi-square test on cross data.
prerequisites: Homologous chromosomes, haploid and diploid cells
How homologues separate in meiosis I and sister chromatids in meiosis II
learningObjectives: Use the terms gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous correctly
Explain the laws of segregation and independent assortment in terms of chromosome behaviour in meiosis, and say when independent assortment applies
Predict genotypic and phenotypic ratios from monohybrid, dihybrid and test crosses, using Punnett squares or the sum and product rules
Use a test cross or a pedigree to decide whether an allele is dominant or recessive and to infer genotypes
State a null hypothesis for a cross, calculate chi-square and decide whether to reject or fail to reject it
resources.calculatorNote: Chi-square critical values at p = 0.05: 3.84 (1 degree of freedom), 5.99 (2), 7.81 (3). Keep probabilities as fractions until the last step
keyPoints: Each diploid organism carries two alleles of each gene. The two alleles separate into different gametes (segregation), because homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I.
Genes on different chromosomes are sorted into gametes independently of each other (independent assortment). Genes close together on one chromosome are not.
For independent events, multiply probabilities (product rule). For mutually exclusive ways of getting the same result, add them (sum rule).
A genotypic ratio counts allele combinations (1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa); a phenotypic ratio counts visible traits (3 dominant : 1 recessive). Never mix them up.
Chi-square compares observed counts with the counts your null hypothesis predicts. If χ² is above the critical value, reject the null hypothesis; otherwise fail to reject it.

faqs.question: Does dominant mean the allele is more common or better?
faqs.answer: No. Dominant only means that one copy is enough to produce the phenotype. A dominant allele can be rare, and it can cause a disorder. How common an allele is depends on the population, not on dominance.

faqs.question: If chi-square tells me to fail to reject, have I proved my hypothesis?
faqs.answer: No. You have only shown that the difference between observed and expected counts is small enough to be explained by chance. Your hypothesis is supported, not proved.

resources.title: Non-Mendelian Genetics: Study Guide (Biology 5.4)
resources.description: Why some traits break Mendel's ratios: linked genes and gene mapping, sex-linked traits, incomplete dominance, codominance, pleiotropy and maternal inheritance of mitochondria and chloroplasts.
prerequisites: Mendel's laws, Punnett squares and the product rule
The chi-square test for cross data
Crossing over in prophase I of meiosis
learningObjectives: Use a chi-square test to show that observed offspring ratios differ from Mendelian predictions
Explain genetic linkage and calculate recombination frequency and map distance from cross data
Distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance and predict ratios for each
Predict and explain the inheritance of X-linked and Y-linked traits, and describe ZW and haplodiploid sex determination
Explain pleiotropy and non-nuclear (mitochondrial and chloroplast) inheritance
resources.calculatorNote: Recombination frequency = recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring × 100%; 1% = 1 map unit. Chi-square critical values at p = 0.05: 3.84 (1 df), 5.99 (2 df), 7.81 (3 df)
keyPoints: Many traits do not follow Mendel's ratios. You show this quantitatively: a chi-square test rejects the Mendelian expectation.
Genes close together on one chromosome are linked. Recombinant offspring come from crossing over; the percentage of recombinants gives the map distance (1% = 1 map unit).
Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is a blend. Codominance: the heterozygote shows both phenotypes. Both give a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotypic ratio from two heterozygotes.
Males (XY) have one X, so X-linked recessive traits appear more often in males than in females. Birds (ZW) and bees (haplodiploidy) use other systems.
Pleiotropy: one gene affects several traits. Mitochondrial and chloroplast genes are usually inherited only from the mother.

faqs.question: Are non-Mendelian patterns exceptions that disprove Mendel?
faqs.answer: No. Segregation still happens for every nuclear gene. The ratios change because of where the gene is (same chromosome, sex chromosome, organelle) or how its alleles interact, not because alleles stop separating.

faqs.question: Can a map distance be more than 50 map units?
faqs.answer: Two genes can be more than 50 units apart on a map built by adding up short distances, but a single cross never shows more than about 50% recombinants. Genes that far apart look as if they assort independently.

resources.description: Learn how temperature, light, soil chemistry, diet and other organisms change gene expression, so that one genotype can produce different phenotypes, with reaction norms and sex determination by temperature.
prerequisites: Genotype, phenotype, alleles and dominance
Enzymes are proteins whose activity depends on temperature and pH

learningObjectives: Explain why a phenotype depends on both the genotype and the conditions in which the organism develops
Explain how an environmental signal can change which genes are expressed, or how active their products are, without changing the DNA sequence

keyPoints: Phenotype = genotype acting in an environment. The same alleles can give different traits under different conditions.
The environment works mainly by changing gene expression (which genes are switched on, and how strongly) or by changing how active a gene product is. The DNA sequence is not changed.
Phenotypic plasticity is the ability of one genotype to produce different phenotypes. A reaction norm graph shows it: phenotype against environment, one line per genotype.
To show an effect is environmental, keep the genotype the same (clones, identical twins, inbred lines) and change only the environment.

faqs.question: If the environment changes a phenotype, is the change passed to the offspring?
faqs.answer: Not through the DNA sequence. A tan, a larger muscle or a winter coat is a change in gene expression in body cells. The alleles in the gametes are the same, so offspring inherit the genotype, not the tan.

faqs.question: Is phenotypic plasticity always helpful?
faqs.answer: Often it is, because the phenotype can match the conditions, such as a white coat in a snowy winter. But it is not always helpful: a cue can mislead the organism, and a trait like sex ratio can be pushed too far by unusual temperatures.

resources.description: How DNA and RNA carry hereditary information: circular and linear chromosomes, histones, plasmids, purines and pyrimidines, and why purine–pyrimidine pairing keeps the helix even.
prerequisites: Nucleotides, the 5′ and 3′ ends of a strand, and A–T / C–G base pairing (Topic 1.6)
Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell structure, including the nucleus (Topic 2.1)
Chromosomes in mitosis and meiosis (Topics 4.5 and 5.1)
learningObjectives: Explain that DNA, and in some viruses RNA, is the molecule that stores genetic information and passes it to the next generation
Compare how genetic material is organised in prokaryotes (a circular chromosome) and eukaryotes (several linear chromosomes packed with histones)
Describe plasmids and explain how genes carried on them can be passed between cells
Sort the bases into purines (double ring) and pyrimidines (single ring) and explain why each base pair contains one of each

keyPoints: Hereditary information is stored in DNA in all cells. Some viruses use RNA as their genetic material instead.
Prokaryotes typically have one circular chromosome. Eukaryotes typically have several linear chromosomes, wound around histone proteins so they fit in the nucleus.
Plasmids are small, extra circles of DNA, separate from the chromosomes. They are common in bacteria and also occur in some eukaryotes, such as yeasts.
Purines (A, G) have a double ring; pyrimidines (C, T, U) have a single ring. Every base pair is one purine plus one pyrimidine: A with T (or U in RNA), G with C.
Purine–pyrimidine pairing keeps the double helix the same width all along and is shared by all known cellular life, which is evidence of common ancestry.

faqs.question: Is a chromosome the same as a DNA molecule?
faqs.answer: A chromosome is one long DNA molecule together with the proteins that pack it. A eukaryotic chromosome that has been copied before division contains two identical DNA molecules (sister chromatids) until they separate.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw the ring structures of the bases?
faqs.answer: No. You need to know which bases are purines (double ring) and which are pyrimidines (single ring), and why a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. The full chemical structures are not required.

faqs.question: Do mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each has its own small circular DNA, similar to a bacterial chromosome. This is part of the evidence for endosymbiosis that you met in Topic 2.10.

resources.title: DNA Replication: Study Guide (Biology 6.2)
resources.description: How DNA is copied: semiconservative replication, 5′ to 3′ synthesis, helicase, topoisomerase, RNA primers, DNA polymerase, leading and lagging strands, and ligase.
prerequisites: Antiparallel strands, 5′ and 3′ ends, and complementary base pairing (Topics 1.6 and 6.1)
Enzymes as specific catalysts (Topic 3.1)
DNA is copied before a cell divides (Topic 4.5)
learningObjectives: Explain what semiconservative replication means and how density-label data support it over other models
Explain why new DNA can only be built in the 5′ to 3′ direction and why DNA polymerase needs an RNA primer to start
Describe the jobs of helicase, topoisomerase, DNA polymerase and ligase at a replication fork
Explain why one new strand is made continuously (leading) and the other in fragments (lagging)
Write the new strands made at a fork, with 5′ and 3′ ends labelled

resources.calculatorNote: Replication rates and sizes in the examples are model values for fictional organisms. Convert seconds to minutes or days only at the end
keyPoints: Replication is semiconservative: each new DNA molecule has one original (template) strand and one newly made strand.
DNA polymerase only adds nucleotides to a free 3′ end, so new DNA always grows 5′ → 3′. It cannot start a strand from nothing, so it needs a short RNA primer.
Helicase separates the two strands at the fork. Topoisomerase relieves the overwinding (supercoiling) that builds up ahead of the fork.
The leading strand is made continuously towards the fork. The lagging strand is made in short fragments away from the fork, each with its own primer.
Primers are replaced with DNA, and ligase joins the fragments of the lagging strand into one continuous strand.

faqs.question: Which enzyme names do I need to know?
faqs.answer: DNA polymerase, helicase, topoisomerase and ligase for replication (and RNA polymerase, which you will meet in transcription). Other enzymes, such as the one that makes primers, and the names of the stages are not required, although you should know what they do.

faqs.question: Why does the cell use an RNA primer, not a DNA one?
faqs.answer: DNA polymerase cannot start a new chain; it can only extend an existing one from its 3′ end. The enzyme that makes primers is a kind of RNA polymerase, which can start a chain from scratch. The RNA is later removed and replaced with DNA.

faqs.question: Is replication the same in prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
faqs.answer: The core mechanism is the same: semiconservative, 5′ → 3′, with primers, leading and lagging strands and ligase. The main difference in this course is scale: a circular bacterial chromosome usually has one starting point, while each linear eukaryotic chromosome has many.
