resources.title: Transcription and RNA Processing: Study Guide (Biology 6.3)
resources.description: How RNA polymerase copies one DNA strand into RNA, what mRNA, tRNA and rRNA each do, and how eukaryotic cells cap, tail and splice mRNA, including alternative splicing.
prerequisites: The structure of DNA and RNA: nucleotides, base pairing and 5′ and 3′ ends
How DNA is replicated, including the 5′ to 3′ direction of synthesis
learningObjectives: Describe the flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein
Describe the jobs of mRNA, tRNA and rRNA, and explain how each RNA's base sequence and shape suit its job
Explain how RNA polymerase uses one DNA strand as a template, reading it 3′ to 5′ and building RNA 5′ to 3′
Write the RNA transcript, with labelled ends, from a template or coding strand sequence
Describe how eukaryotic pre-mRNA is capped, given a poly-A tail and spliced, and explain why each change matters
Explain how alternative splicing lets one gene produce several different mature mRNAs
resources.calculatorNote: Only simple sums and percentages of sequence lengths. Lengths are given in nucleotides (nt)
keyPoints: Genetic information flows from DNA to RNA (transcription) and from RNA to protein (translation).
mRNA carries a gene's message to the ribosome; tRNA brings amino acids and pairs with mRNA codons through its anticodon; rRNA is a structural and working part of the ribosome.
RNA polymerase reads ONE strand of DNA, the template strand, from 3′ to 5′, and builds RNA from 5′ to 3′. The RNA matches the other (coding) strand, with U in place of T.

In eukaryotes the first transcript is processed in the nucleus: a 5′ cap helps the ribosome recognise the mRNA, a poly-A tail at the 3′ end makes it more stable, and introns are cut out while exons are joined.
Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons, so one gene can give several different mature mRNAs and proteins.

faqs.question: Is the coding strand ever read by RNA polymerase?
faqs.answer: Not for that gene. RNA polymerase reads only the template strand. The coding strand is useful to us because its sequence matches the mRNA (with T instead of U). For a different gene on the same chromosome, the other strand may be the template.

faqs.question: Do prokaryotes splice their mRNA?
faqs.answer: In general, no. Bacterial genes rarely contain introns, and bacterial mRNA is not given a eukaryotic-style cap and poly-A tail. With no nucleus, bacteria can start translating an mRNA while it is still being made, which you will meet in Topic 6.4.

faqs.question: Why does the course call it a GTP cap?
faqs.answer: The cap is built from a guanine nucleotide, supplied as GTP, attached to the 5′ end of the mRNA in an unusual way and then chemically modified. You only need to know that it is added to the 5′ end and helps the ribosome recognise the mRNA.

resources.title: Translation: Study Guide (Biology 6.4)
resources.description: How ribosomes read mRNA codons to build a polypeptide: where translation happens, the genetic code, initiation, elongation and termination, and the reverse flow of information in retroviruses.
prerequisites: The jobs of mRNA, tRNA and rRNA, and how mRNA is made and processed
Amino acids are joined into polypeptides; sequence determines protein structure
learningObjectives: State where translation happens in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and explain why prokaryotes can translate an mRNA while it is still being transcribed
Use a genetic code table to translate an mRNA, starting at AUG and stopping at a stop codon
Describe initiation, elongation and termination, including the roles of rRNA, tRNA anticodons and codons
Explain how a shared genetic code is evidence for the common ancestry of living things
Describe how retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to copy RNA into DNA, and predict the effects of disrupting a step in information flow
resources.calculatorNote: Only counting and simple arithmetic: 3 nucleotides per codon. A genetic code table is provided; you do not need to memorise it
keyPoints: Translation turns the base sequence of an mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide. It happens on ribosomes: free in the cytoplasm of all cells, and on the surface of the rough ER in eukaryotes.
mRNA is read in non-overlapping triplets called codons. Translation starts at AUG (methionine) and ends at a stop codon. Many amino acids have more than one codon.
Each tRNA carries one kind of amino acid and has an anticodon that base-pairs with a codon. The ribosome adds each new amino acid to the growing chain.
Nearly all organisms use the same genetic code, which is evidence that all living things share a common ancestor.
Retroviruses reverse the usual flow: reverse transcriptase copies their RNA genome into DNA, which joins the host's DNA and is then transcribed and translated.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn the whole genetic code?
faqs.answer: No. You only need to know that AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine. Exam-style questions provide a genetic code table when you need one. You do need to be able to read the table quickly.

faqs.question: Is the start codon the first three bases of the mRNA?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most mRNAs have a stretch of bases before the start codon that is not translated. The ribosome finds the start codon, and from there the mRNA is read in groups of three.

faqs.question: Why do proteins made on the rough ER end up in different places from proteins made on free ribosomes?
faqs.answer: Background: ribosomes that make proteins for secretion, for membranes or for some organelles are held on the rough ER, so the new polypeptide passes into the ER and then on through the endomembrane system. Ribosomes in the cytosol mostly make proteins that stay in the cytosol.

resources.title: Regulation of Gene Expression: Study Guide (Biology 6.5)
resources.description: How cells switch genes on and off: regulatory sequences and proteins, constitutive and inducible genes, the lac and trp operons, coordinate control in eukaryotes, and epigenetic marks on DNA and histones.
prerequisites: Transcription by RNA polymerase, starting at a promoter
Translation of mRNA into a polypeptide at a ribosome
DNA is wrapped around histone proteins in eukaryotic chromosomes
learningObjectives: Describe how regulatory proteins bind to regulatory DNA sequences to turn transcription up or down
Tell constitutive, inducible and repressible genes apart, with an example of each
Explain how the position of the operator in the lac and trp operons lets one repressor control several genes at once
Explain how eukaryotic genes on different chromosomes can be switched on together by the same transcription factor
Describe how reversible DNA methylation and histone acetylation change gene expression without changing the DNA sequence
Make a claim about how a gene is regulated from mutant or drug-treatment data, and back it with evidence and reasoning
resources.calculatorNote: Only ratios and percentages are needed. Fold change = expression in the test condition ÷ expression in the reference condition
keyPoints: Every cell carries many genes it is not using. Regulatory proteins bind to regulatory DNA sequences and decide which genes are transcribed, and how much.
Constitutive genes are expressed all the time. Inducible genes are off until a signal switches them on; repressible genes are on until a signal switches them off.

In bacteria, genes for one job often sit together in an operon under one promoter and one operator, so a single repressor controls them all. The lac operon is inducible; the trp operon is repressible.
In eukaryotes, genes scattered across chromosomes can be switched on together because they share the same control sequence for one transcription factor.
Epigenetic changes, such as DNA methylation (usually silencing) and histone acetylation (usually activating), alter expression without changing the DNA sequence, and they can be reversed.
A cell's phenotype depends on which genes it expresses and at what levels.

faqs.question: Is epigenetics the same as a mutation?
faqs.answer: No. A mutation changes the sequence of bases. An epigenetic change adds or removes chemical groups on the DNA or on histones; the base sequence stays the same, and the change can be reversed.

faqs.question: Do eukaryotes have operons?
faqs.answer: Almost never in the bacterial sense. Eukaryotic genes usually have their own promoters. They are coordinated instead by sharing control sequences that the same transcription factor recognises.

resources.title: Gene Expression and Cell Specialization: Study Guide (Biology 6.6)
resources.description: How cells with the same genome become different: transcription factors at promoters and enhancers, repressors that block transcription, combinations of regulators, and small RNAs that silence genes.
prerequisites: Regulatory sequences, regulatory proteins and operons
Transcription by RNA polymerase and translation at the ribosome
Epigenetic marks on DNA and histones
learningObjectives: Explain how general transcription factors and RNA polymerase assemble at a promoter, and how activators at enhancers raise the rate of transcription
Explain why an enhancer can work from far upstream or downstream of the start site
Explain how repressor proteins bound to DNA block transcription
Use the idea of combinations of transcription factors to predict which genes a cell type expresses

resources.calculatorNote: Only percentages and ratios are needed. Percentage of full activity = test value ÷ full-construct value × 100
keyPoints: Almost every cell in your body has the same genes. Cells specialise because they express different genes, at different levels: differential gene expression.
RNA polymerase and general transcription factors bind the promoter. Activators bind enhancers, which can sit far upstream or downstream of the start site, and greatly raise the rate of transcription.
Negative regulators (repressors) bind DNA and block transcription, for example at silencer sequences.
Each gene needs a particular combination of transcription factors. Each cell type has its own set, so it switches on its own set of genes.
Small RNAs, such as microRNAs and siRNAs, base-pair with mRNA and block translation or cause the mRNA to be broken down.

faqs.question: If every cell has the same genes, why does a nerve cell not make insulin?
faqs.answer: The insulin gene is present in a nerve cell, but the nerve cell lacks the combination of activators the insulin gene's control region needs, and the gene's chromatin is packed away. So the gene is not transcribed.

faqs.question: Is an enhancer a gene?
faqs.answer: No. An enhancer is a regulatory DNA sequence. It does not code for a protein. It is a binding site for activator proteins that make transcription of a nearby gene more likely.

resources.title: Mutations: Study Guide (Biology 6.7)
resources.description: Learn the types of mutation, how changes in DNA alter protein type or amount and phenotype, how chromosome errors arise, and how mutations and gene transfer feed natural selection.
prerequisites: Transcription and translation, and how to read a codon table

learningObjectives: Classify a change in DNA as a substitution, insertion or deletion, and as silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift
Predict how a mutation changes the amino acid sequence, the amount of protein, and the phenotype

resources.calculatorNote: Only simple ratios and percentages are needed. A codon table is given wherever you need one
keyPoints: A mutation is any change in the DNA sequence. It can change the type of protein made, the amount made, or nothing at all.
Point (substitution) mutations can be silent, missense or nonsense. Insertions or deletions that are not a multiple of three shift the reading frame.
Mutations are random. Whether one is beneficial, harmful or neutral depends on its effect and on the environment.
Nondisjunction in meiosis gives gametes with an extra or missing chromosome; changes in chromosome number or structure often affect development.
Mutation, plus gene transfer between prokaryotes and recombination between viruses, creates the variation that natural selection acts on.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn the names of specific genetic disorders?
faqs.answer: No. Knowledge of specific mutations, and of specific disorders caused by changes in chromosome number, is outside the scope of the exam. You need the general principles and the ability to reason from a sequence or data you are given.

faqs.question: Is a mutation always bad?
faqs.answer: No. Many mutations have no effect on the protein or phenotype. Some help in one environment and harm in another. Only the effect in context decides.

resources.title: Introduction to Natural Selection: Study Guide (Biology 7.1)
resources.description: Learn the steps of Darwin's argument, what evolutionary fitness really measures, how to calculate relative fitness, and why changing environments alter the speed and direction of evolution.
prerequisites: Genes, alleles and how traits are inherited (Unit 5)
Mutation as a source of new DNA sequences (Topic 6.7)
learningObjectives: Define evolution and place natural selection among the processes that cause it
Set out the steps of Darwin's argument: overproduction, competition, heritable variation and differential survival and reproduction
Explain why fitness is measured by reproductive success, and calculate relative fitness from data
Explain how changes in biotic and abiotic conditions alter the rate and direction of evolution
Describe what a histogram or flowchart of natural selection shows, including its axes, groups and trends
resources.calculatorNote: You need means, percentages and ratios. Give relative fitness to 2 or 3 decimal places
keyPoints: Evolution is a change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations. Natural selection is one major cause; random processes are others.

Darwin's argument: more offspring are born than resources can support, individuals vary, much of that variation is inherited, so individuals with favourable traits survive and reproduce more, and those traits become more common.
Fitness means reproductive success: the number of offspring an individual leaves that themselves survive to breed. Long life or strength counts only if it leads to more offspring.
Relative fitness = mean offspring of a phenotype ÷ mean offspring of the most successful phenotype.
Biotic and abiotic conditions change, so the trait that is favoured can change from one generation to the next. This alters both the speed and the direction of evolution.

faqs.question: Do individuals evolve?
faqs.answer: No. An individual's genes do not change in response to its environment. Populations evolve, because the mix of heritable traits changes from one generation to the next.

faqs.question: Is natural selection the only cause of evolution?
faqs.answer: No. It is a major mechanism, but random processes such as mutation, genetic drift and gene flow also change populations. You meet those in Topic 7.4.

Recall the differences between allopatric and sympatric speciation and between the two models of rate
keyPoints: Speciation = two populations become reproductively isolated, so gene flow between them stops.
Pre-zygotic barriers act before a zygote forms; post-zygotic barriers act on hybrids.
Allopatric: separated by geography. Sympatric: same area, isolated by polyploidy, host shift or mate choice.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Speciation: Study Guide (Biology 7.10)
resources.description: Learn the biological species concept, the barriers that keep species apart, allopatric and sympatric speciation, gradualism and punctuated equilibrium, adaptive radiation and convergent evolution.
prerequisites: Natural selection, genetic drift and gene flow change allele frequencies
Meiosis: homologous chromosomes pair before they separate
Reading a phylogenetic tree: nodes and branches
learningObjectives: Define a species with the biological species concept and explain why reproductive isolation is the key to speciation
Classify reproductive barriers as pre-zygotic or post-zygotic and explain how each blocks gene flow
Compare allopatric and sympatric speciation, including speciation by polyploidy
Contrast gradualism with punctuated equilibrium and explain why adaptive radiation can be rapid
Distinguish divergent from convergent evolution and predict how a change in conditions affects gene flow between populations
resources.calculatorNote: You need simple chromosome counts and percentages. Give percentages to 1 decimal place
keyPoints: A new species arises when two populations become reproductively isolated, so genes no longer flow between them.
Biological species concept: a species is a group whose members can interbreed and produce viable, fertile offspring. It applies to sexually reproducing organisms.
Pre-zygotic barriers stop a zygote forming (habitat, timing, behaviour, mechanical, gametic). Post-zygotic barriers act after (hybrids die, are sterile, or their offspring fail).
Allopatric speciation follows a geographic split. Sympatric speciation happens in the same area, for example by polyploidy in plants or a switch to a new host.
Speciation can be slow and steady (gradualism) or quick after long stasis (punctuated equilibrium). It is fastest in adaptive radiations into new habitats.

faqs.question: If two animals produce a hybrid, are they the same species?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Under the biological species concept the offspring must be viable and fertile, and the groups must exchange genes in nature. A horse and a donkey produce mules, but mules are almost always sterile, so horses and donkeys are separate species.

faqs.question: Does speciation need a physical barrier?
faqs.answer: No. Allopatric speciation does, but sympatric speciation happens with no geographic barrier, for example when polyploidy makes offspring unable to breed with the parent population.

resources.title: Variations in Populations: Study Guide (Biology 7.11)
resources.description: Learn how the genetic diversity of a population affects its ability to survive disease, climate change and other pressures, and why an allele that helps in one setting can harm in another.
prerequisites: Natural selection acts on heritable variation in a population
Allele and genotype frequencies, and the Hardy–Weinberg equations p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1
learningObjectives: Explain what genetic diversity is and describe simple ways to compare it between populations
Explain why species and populations with little genetic diversity are at greater risk of decline or extinction
Explain why a genetically diverse population is more likely to contain individuals that survive a new environmental pressure
Use allele frequencies to predict what fraction of a population could survive a selective pressure
Explain, with data, why an allele that is adaptive in one environment can be harmful in another
Build a claim–evidence–reasoning argument that links population data to the theory of natural selection
resources.calculatorNote: Only squares, products and percentages are needed. All data sets in the worked examples are fictional
keyPoints: Genetic diversity is the variety of alleles in a population. It is the raw material natural selection works with.
Populations with little genetic diversity are at risk of decline or extinction, because a new disease or change in the environment can affect almost every individual in the same way.
Diverse populations are more resilient: they are more likely to already contain some individuals that can survive a new pressure.
Whether an allele is helpful depends on the environment. An allele that is adaptive under one set of conditions may be harmful under another.
Selection acts on variation that already exists. A population cannot produce the right allele on demand when the pressure arrives.

faqs.question: Is a small population always low in genetic diversity?
faqs.answer: Not always, but usually over time. A small population loses alleles by chance and through inbreeding, and it has fewer individuals carrying rare alleles in the first place. A population that recently shrank may still hold much of its old diversity for a while.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn the details of particular endangered species?
faqs.answer: You need the principle, not a list of facts. Exam questions give you the data. Named examples, such as condors or potato blight, help you remember and explain the idea.

prerequisites: The structure of RNA and DNA, and complementary base pairing

learningObjectives: Use the dates of Earth's formation, of conditions becoming suitable for life and of the earliest fossils to state a plausible time range for the origin of life

resources.calculatorNote: Only subtraction, ratios and simple scaling are needed. Course dates: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago (bya); conditions became suitable about 3.9 bya; earliest fossil evidence about 3.5 bya
keyPoints: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago (bya). It was too hostile for life until about 3.9 bya. The earliest fossil evidence of life is about 3.5 bya.
Together these dates give a plausible window for the origin of life: roughly between 3.9 and 3.5 bya.
The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA was the first genetic material, because RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions.
Its three assumptions: RNA replication once carried genetic information between generations; that replication depended on base pairing; and genetically encoded proteins were not yet the catalysts.

faqs.question: Do I need to know the Miller–Urey experiment?
faqs.answer: It is not part of the required content for this topic, but it is a useful example of how scientists test ideas about early Earth chemistry. This guide includes it as labelled background.

faqs.question: Has the RNA world hypothesis been proven?
faqs.answer: No. It is a well-supported model, not a proven fact. Several observations fit it, and laboratory experiments show that parts of it are possible, but no one has shown how the first self-copying RNA arose.

resources.title: Natural Selection: Study Guide (Biology 7.2)
resources.description: Learn why selection acts on phenotypes, how changing environments create selective pressures, why one trait can help in one place and harm in another, and how molecular variation affects fitness.
prerequisites: The steps of natural selection and the meaning of relative fitness (Topic 7.1)
How a change in DNA can change a protein (Topic 6.7)
Membrane structure and enzyme activity (Units 2 and 3)
learningObjectives: Explain why natural selection acts on phenotypes and why only heritable variation changes the next generation
Identify biotic and abiotic selective pressures and explain how a changing environment creates them
Explain, with examples, how the same phenotype can raise fitness in one environment and lower it in another

keyPoints: Natural selection acts on phenotypes: predators, drought and disease meet the organism, not its alleles. Only the heritable part of the variation is passed on.
A selective pressure is any feature of the environment that makes some phenotypes survive or reproduce better than others. When the environment changes, new pressures appear.
Fitness depends on the environment. The sickle-cell carrier phenotype is favoured where malaria is common but gives no advantage where it is absent.

Variation in the types and numbers of molecules in cells, such as enzyme variants, membrane lipids or extra copies of a detoxifying enzyme, lets some individuals survive and reproduce when conditions change.

faqs.question: Does insecticide resistance count as artificial selection?
faqs.answer: No. Humans apply the insecticide, but they do not choose which insects breed. The insects that happen to survive leave the offspring, so this is natural selection in a human-changed environment. Artificial selection, in Topic 7.3, is when humans pick the parents.

faqs.question: Do I need to know the details of each example?
faqs.answer: You need to explain how the variation affects fitness in a given environment. The examples here are illustrations; an exam question can use any organism and will give you the details you need.

resources.title: Artificial Selection: Study Guide (Biology 7.3)
resources.description: Learn how human choice of which individuals breed changes traits and genetic variation in other species, how to describe data from selection experiments, and why uniform crops are at risk.
prerequisites: Natural selection: heritable variation, differential reproduction and fitness
Alleles, genotypes and phenotypes
learningObjectives: Explain artificial selection as the same process as natural selection, with human choice deciding which individuals reproduce
Explain why artificial selection can only work on heritable variation that already exists
Explain how artificial selection changes the mean of a trait and reduces genetic variation within a selected population
Describe data from a selection experiment: quote values, describe trends and compare selected lines with a control
Explain why genetically uniform crops and livestock are more vulnerable to disease and changing conditions
resources.calculatorNote: You need means, differences and percentage changes only. Round to the precision of the data
keyPoints: Artificial selection: humans choose which individuals breed, based on traits they want. The selected traits become more common in the next generations.
It works exactly like natural selection (heritable variation plus unequal reproduction); only the 'judge' is different: human choice instead of the environment.
Selection can only use heritable variation that already exists. New variation comes from mutation and from crossing with other populations.
Within a selected population, genetic variation usually falls: alleles for unwanted traits are lost, and few parents are used. Between breeds or varieties, differences grow.
Uniform crops and livestock can be wiped out by one disease, because no individuals carry alleles for resistance.

faqs.question: Is artificial selection the same as genetic engineering?
faqs.answer: No. Artificial selection only chooses which whole organisms breed; it uses variation already present. Genetic engineering (Topic 6.8) changes DNA directly, for example by inserting a gene.

faqs.question: Do I need to know a formula for the response to selection?
faqs.answer: No formula is needed for this topic. You should be able to describe data from a table or graph: pick out values, describe trends and compare a selected group with a control.

faqs.question: Does reading about selection count as the selection lab?
faqs.answer: No. Reading and simulations do not meet the course's laboratory requirement. An artificial selection investigation is one you should carry out with your teacher.

resources.title: Population Genetics: Study Guide (Biology 7.4)
resources.description: Learn how mutation, genetic drift, bottlenecks, founder events and gene flow change allele frequencies, how to calculate allele frequencies from counts, and why these changes count as evolution.
prerequisites: Alleles, genotypes, homozygous and heterozygous
Natural and artificial selection change populations over generations
learningObjectives: Explain how mutation adds new genetic variation and why it is a random process
Explain genetic drift as chance change in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations
Distinguish the bottleneck effect from the founder effect, with an example of each
Explain how gene flow adds or removes alleles and keeps connected populations similar
Calculate allele frequencies from genotype counts and use changes in them as evidence of evolution
State a null hypothesis and predict results for an investigation of drift or gene flow
resources.calculatorNote: Allele frequency = copies of the allele ÷ total copies of that gene (2 per diploid individual). Give frequencies to 2 or 3 decimal places
keyPoints: A population evolves when its allele frequencies change from one generation to the next. Selection is one cause; random processes are others.
Mutation is random and adds new alleles, the raw material for selection. On its own it changes frequencies very slowly.
Genetic drift is chance change in allele frequencies. It is strongest in small populations and can fix or remove an allele regardless of its effect.
Bottleneck: a population is cut to a few survivors. Founder effect: a few individuals start a new, separate population. Both are forms of drift.
Gene flow (migration) moves alleles between populations. It keeps them similar and works against their splitting into separate species.

faqs.question: Is genetic drift the same as natural selection?
faqs.answer: No. Selection favours alleles because of their effect on survival and reproduction. Drift changes allele frequencies by chance, whatever the alleles do. A harmful allele can increase by drift in a small population.

faqs.question: Do I need the Hardy–Weinberg equations for this topic?
faqs.answer: Not yet. Here you calculate allele frequencies by counting alleles. Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, and what it predicts, is Topic 7.5.

resources.title: Hardy–Weinberg Equilibrium: Study Guide (Biology 7.5)
resources.description: Learn the Hardy–Weinberg model of a non-evolving population: its five conditions, how to calculate allele and genotype frequencies, and how to use it as a null hypothesis.
prerequisites: Alleles, genotypes, dominant and recessive (Topic 5.3)
Mutation, genetic drift, gene flow and natural selection as causes of change (Topics 7.2–7.4)
The chi-square test (Topic 5.3)
learningObjectives: State the five conditions a population must meet for its allele and genotype frequencies to stay constant
Predict which frequencies change, and in which direction, when each condition is broken
Calculate allele frequencies by counting alleles from genotype data
Use p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 to predict genotype frequencies, including carrier frequency for a recessive trait
Use the Hardy–Weinberg prediction as a null hypothesis and test it against observed data with chi-square
Interpret graphs of allele frequency over time
resources.calculatorNote: Square roots are needed. Chi-square critical values at p = 0.05: 3.84 (1 degree of freedom), 5.99 (2). Give frequencies as decimals to 2 or 3 decimal places
keyPoints: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium is a model of a population that is not evolving: allele and genotype frequencies stay the same from one generation to the next.
For two alleles with frequencies p and q: p + q = 1, and the genotype frequencies are p² (homozygous one way), 2pq (heterozygous) and q² (homozygous the other way).
The five conditions are a large population, no migration, no new mutations, random mating and no natural selection. Real populations never meet all five.
Because the conditions are never fully met, the model is a null hypothesis: if observed data differ clearly from its prediction, at least one condition is being broken.
Count alleles to get p from genotype data. Use q = √(q²) only if you assume the population is in equilibrium.

faqs.question: Is the Hardy–Weinberg equation given in the exam?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 appear on the equations and formulas sheet. You still need to know what each term means and when you may use it.

faqs.question: Does a dominant allele always become more common over time?
faqs.answer: No. Dominance describes how alleles show up in the phenotype of a heterozygote. It says nothing about frequency. If the five conditions hold, a dominant allele at 0.1 stays at 0.1.

faqs.question: If a population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, does that mean it is not evolving at all?
faqs.answer: Only for the gene you tested. A population can be in equilibrium for one gene and evolving at another, for example where selection acts on a different trait.

resources.title: Evidence of Evolution: Study Guide (Biology 7.6)
resources.description: Learn how fossils, rock layers, radiometric dating, homologous and vestigial structures, DNA and protein sequences and biogeography show that organisms have changed over time.
prerequisites: DNA, the genetic code and how mutations change sequences (Unit 6)
Allele frequencies and how populations change (Topics 7.4–7.5)
learningObjectives: Name the kinds of data (geographical, geological, physical, biochemical and mathematical) that support evolution, with an example of each
Explain how fossils are dated using rock layers, radioactive decay and comparisons between sites
Calculate the age of a sample from the fraction of carbon-14 left, using its half-life
Explain how homologous and vestigial structures provide evidence of common ancestry, and tell them apart from analogous structures
Compare DNA or amino acid sequences and use the number of differences to judge relatedness
Describe data in a table or graph by quoting specific values, trends and relationships
resources.calculatorNote: Half-life of carbon-14: take 5,700 years (older books use 5,730; answers differ by under 1%). Fraction left after n half-lives = (1/2)ⁿ
keyPoints: Evidence for evolution comes from many independent sciences: geology, physics, biochemistry, geography and mathematics. They point to the same conclusion.
Fossils are dated by their position in rock layers (lower is usually older), by radioactive decay of isotopes such as carbon-14, and by matching layers and fossils between sites.
Each half-life halves the amount of a radioactive isotope. Carbon-14 (half-life about 5,700 years) dates once-living material up to about 50,000 years old.
Homologous structures (same basic parts, different uses) and vestigial structures (reduced remnants) show common ancestry.
The fewer differences between two species' DNA or protein sequences, the more recently they shared a common ancestor.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise half-lives of isotopes?
faqs.answer: No. A question will give you the half-life it wants you to use. You need to know what a half-life means and how to work out the number of half-lives from the fraction remaining.

faqs.question: Does vestigial mean useless?
faqs.answer: No. A vestigial structure is reduced compared with the same structure in related species and has lost its original main function. Some still have a minor use, such as the human tailbone, which anchors muscles.

resources.title: Common Ancestry: Study Guide (Biology 7.7)
resources.description: Learn how membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes and genes with introns show that all eukaryotes share a common ancestor, and how to predict effects from that shared design.
prerequisites: The difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts
Transcription and RNA processing, including what introns and exons are
learningObjectives: Describe the cell-level and molecular features that every eukaryote shares: membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes and genes interrupted by introns
Explain why a set of shared, complex features is better explained by one common ancestor than by many separate origins
Tell apart features shared by all life from features shared only by eukaryotes
Compare gene structures and use shared intron positions as evidence, while noting that introns can be gained or lost
Predict the effects of disrupting a shared eukaryotic system, such as splicing, on different groups of organisms
resources.calculatorNote: Only simple percentages are needed. All data sets are fictional
keyPoints: All eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi and protists) share three features at the cell and molecular level: membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes, and genes that contain introns.
These features are complex and built the same way in every eukaryote. One shared ancestor that already had them explains this far better than many separate origins.
Most bacteria and archaea lack all three: no nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles, usually one circular chromosome, and protein-coding genes without spliceosomal introns.
Shared design lets you predict: a drug or mutation that disrupts splicing affects yeast, plants and human cells, but not bacteria.

faqs.question: Does common ancestry mean humans evolved from yeast?
faqs.answer: No. Humans and yeast are both modern species. They share an ancestor that lived long ago, and each lineage has changed since then. Neither is the ancestor of the other.

faqs.question: Do bacteria and eukaryotes also share a common ancestor?
faqs.answer: Yes. All life shares features such as DNA, the genetic code and ribosomes. This topic focuses on the extra features that only eukaryotes share, which point to a more recent common ancestor of all eukaryotes.

resources.title: Continuing Evolution: Study Guide (Biology 7.8)
resources.description: Learn why all species are still evolving, using genome change, the fossil record, resistance to antibiotics, pesticides, herbicides and cancer drugs, and new diseases.
prerequisites: Natural selection: variation, inheritance and differential survival and reproduction
Mutations as the source of new alleles
learningObjectives: Explain why evolution is an ongoing process in every population, including humans
Use mutation rates and population sizes to show how genomes change from one generation to the next
Interpret fossil data that show continuous change in a lineage
Explain resistance to antibiotics, pesticides, herbicides and chemotherapy drugs as natural selection on existing variation
Explain how pathogens evolve and how this can lead to new or re-emerging diseases
Evaluate an investigation into evolving resistance and propose a better-designed follow-up investigation
resources.calculatorNote: Standard form (powers of ten) is used for population sizes and mutation rates. Model values are round numbers chosen for clarity; all data sets are fictional unless a source is named
keyPoints: Every species is still evolving: new mutations arise each generation, and environments keep changing what is favoured.
Evidence includes changes in genomes over time, continuous change in fossil lineages, resistance to drugs and pesticides, and pathogens that cause new diseases.
Resistance is not caused by the drug. The drug selects variants that already exist, so they survive, reproduce and become common.
Large populations with short generations, such as bacteria, viruses and tumour cells, evolve fastest.

faqs.question: Have humans stopped evolving?
faqs.answer: No. New mutations arise in every human generation, and allele frequencies keep changing through selection, drift and migration. Human evolution is simply slow to see because a human generation is long.

faqs.question: Does an antibiotic make bacteria mutate into resistant forms?
faqs.answer: No. Resistant variants arise by random mutation, usually before the drug is present. The antibiotic kills susceptible cells, so the resistant ones are left to multiply.

resources.title: Phylogeny: Revision Notes (Biology 7.9)
resources.description: One-page recap of how to read and build cladograms and phylogenetic trees, the evidence behind them, molecular clocks, and the mistakes that cost marks.
learningObjectives: Recall the parts of a tree and how to judge relatedness from nodes
Recall how shared derived characters, an outgroup and a molecular clock are used
keyPoints: A node is the most recent common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it; relatedness depends on how recent that node is.
Cladogram = branching order only. Phylogenetic tree = branching order plus time or change, calibrated by fossils or a molecular clock.
Shared derived characters (gains or losses) define clades; the outgroup shows the ancestral state.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Phylogeny: Study Guide (Biology 7.9)
resources.description: Learn to read and build cladograms and phylogenetic trees, use shared derived characters and an outgroup, weigh molecular against body-form evidence and date splits with a molecular clock.
prerequisites: Common ancestry and the evidence for evolution: homologous structures, fossils and shared DNA
Mutations change DNA sequences and are passed on to offspring
learningObjectives: Read a tree: identify the root, nodes, clades and sister groups, and judge relatedness from the most recent common ancestor
Explain how a phylogenetic tree differs from a cladogram, including how time is calibrated with fossils or a molecular clock
Build a cladogram from a table of traits gained or lost, using an outgroup and shared derived characters
Compare morphological, fossil, DNA and protein evidence and explain why molecular data are usually more reliable
Explain why every tree is a testable hypothesis that is revised when new evidence appears
resources.calculatorNote: You need simple division for percentages and molecular-clock rates. Give dates to 2 significant figures; they are estimates
keyPoints: A tree is a hypothesis about how lineages are related. Each node stands for the most recent common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it, and marks a speciation event.
Judge relatedness by how recently two lineages share an ancestor, not by how close their tips are drawn. Branches can rotate at a node without changing the tree.
A cladogram shows only the branching order. A phylogenetic tree also shows time or amount of change, calibrated by dated fossils or a molecular clock.
Shared derived characters (traits gained or lost) group lineages; the outgroup shows which state is ancestral. Traits every group shares, or that only one lineage has, do not help.
Molecular data (DNA and protein sequences) usually give more reliable trees than body form, because they provide many characters and are less often misled by convergent evolution.

faqs.question: Is a cladogram the same as a phylogenetic tree?
faqs.answer: Both show branching order. In this course a phylogenetic tree also shows time or amount of change along its branches; a cladogram does not, so its branch lengths mean nothing.

faqs.question: Does the outgroup represent the ancestor of the other species?
faqs.answer: No. The outgroup is a living (or fossil) lineage that is less closely related to the ingroup than ingroup members are to each other. It shows which character states are probably ancestral.

resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Responses to the Environment: Study Guide (Biology 8.1)
resources.description: Learn how organisms respond to internal and external changes through behaviour and physiology, how they signal to each other, and how responses and cooperation affect fitness.
prerequisites: Natural selection: heritable variation and differential reproductive success
Cell communication: a signal is received and causes a response
Chi-square: comparing observed and expected counts
learningObjectives: Explain how a behavioural or physiological response is linked to a change in an organism's internal or external environment
Tell taxis from kinesis and innate from learned behaviour, using evidence
Describe the kinds of signals organisms use (visual, sound, touch, electrical, chemical) and what the signals achieve
Explain how signalling and cooperative behaviour change survival and reproductive success, and so take part in natural selection
Identify the independent and dependent variables in a behaviour experiment, and choose and justify suitable controls
resources.calculatorNote: Chi-square: χ² = Σ (o − e)² ÷ e, with degrees of freedom = number of categories − 1. Critical values at p = 0.05: 3.84 (1 df), 5.99 (2 df), 7.81 (3 df)
keyPoints: Organisms respond to changes inside them (hunger, dehydration, hormones) and outside them (light, temperature, predators) with behavioural responses (what they do) and physiological responses (changes inside the body).
Taxis is movement directed toward or away from a stimulus. Kinesis is a change in speed or turning rate that is not directed.
Organisms communicate with visual, sound, touch, electrical and chemical signals. Signals change the receiver's behaviour and can change who survives and reproduces.
Natural selection favours innate and learned behaviours that raise survival and reproduction. Cooperation often raises individual fitness and helps the population survive.
A good behaviour experiment changes one variable, counts or measures the response, and uses a control that rules out other explanations, such as a side bias in the apparatus.

faqs.question: Do I need to know how each response works inside the body?
faqs.answer: No. You need to link a response to the change that triggers it and to its effect on survival and reproduction. The detailed mechanisms of specific behaviours, and of specific communication systems, are outside the scope of the exam.

faqs.question: Does reading about choice-chamber experiments count as doing the lab?
faqs.answer: No. Reading and simulations do not meet the course's laboratory requirement. Behaviour investigations are lab work you should carry out with your teacher.

resources.title: Energy Flow Through Ecosystems: Study Guide (Biology 8.2)
resources.description: Learn how organisms gain and use energy, how energy flows through trophic levels while carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water cycle, and how changes in energy supply affect ecosystems.
prerequisites: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration: what goes in and what comes out
Behavioural and physiological responses to the environment
Percentages and simple ratios
learningObjectives: Compare how endotherms and ectotherms control body temperature, and link net energy gain or loss to growth, reproduction and survival
Explain why energy flows through an ecosystem while matter cycles, and describe the water, carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles
Calculate energy passed between trophic levels and use the result to explain the shape of energy pyramids
Predict how a change in sunlight or producer biomass affects the number and size of trophic levels and population sizes
Explain how photosynthetic and chemosynthetic autotrophs and the different kinds of heterotroph allow energy to enter and move through an ecosystem
resources.calculatorNote: Model values: about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next; 1 mL of oxygen used in respiration releases about 20 J; dry food yields about 17 kJ per gram. Round to the precision of the data
keyPoints: Energy flows one way: in as light (or chemical energy), out as heat. Matter cycles: atoms of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water are reused again and again.
Endotherms use heat from their own metabolism to keep body temperature steady, so they need much more food than ectotherms of the same size. Ectotherms control temperature mainly by behaviour.
A net energy gain allows storage, growth and more reproduction; a net loss leads to loss of mass, less reproduction and eventually death.
Only a small fraction (often about 10%) of the energy at one trophic level ends up in the next, so food chains are short and higher levels are small.
Autotrophs capture energy from sunlight (photosynthesis) or from inorganic molecules (chemosynthesis). Heterotrophs get energy by eating organic matter that came from autotrophs.

faqs.question: Is the 10% figure a law?
faqs.answer: No. It is a rough average. Real transfer efficiencies vary, often between about 5% and 20%, depending on the organisms and the ecosystem. Use the figure a question gives you.

faqs.question: Do I need the names of the bacteria in the nitrogen cycle?
faqs.answer: No. You need the steps (fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification, denitrification), what each one converts into what, and that soil microorganisms carry them out.

resources.description: One-page recap of populations, births and deaths, per capita rates and exponential growth, with dN/dt = B − D, dN/dt = rₘₐₓN, graphing tips and the mistakes that cost marks.

keyPoints: Population: one species, one area, one time, interacting with each other and the environment.
dN/dt = B − D; per capita r = (B − D) ÷ N.
No limits on reproduction: dN/dt = rₘₐₓN, a J-shaped curve that is a straight line on a log scale.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Population Ecology: Study Guide (Biology 8.3)
resources.description: Learn what a population is, how births, deaths and population size set its growth rate, how to use dN/dt = B − D and dN/dt = rₘₐₓN, and how to graph exponential growth.
prerequisites: Energy flow and how organisms obtain energy and matter from their environment
Reading line graphs and calculating rates of change
learningObjectives: Define a population and describe how its members interact with each other and with their environment
Explain how birth rate, death rate and population size together set the rate of population growth
Use dN/dt = B − D and per capita rates to calculate and compare population growth
Describe exponential growth, use dN/dt = rₘₐₓN and say when it applies
Link adaptations for obtaining and using energy and matter to births and deaths
Construct a suitable graph of population data, including a log scale and error bars where appropriate
resources.calculatorNote: You need subtraction, multiplication, division and powers. Use logarithms only for a log-scale axis. Keep full values until the last step
keyPoints: A population is all the individuals of one species in one area that interact with each other and with their environment.
Population growth depends on birth rate, death rate and population size: dN/dt = B − D, where B and D are births and deaths per unit time.
Per capita growth rate r = (B − D) ÷ N. With no limits on reproduction, r stays at its maximum, rₘₐₓ, and growth is exponential: dN/dt = rₘₐₓN.
In exponential growth the population adds more individuals each time step, but the per capita rate and the doubling time stay constant. On a log scale the curve becomes a straight line.
Births and deaths depend on how well organisms obtain and use energy and matter, so adaptations for feeding and energy use shape population growth.

faqs.question: What is the difference between B and b?
faqs.answer: B is the number of births per unit time in the whole population (for example 96 births per month). The per capita birth rate, b, is births per individual per unit time: b = B ÷ N. The same goes for D and d.

faqs.question: Do I need to include immigration and emigration?
faqs.answer: The equation in this topic uses only births and deaths, as if the population were closed. Real populations also gain and lose individuals by movement. Include them only if a question gives you the numbers.

faqs.question: Does reading about population growth count as a lab?
faqs.answer: No. Reading and simulations do not meet the course's laboratory requirement. Counting a growing yeast or duckweed culture is a good investigation to carry out with your teacher.

resources.description: One-page recap of population density, carrying capacity, density-dependent and density-independent factors and logistic growth, with the key equation, calculation tips and mistakes that cost marks.
learningObjectives: Recall carrying capacity and the two kinds of limiting factor
Recall dN/dt = rₘₐₓN(K − N)/K and what it predicts at different population sizes
keyPoints: K = the population size the environment's total resources can sustain.
Density-dependent: fraction affected rises with density. Density-independent: same fraction at any density.
Logistic: dN/dt = rₘₐₓN(K − N)/K; S-shaped curve, fastest at K/2, zero at K.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Effect of Density on Populations: Study Guide (Biology 8.4)
resources.description: Learn what carrying capacity is, how density-dependent and density-independent factors limit growth, and how to use the logistic equation and calculate means, ratios and percentages from population data.
prerequisites: Births, deaths and per capita growth rates (dN/dt = B − D)
Exponential growth and the equation dN/dt = rₘₐₓN
learningObjectives: Define population density and carrying capacity, and explain how resources set carrying capacity
Explain how a rising density reduces the resources available to each individual and so lowers births and raises deaths
Distinguish density-dependent from density-independent factors, with examples and data
Use dN/dt = rₘₐₓN(K − N)/K to calculate growth rates and describe the S-shaped logistic curve
Calculate means, rates, ratios, percentages and percentage changes from population data
resources.calculatorNote: Logistic growth: dN/dt = rₘₐₓN(K − N)/K. Work out (K − N)/K first. Keep full values until the last step
keyPoints: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area or volume. Resources set how many individuals an area can support, and density sets how much of each resource each individual gets.
Carrying capacity (K) is the largest population size the environment's total resources can support in the long term.

Density-dependent factors (competition, predation, disease, waste) hit a larger fraction of the population as density rises. Density-independent factors (storms, frost, fire) hit about the same fraction at any density.
As these limits take hold, growth usually becomes logistic: dN/dt = rₘₐₓN(K − N)/K. The curve is S-shaped, growth is fastest at N = K/2 and stops at N = K.

faqs.question: Is carrying capacity a fixed number for a species?
faqs.answer: No. K belongs to a species in a particular environment. If food, water or space changes, for example in a drought or a good rainy season, K changes too.

faqs.question: Can a population be larger than K?
faqs.answer: For a short time, yes. Then (K − N)/K is negative, so the logistic equation gives a negative dN/dt and the population falls back toward K.

faqs.question: Does reading about density effects count as a lab?
faqs.answer: No. Reading and simulations do not meet the course's laboratory requirement. Growing cultures at different densities is a good investigation to carry out with your teacher.

resources.title: Community Ecology: Study Guide (Biology 8.5)
resources.description: Learn how to describe a community by its species composition and diversity, calculate Simpson's diversity index, and explain how competition, predation and symbioses shape communities.
prerequisites: Populations, carrying capacity and density-dependent factors
Food chains, trophic levels and the flow of energy through an ecosystem
Mean and standard deviation of a small data set
learningObjectives: Describe a community by the species it contains (composition) and by its species diversity
Calculate and interpret Simpson's diversity index, separating richness from evenness
Classify interactions between populations by their positive, negative or neutral effect on each species
Explain how predation, competition, niche partitioning, trophic cascades and symbioses change population sizes and community structure
Use error bars of mean ± 2 SE to judge whether two sample means are likely to be different
resources.calculatorNote: Simpson's diversity index = 1 − Σ(n/N)². Standard error SE = s ÷ √n, using the sample standard deviation s; error bars are mean ± 2 SE. Give indices to 2 decimal places
keyPoints: A community is all the interacting populations of different species in one area. Describe it by composition (which species) and diversity (how many species and how evenly individuals are spread among them).
Simpson's diversity index = 1 − Σ(n/N)². It runs from 0 (one species) towards 1. Higher means more diverse: more species, more evenly represented.
Every interaction can be written as a pair of effects: competition (−/−), predation, herbivory and parasitism (+/−), mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0).
Interactions decide which species get energy and matter, so they drive population changes: predator–prey cycles, competitive exclusion, niche partitioning and trophic cascades.
If error bars of mean ± 2 SE do not overlap, the two means are probably different; if they overlap a lot, the data do not show a difference.

faqs.question: Is a high Simpson's index always better?
faqs.answer: No. The index describes a community; it is not a score. A salt marsh or a desert spring can be healthy with few species. Compare indices only between similar habitats sampled in the same way.

faqs.question: What is the difference between predation and parasitism?
faqs.answer: Both are +/− interactions. A predator usually kills and eats its prey quickly. A parasite usually lives on or in its host and feeds on it over a long time, often without killing it.

resources.title: Biodiversity: Study Guide (Biology 8.6)
resources.description: Learn why diverse ecosystems resist and recover from change better, what makes a keystone species, and how to predict the short- and long-term effects of adding or removing a part of an ecosystem.
prerequisites: Food webs, producers and trophic levels
Community structure, Simpson's diversity index and interactions between species
learningObjectives: Explain why ecosystems with more parts, and more variety among those parts, are usually more resilient to environmental change
Describe how keystone species, producers and essential biotic and abiotic factors keep an ecosystem diverse
Use data to identify a keystone species from its effect relative to its abundance
Predict the short-term and long-term effects of adding or removing a component of an ecosystem
Calculate percentage changes to compare how much ecosystems are disturbed and how far they recover
resources.calculatorNote: Percentage change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100. Give percentages to 3 significant figures or to the nearest whole number
keyPoints: Ecosystems with few components, or little variety among them, are often less resilient: a change hits them harder and they recover more slowly.
Diversity gives back-up: if one species fails, another that does a similar job can take over (functional redundancy).
A keystone species has an effect far larger than its abundance suggests. Remove it and the ecosystem often collapses.
Producers, keystone species and essential abiotic factors (water, light, nutrients, temperature) hold up the diversity of an ecosystem.
Adding or removing any component changes the ecosystem's structure; short-term effects (on direct partners) and long-term effects (on the whole community) can differ.

faqs.question: Is resilience the same as resistance?
faqs.answer: Not quite. Resistance is how little an ecosystem changes when it is disturbed. Resilience is how quickly and fully it returns afterwards. Diverse ecosystems often score better on both, and exam answers about recovery are about resilience.

faqs.question: Is a keystone species always a predator?
faqs.answer: No. Many famous examples are predators, but a herbivore, a pollinator, a fruiting tree or an animal that alters its habitat can also have a large effect relative to its abundance.

resources.title: Disruptions in Ecosystems: Study Guide (Biology 8.7)
resources.description: Learn how the environment selects among random variation, how invasive species, human activity, biomagnification and eutrophication disrupt ecosystems, and how to test claims with chi-square.
prerequisites: Natural selection acts on heritable variation (Unit 7)
Energy flow and trophic levels in food chains (Topic 8.2)
Biodiversity, keystone species and ecosystem resilience (Topic 8.6)
The chi-square test and the null hypothesis (Topic 5.3)
learningObjectives: Explain how a changing environment selects among variations that already exist, including heterozygote advantage, and why mutations are not caused by the need for them
Explain how an invasive species can spread by exploiting a niche free of predators or competitors, or by outcompeting native species
Describe how human activities, including biomagnification and eutrophication, change ecosystems and can cause extinctions
Explain how geological and meteorological events change habitats and where species live
Use a chi-square test to reject or fail to reject a null hypothesis about an ecological or evolutionary disruption
resources.calculatorNote: Chi-square critical values at p = 0.05: 3.84 (1 degree of freedom), 5.99 (2), 7.81 (3). Concentration ratios are given to 2 or 3 significant figures
keyPoints: Variation comes first; selection comes second. Mutations arise at random. A change in the environment then favours the variants that happen to suit it.
Heterozygote advantage: the heterozygous genotype has a higher relative fitness than either homozygote, so both alleles stay in the population.
An invasive species spreads when it finds a niche free of its usual predators or competitors, or outcompetes native species for resources.
Biomagnification: a persistent, fat-soluble toxin becomes more concentrated at each trophic level. Eutrophication: extra nutrients cause an algal bloom, then decomposers use up the oxygen.
Geological and meteorological events, such as continental drift, El Niño and meteor impacts, change habitats and where species are found.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise the named examples, such as kudzu or potato blight?
faqs.answer: You need to be able to explain a disruption using one or two real examples. The exam usually gives you a scenario with data. What matters is the mechanism: what changed, which organisms gained or lost, and why.

faqs.question: Is a chi-square test the only statistics I need here?
faqs.answer: It is the most common test for count data in this topic. You may also be asked to judge a claim from a graph, means or error bars. In every case, decide whether the data support the claim, and state what the data cannot show.

resources.title: Experimental Design and Data Analysis: Exam Skills Guide (Biology)
resources.description: How to name variables and controls, state a null hypothesis, choose and draw the right graph, do the course calculations and write a claim backed by evidence and reasoning.
prerequisites: You have studied at least the first three units of the course
You can calculate a mean and a percentage with a calculator
learningObjectives: Identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables, a suitable control and a testable null hypothesis for an experiment
Choose the right type of graph for a data set and draw it with labelled axes, units, even scales and error bars
Carry out the course calculations: rates, percent change, mean, standard deviation, standard error, chi-square, Hardy–Weinberg and water potential
Use error bars or a chi-square result to decide whether to reject or fail to reject a null hypothesis
Write a claim supported by numerical evidence and biological reasoning, and justify a prediction
resources.calculatorNote: SE = s ÷ √n with s the sample standard deviation; error bars are mean ± 2 SE. χ² = Σ (o − e)² ÷ e; critical values at p = 0.05: 3.84 (1 df), 5.99 (2 df), 7.81 (3 df). Ψs = −iCRT with R = 0.0831 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T = °C + 273
keyPoints: Every experiment question rests on four labels: the independent variable you change, the dependent variable you measure, the variables you keep the same, and the control you compare against.
A null hypothesis says the independent variable has no effect. Data let you reject it or fail to reject it; data never prove a hypothesis.
Graph points come from the right graph type, labelled axes with units, even scales and correctly plotted points with error bars when the table gives them.
Show every calculation: the formula, the numbers substituted, the answer with units and sensible rounding.
A strong argument has a claim, numbers from the data as evidence, and a biological reason that links the two.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise the chi-square table and the formulas?
faqs.answer: No. A formula sheet with the chi-square table, standard error, Hardy–Weinberg and water potential equations is provided. You do need to know when to use each one and how to set it out.

faqs.question: Is it ever right to say the data prove my hypothesis?
faqs.answer: No. Say the data support the claim, or that you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis. One experiment with a small sample can never prove a general rule.

faqs.question: How many decimal places should my answer have?
faqs.answer: Match the precision of the data, usually 2 or 3 significant figures, and keep full calculator values until the final step.

resources.title: Task Verbs and Free-Response Technique: Exam Skills Guide (Biology)
resources.description: What each free-response task verb asks for and how much to write, how to read multi-part questions, plan your time and set out calculations, with three worked answers shown weak and strong.
prerequisites: You have studied at least half of the course content
You can read a data table and a line or bar graph
learningObjectives: Say what each free-response task verb requires and match the length of your answer to it
Break a multi-part question into its parts and give each part the number of separate points it is worth
Plan your time across the six free-response questions
Set out calculations, chi-square tests and error-bar comparisons so that every step can be followed
Turn a weak answer into one that makes a claim, uses the data and gives reasoning
resources.calculatorNote: χ² = Σ (o − e)² ÷ e, critical value 3.84 at p = 0.05 with 1 degree of freedom; Ψs = −iCRT with R = 0.0831 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T = °C + 273; p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Keep full calculator values until the last step
keyPoints: The verb decides the answer. Identify and describe need no reason; explain and justify need a because-link; predict needs a direction.
Count the points before you write. A 3-point part needs three separate correct ideas, not one long sentence.
The six questions carry 34 points in 90 minutes, about 2.6 minutes a point: roughly 22–24 minutes for each long question and 10 for each short one.
Show every calculation as formula, substitution with units, then answer with units. In chi-square, divide by the expected value.
Use the scenario's own numbers and terms. An answer that could fit any experiment rarely earns the point.

faqs.question: Do I lose marks for writing too much?
faqs.answer: Extra correct material usually earns nothing, and it costs time. Extra material that contradicts your answer can cost the point. Answer the verb, then stop.

faqs.question: Do I need full sentences?
faqs.answer: Yes. Outlines, bullet lists or a diagram on its own are not scored, unless a part asks you to draw or graph.

faqs.question: What if I cannot finish an early part that a later part depends on?
faqs.answer: Make a sensible assumption, say what it is in one line, and answer the later part. A blank part earns nothing.

prerequisites: Function notation, such as f(3) and f(3 + h)

learningObjectives: Calculate an average rate of change over an interval and state its units

keyPoints: An average rate of change is (change in output) ÷ (change in input) over an interval.
At a single instant the change in input is 0, so the average-rate formula gives 0/0 and cannot be used directly.
Average rates over smaller and smaller intervals containing the instant approach one value. That value is the instantaneous rate of change.

faqs.question: If nothing moves during an instant, how can there be a speed at that instant?
faqs.answer: The speed at an instant is not measured during the instant. It is the value that average speeds approach as the time interval around that instant shrinks.

faqs.question: Do I need formal limits for this topic?
faqs.answer: No. Topic 1.1 builds the idea. Limit notation is defined properly in Topic 1.2.

resources.title: Exploring Types of Discontinuities: Study Guide (Calculus AB 1.10)
resources.description: Learn to recognise removable, jump and vertical-asymptote discontinuities from graphs, tables and formulas, and to justify each type with one-sided limits.
prerequisites: One-sided limits and limit notation (Topics 1.2 to 1.4)
Algebraic manipulation of 0/0 limits, especially factoring (Topic 1.6)
Reading limits from graphs, tables and formulas (Topic 1.9)
learningObjectives: Describe what it means for a graph to be broken at a point, and name the three things that must all hold for it to be unbroken there
Classify a discontinuity as removable, jump or due to a vertical asymptote
Use left-hand and right-hand limits, together with the function value, to justify the type
Find and classify the discontinuities of rational and piecewise-defined functions
Recognise each type in a graph, a table of values and a formula
resources.calculatorNote: Practise every example here without a calculator. Tables of values are a check, not a justification.
keyPoints: A discontinuity at x = c is a break in the graph: f(c) is missing, the limit at c does not exist, or the limit and f(c) disagree.
Removable: the two-sided limit exists (a finite number) but f(c) is undefined or different. On a graph it is a hole.
Jump: both one-sided limits are finite numbers but they are different.
Vertical asymptote: f(x) grows without bound on at least one side of c.
Justify the type with the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and f(c), not with a picture alone.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 1.10 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: If f(c) is defined, can there still be a discontinuity at c?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the limit at c exists but is different from f(c), the discontinuity is removable. If the one-sided limits are finite but different, it is a jump, whatever f(c) is.

faqs.question: Does a zero in the denominator always mean a vertical asymptote?
faqs.answer: No. If the factor that makes the denominator zero cancels with the numerator, the graph has a hole instead. Factor first, then decide.

faqs.question: Is 'I can draw it without lifting my pencil' a good enough reason?
faqs.answer: It is a helpful picture, but it is not a justification. In a written answer, show that f(c) exists, that the limit exists, and that the two are equal, with their values.

faqs.question: If the formula for f gives 0/0 at x = c, is f automatically discontinuous there?
faqs.answer: Not always. If f(c) is given separately (for example in a piecewise definition) and it equals the limit, f is continuous at c. Always check all three conditions.

faqs.question: Is 1/x a continuous function?
faqs.answer: It is continuous at every point of its domain, so it is continuous on (−∞, 0) and on (0, ∞). It is not continuous on any interval that contains 0, such as [−1, 1], because it is not defined at 0.

faqs.question: Do I have to check every point of an interval one by one?
faqs.answer: No. The family facts cover all the points inside each piece at once. You only test special points: where a piece changes, where the formula is undefined, and the endpoints of the interval you were asked about.

resources.description: Learn when a discontinuity can be removed, how to redefine a function at a hole, and how to solve for parameters that make a piecewise function continuous.
prerequisites: The three conditions for continuity at a point (Topic 1.11)
Types of discontinuity: removable, jump and vertical asymptote (Topic 1.10)
Finding 0/0 limits by factoring and conjugates (Topic 1.6)
Solving linear and quadratic equations, and pairs of simultaneous equations
learningObjectives: Decide whether a discontinuity can be removed by checking whether the limit at that point exists
Remove a discontinuity by defining or redefining the function value to equal the limit
Write the condition that makes a piecewise function continuous at a boundary
Solve for one or two parameters that make a piecewise function continuous, or show that no value works
resources.calculatorNote: Practise every example here without a calculator. Give exact values (fractions, not decimals).
keyPoints: A discontinuity at x = c can be removed only if lim (x → c) f(x) exists as a finite number.
To remove it, define (or redefine) f(c) to be that limit. Jumps and vertical asymptotes cannot be removed this way.
A piecewise function is continuous at a boundary c when the left expression at c, the right expression at c and f(c) are all equal.
One unknown parameter needs one equation; two unknowns need two equations, usually one from each boundary.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 1.13 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: Why can I not remove a jump by choosing a better value of f(c)?
faqs.answer: At a jump the left-hand and right-hand limits are different numbers. One value of f(c) cannot equal both, so the limit does not exist and no choice of f(c) makes f continuous.

faqs.question: Do I need to worry about which piece contains the boundary point?
faqs.answer: Yes. The piece with ≤ or ≥ at the boundary gives f(c). For continuity all three values must agree, so in practice you set the two expressions equal at c, and f(c) then matches automatically.

resources.title: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes: Study Guide (Calculus AB 1.14)
resources.description: Learn what it means for a limit to be infinite, how to find one-sided infinite limits with a sign check, and how to use them to justify a vertical asymptote.
prerequisites: One-sided limits and the ways a limit can fail to exist (Topics 1.2 to 1.4)
Factoring and cancelling in 0/0 limits (Topic 1.6)
Types of discontinuity: removable, jump and vertical asymptote (Topic 1.10)
Graphs of ln x, eˣ and tan x
learningObjectives: Explain what it means to write that a limit equals +∞ or −∞, and why such a limit still does not exist as a number
Find one-sided infinite limits by checking the sign of the numerator and the denominator near the point
Use a one-sided infinite limit to justify that a line x = a is a vertical asymptote
Tell a hole from a vertical asymptote in a rational function by cancelling common factors first
Describe unbounded behaviour near a point from a formula, a table or a graph
resources.calculatorNote: Practise every limit here without a calculator. A table of values can support a conclusion; it does not prove one.
keyPoints: Writing lim (x → a) f(x) = ∞ means f(x) grows without bound as x gets close to a. It describes how the limit fails to exist; ∞ is not a number.
The line x = a is a vertical asymptote of f if at least one one-sided limit at a is +∞ or −∞.
Substitution giving a nonzero number over 0 signals an infinite limit. Check the sign of the bottom on each side to decide +∞ or −∞.
A zero of the denominator gives a hole, not an asymptote, if the factor cancels. Always simplify first.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 1.14 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: If I write lim (x → 2) f(x) = ∞, does the limit exist?
faqs.answer: No. The limit does not exist as a real number. Writing = ∞ gives extra information: it says why it fails to exist (the values grow without bound and are all positive).

faqs.question: Does a vertical asymptote need both one-sided limits to be infinite?
faqs.answer: No. One infinite one-sided limit is enough. For example, e^(1/x) → +∞ as x → 0 from the right but → 0 from the left, and x = 0 is still a vertical asymptote.

resources.title: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes: Study Guide (Calculus AB 1.15)
resources.description: Learn what a limit as x → ∞ means, how it describes end behaviour and horizontal asymptotes, and how to compare how fast functions grow using limits.
prerequisites: Limit notation and one-sided limits (Topics 1.2 to 1.4)
Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes (Topic 1.14)
The squeeze theorem (Topic 1.8)
Degree and leading coefficient of a polynomial; √(x²) = |x|
learningObjectives: Explain what lim (x → ∞) f(x) = L and lim (x → −∞) f(x) = L mean, using values far from zero
Use limits at infinity to describe the end behaviour of a function and to find its horizontal asymptotes
Find limits at infinity of rational functions and of expressions with square roots by dividing by a suitable power of x
Move between a limit statement, a table, a graph and a formula when describing end behaviour
Compare how fast two functions grow by finding the limit of their ratio
resources.calculatorNote: Practise every limit here without a calculator. A table of large x values is a check, not a method.
keyPoints: lim (x → ∞) f(x) = L means f(x) gets as close to L as you like once x is large enough. It describes end behaviour.
The line y = L is a horizontal asymptote if f(x) → L as x → ∞ or as x → −∞. A graph has at most two, one at each end.
Rational functions: divide top and bottom by the highest power of x in the denominator. Compare degrees to predict the answer.
To compare growth, find lim (x → ∞) f(x)/g(x). A limit of 0 means g grows faster; ∞ means f grows faster.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 1.15 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: Can a graph cross its horizontal asymptote?
faqs.answer: Yes. A horizontal asymptote only describes what happens far to the left or far to the right. In the middle, the graph can cross it, even many times.

faqs.question: Is ∞ a number I can substitute?
faqs.answer: No. x → ∞ means x grows without bound. You never put ∞ into a formula. You rewrite the expression so that the terms that shrink to 0 are easy to see.

resources.title: Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem: Study Guide (Calculus AB 1.16)
resources.description: Learn what the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees, why continuity on a closed interval matters, and how to write a full justification from a formula, table or graph.
prerequisites: Continuity at a point and on an interval (Topics 1.11 and 1.12)
Which familiar functions are continuous on their domains: polynomials, rational, root, exponential, log and trig functions
Reading values from a table or a graph
learningObjectives: State the Intermediate Value Theorem with both of its conditions and its conclusion
Check the conditions for a function given by a formula, a piecewise definition, a table or a graph
Use the theorem to show that an equation has a solution in a given interval, and to give a lower bound on the number of solutions
Explain what the theorem does not tell you: where the value occurs, how many times, or anything when a condition fails
