The greatest or least amount occurs where the net rate changes sign or at an endpoint. Compare all candidates.
Every interpretation needs three things: what quantity, over which interval, and in which units.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 8.3 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: How do I know whether to integrate or differentiate?
faqs.answer: Look at what you are given. If you have a rate and want an amount or a change in amount, integrate. If you have an amount and want how fast it changes, differentiate.

faqs.question: What is the difference between net change and total change?
faqs.answer: Net change, ∫ (a to b) r(t) dt, lets increases and decreases cancel. Total change, ∫ (a to b) |r(t)| dt, adds up every increase and every decrease as positive amounts.

This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 8.4 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: What if my answer comes out negative?
faqs.answer: If one curve stays on top between your limits, you subtracted in the wrong order (bottom minus top). Check which curve is higher with a test point between the limits; the area is the positive value. If the curves cross between your limits, split the integral there (Topic 8.6).

faqs.question: Do I need to split the integral where a curve crosses the x-axis?
faqs.answer: No. For the area between two curves only the difference top − bottom matters. You split only where the curves cross each other or where a boundary changes formula.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 8.5 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: How do I know whether to use dx or dy?
faqs.answer: Sketch the region. If every vertical line crosses it from one curve to one other curve, dx is fine. If every horizontal line crosses it from one curve to one other curve, dy is fine. If only one of these is true, use that one.

faqs.question: Is right minus left the same as top minus bottom turned sideways?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each horizontal strip has length (larger x) − (smaller x), so the right curve comes first. A negative answer means you subtracted in the wrong order.

resources.description: Learn how to find the area between curves that cross several times: locate every intersection, split the integral where the top curve changes, or integrate the absolute difference.
prerequisites: Area between curves with vertical strips (Topic 8.4) and horizontal strips (Topic 8.5)
Evaluating definite integrals with antiderivatives and with a calculator
Solving cubic equations by factoring; finding intersections on a graphing calculator
Properties of definite integrals, including splitting at an interior point (Topic 6.6)
learningObjectives: Find every intersection of two curves on an interval and decide which curve is on top between each pair
Write the area as a sum of definite integrals, one for each piece of the region
Write the area as one integral of the absolute value of the difference, and evaluate it with a calculator
Explain why the integral of f − g over the whole interval is a net (signed) value, not the area
Read the information needed for an area from graphs, given integral values or tables
resources.calculatorNote: Worked examples 1 and 3 use no calculator. Worked example 2 is calculator-active: use radians, store unrounded intersection values and give the area to three decimal places.
keyPoints: When curves cross inside the interval, the top curve changes. Split the integral at every crossing and use top − bottom on each piece.
Equivalently, Area = ∫ (a to b) |f(x) − g(x)| dx. On a calculator this one integral does all the splitting for you.
∫ (a to b) [f(x) − g(x)] dx without the absolute value is a net value: pieces where g is on top count as negative and cancel.
Find every intersection first. Missing one gives the wrong area.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 8.6 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: Should I split the integral or use the absolute value?
faqs.answer: Without a calculator, split: you cannot antidifferentiate |f − g| directly. With a calculator, ∫ |f(x) − g(x)| dx is quicker, but you still need the intersection values if they are the limits of the region.

faqs.question: Is |∫ (f − g) dx| the same as ∫ |f − g| dx?
faqs.answer: No. The first takes the absolute value after the pieces have cancelled. The second makes every piece positive before adding. Only the second gives the area.

resources.title: Volumes with Cross Sections: Squares and Rectangles: Study Guide (Calculus AB 8.7)
resources.description: Learn how slicing a solid into thin square or rectangular slabs turns its volume into a definite integral of a cross-sectional area, for slices across x or across y.
prerequisites: The definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums (Topic 6.3)
Evaluating definite integrals with antiderivatives and with a calculator (Topics 6.7 to 6.9)
Area between curves with vertical and horizontal strips (Topics 8.4 to 8.6)
Area of a square (side²) and of a rectangle (base × height)
learningObjectives: Explain why the volume of a solid with known cross sections is the integral of the cross-sectional area A(x) or A(y)
Find the length of the segment that a cross section stands on, as top minus bottom or right minus left
Write A(x) or A(y) for square cross sections and for rectangular cross sections whose height is described in words
Choose dx or dy from the direction of the slices, set the limits, and evaluate the volume exactly or with a calculator
resources.calculatorNote: Worked examples 1 and 2 use no calculator. Worked example 3 is calculator-active: store the intersection value unrounded and give the volume to three decimal places.
keyPoints: Volume = ∫ (a to b) A(x) dx, where A(x) is the area of the cross section at x. Add up thin slabs, each with volume about A(x) Δx.
The cross section stands on a segment in the base. Its length s is top − bottom (slices across x) or right − left (slices across y).
Square cross sections: A = s². Rectangles: A = s × (height), where the question tells you the height.
Slices perpendicular to the x-axis mean dx and x-limits; slices perpendicular to the y-axis mean dy and y-limits.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 8.7 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: Do I need π for square cross sections?
faqs.answer: No. π appears only when the cross sections are circles or parts of circles (Topic 8.8 and the disc method in Topic 8.9). A square slice has area s².

faqs.question: Can I square the top function and the bottom function separately?
faqs.answer: No. Find the side first, s = top − bottom, then square the whole difference. (f − g)² is not f² − g².

keyPoints: V = ∫ A dx (or dy). Find s, write A in terms of s, integrate.

Shared content for Calculus AB and Calculus BC.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Volumes with Cross Sections: Triangles and Semicircles: Study Guide (Calculus AB 8.8)
resources.description: Learn the area formulas for triangular and semicircular cross sections in terms of the side s, and use them in V = ∫ A dx to find volumes of solids built on a base region.
prerequisites: Volumes with square and rectangular cross sections, V = ∫ A(x) dx (Topic 8.7)
Area between curves with vertical and horizontal strips (Topics 8.4 to 8.6)
Pythagoras' theorem; areas of a triangle and a circle
learningObjectives: Derive the area of an equilateral triangle, an isosceles right triangle (leg or hypotenuse in the base) and a semicircle in terms of the side s that lies in the base
Write and evaluate volume integrals for solids with triangular and semicircular cross sections, perpendicular to the x-axis or the y-axis
Find volumes for other cross sections described by a shape or by a given area function
Use a calculator to evaluate a cross-section volume when the limits or the integral need one
resources.calculatorNote: Worked examples 1 and 2 use no calculator. Worked example 3 is calculator-active: store the intersection value unrounded and give the volume to three decimal places.
keyPoints: The method is the same as Topic 8.7: V = ∫ A dx (or dy). Only the area formula changes.
Equilateral triangle on side s: A = (√3/4)s². Isosceles right triangle, leg in base: A = s²/2. Hypotenuse in base: A = s²/4.
Semicircle with its diameter in the base: radius s/2, so A = (1/2)π(s/2)² = (π/8)s².
Every formula is a constant times s², so the constant comes out of the integral: V = c ∫ s² dx.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 8.8 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise the area formulas?
faqs.answer: It helps, but you should also be able to derive each one in a line from the triangle and circle area formulas. Deriving it on paper also shows the reader where your constant came from.

faqs.question: What does 'leg in the base' versus 'hypotenuse in the base' change?
faqs.answer: Only the area. With a leg of length s in the base, A = s²/2. With the hypotenuse of length s in the base, each leg is s/√2, so A = s²/4: half as much.

resources.title: Volume with the Disc Method: Revolving Around the x- or y-Axis: Study Guide (Calculus AB 8.9)
resources.description: Learn why spinning a region about the x- or y-axis gives circular slices, how to write the disc integral π∫r² with the right variable and limits, and how to evaluate it with and without a calculator.
prerequisites: Volumes from known cross sections, V = ∫ A(x) dx (Topics 8.7 and 8.8)
Evaluating definite integrals with antiderivatives and with a calculator (Unit 6)

learningObjectives: Explain why a region spun about the x-axis or y-axis has circular cross sections, and why each slice's area is π times the radius squared
Write the disc-method integral for a solid of revolution about the x-axis (in x) or the y-axis (in y), with correct radius, limits and differential
Evaluate disc-method volumes exactly, or with a graphing calculator when the integral has no simple antiderivative
Recognise when the disc method applies (the region touches the axis all the way along) and check an answer against a simple cylinder
resources.calculatorNote: Worked examples 1 and 2 use no calculator. Worked example 3 is calculator-active: use radians, store unrounded values and give the volume to three decimal places.
keyPoints: Spinning a region about an axis it touches makes a solid whose slices, cut at right angles to the axis, are circular discs.
About the x-axis: V = π ∫ (a to b) [f(x)]² dx. About the y-axis: V = π ∫ (c to d) [g(y)]² dy, where x = g(y) describes the curve.
The radius is the distance from the axis to the curve. Square the radius before you integrate, and keep the π.
Slice at right angles to the axis: x-axis means dx and x-limits; y-axis means dy and y-limits.
This topic is shared by Calculus AB and Calculus BC students.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Topic 8.9 is common content, so the same page serves AB and BC students.

faqs.question: Do I need the shell method?
faqs.answer: No. Every volume of revolution in this course can be set up with discs (and, from Topic 8.11, washers). The shell method is not part of the course framework.

faqs.question: What if the curve is below the x-axis?
faqs.answer: The radius is a distance, so it is |f(x)|. Because you square it, π[f(x)]² is still correct. The volume is always positive.

resources.title: Notation, Justification and Communication: Exam Skills Guide (Calculus AB and BC)
resources.description: How to write calculus answers that earn credit: clear notation, theorem conditions, sign-chart justifications, units in context, and calculator set-ups.
prerequisites: You have studied most of the course, or at least Units 1 to 5
You can find derivatives and definite integrals with and without a graphing calculator
learningObjectives: Write limits, derivatives, integrals and their units in notation a marker can follow line by line
Check and state the conditions of the Intermediate Value, Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems before using them
Turn a sign chart or a second-derivative value into a written justification that names the function and the reason
Interpret a derivative, an integral or an approximation in context, with the time, the units and the direction of change
Show the set-up a calculator-active answer needs and the steps a calculator-free answer needs
resources.calculatorNote: Worked example 4 needs a graphing calculator; everything else is calculator-free. Store unrounded values and give calculator answers to three decimal places unless a question says otherwise.
keyPoints: A correct number with no supporting work can lose credit: write the expression, then the value.
Before you use a theorem, name it and state that its conditions hold for this function on this interval.
A sign chart is evidence, not a justification. Write a sentence: name the function, the x-value and the sign change.
In context, say what is changing, at what time, in which direction, and in which units.
Shared guide for Calculus AB and Calculus BC students; one short section is BC only and is labelled.

faqs.question: Is this guide for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. Everything is shared content except one short section on series, parametric and polar notation, which is labelled BC only.

faqs.question: Will I lose credit for writing dy/dx instead of f′(x)?
faqs.answer: Either notation is fine if it is correct and clear. What costs credit is notation that is wrong, such as dropping the limit symbol or the differential, or writing an equals sign between things that are not equal.

faqs.question: How many decimal places should I give?
faqs.answer: Unless the question says otherwise, give calculator answers correct to three decimal places, and keep full accuracy in the calculator until the final step.

resources.title: Task Verbs and Free-Response Technique: Exam Skills Guide (Calculus AB and BC)
resources.description: What each free-response task verb asks you to do, how much to write, how to plan your time and show work, and what earns or loses credit, with original worked examples.
prerequisites: You have studied most of the course, at least Units 1 to 6
You can use a graphing calculator to evaluate a definite integral and a derivative at a point
learningObjectives: Say what each task verb in a free-response question requires and how much to write for it
Break a multi-part question into its stem, shared information and separate tasks
Show the set-up for every calculation, including calculator results, and round to three decimal places
Write justifications that name a definition, theorem or test, check its conditions and draw the conclusion
Plan your time across the calculator and no-calculator parts of the free-response section
resources.calculatorNote: Worked example 2 is a calculator question; everything else is done by hand. Calculator answers are given to three decimal places, and angles are in radians.
keyPoints: The task verb tells you what to hand in: a value, an expression, a reason, a sentence in context, or a picture.
Every calculation needs its set-up on the page. A bare calculator number can lose the point even when it is right.
A justification names the theorem or test, checks that it applies, and states the conclusion about the function in the question.
Give decimal answers to three places, and store unrounded values in your calculator.
Calculus AB and Calculus BC use the same verbs; BC adds series, parametric, polar and vector content to the same habits.

faqs.question: Is this page for Calculus AB or Calculus BC?
faqs.answer: Both. The free-response section has the same structure and the same task verbs in both courses. Where the BC exam differs, this page says so.

faqs.question: Do I lose credit for writing more than the question asks?
faqs.answer: Extra correct work does not hurt, but extra wrong statements can. If you add a reason that is false, a marker may not be able to award the point. Write what the verb asks for, clearly, and stop.

faqs.question: What if I cannot answer part (a) but need its value in part (b)?
faqs.answer: Write down a value you will use, say it is your value from part (a) or an assumed value, and carry on. A marker can only credit a method they can see.

resources.title: Defining Convergent and Divergent Infinite Series: Study Guide (Calculus BC 10.1)
resources.description: Learn what an infinite series is, how partial sums are built, and how the limit of the partial sums decides whether a series converges or diverges, with telescoping examples.
prerequisites: Limits at infinity, including limits of rational functions (Topic 1.15)
Sigma (summation) notation
Partial fractions (Topic 6.12), for splitting terms such as 2/((n + 1)(n + 3))
Laws of logarithms, such as ln a − ln b = ln(a/b)
learningObjectives: Tell the difference between a sequence of terms, a series and its sequence of partial sums
Write and evaluate the nth partial sum of a series
Decide whether a series converges or diverges by finding the limit of its partial sums, and state the sum when it exists
Recover individual terms of a series from a formula for its partial sums
Explain why terms that approach 0, or a table of partial sums, do not on their own prove convergence
resources.calculatorNote: Everything on this page is done by hand. A calculator can list partial sums as evidence, but the decision must come from the limit of the partial sums.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
The nth partial sum Sₙ is the sum of the first n terms of the series.
A series converges to S exactly when the sequence of partial sums S₁, S₂, S₃, … has the limit S. Otherwise it diverges.
Terms and partial sums are different sequences: aₙ → 0 does not guarantee that the series converges.
From partial sums you can get the terms back: a₁ = S₁ and aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 2.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Infinite series are BC-only content. Calculus AB ends with Unit 8, so AB students can skip all of Unit 10.

faqs.question: Is the sum of a convergent series really an exact number, not an approximation?
faqs.answer: Yes. By definition, the sum is the limit of the partial sums, and that limit is an exact number such as 5/6. Each partial sum is only an approximation to it.

faqs.question: If I add up the first 1,000 terms on a calculator and the total settles down, has the series converged?
faqs.answer: Not as a proof. A table of partial sums is evidence only. The series Σ ln((n + 1)/n) grows so slowly that it looks settled, yet it diverges. You need the limit of Sₙ or a convergence test.

If Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ aₙ meets the conditions of the alternating series test, then |S − Sₙ| ≤ aₙ₊₁: the error is at most the first term you left out.
Check the conditions first: terms positive in size, decreasing and approaching 0.
The sum S lies between two consecutive partial sums Sₙ and Sₙ₊₁.
The error has the same sign as the first omitted term, which tells you whether Sₙ is too big or too small.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. The alternating series error bound is BC-only content.

faqs.question: Is the bound the actual error?
faqs.answer: No. It is a guaranteed maximum. The actual error is usually smaller, often around half the bound.

faqs.question: Can I use this bound for any series?
faqs.answer: Only for an alternating series whose term sizes decrease to 0, which is exactly the setting of the alternating series test. For other approximations, such as many Taylor polynomials, you need a different tool (the Lagrange error bound, Topic 10.12).

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Taylor polynomials are BC-only content. AB students meet only the tangent line, which is the first-degree case.

faqs.question: What is a Maclaurin polynomial?
faqs.answer: A Taylor polynomial centred at x = 0. The formula is the same with a = 0, so the powers are simply x, x², x³, …

faqs.question: Is a third-degree polynomial the same as the first three nonzero terms?
faqs.answer: Not always. Degree counts the highest power. For sin x about 0 the third-degree polynomial is x − x³/6, which has only two nonzero terms. Read the question carefully.

|f(x) − Pₙ(x)| ≤ M · |x − a|ⁿ⁺¹ / (n + 1)!, where M is at least the largest value of |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| between a and x.
Use the (n + 1)th derivative, the next one after the polynomial stops.
The bound is a guarantee, not the actual error: the true error is usually smaller.
f(x) lies between Pₙ(x) − bound and Pₙ(x) + bound.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. The Lagrange error bound is BC-only content.

faqs.question: Does M have to be the exact maximum?
faqs.answer: No. Any number that is at least as big as |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(z)| for every z between a and x works. A bigger M gives a safe but weaker bound. A smaller one is not allowed.

faqs.question: Which bound should I use, Lagrange or alternating series?
faqs.answer: Use whichever the question asks for. If it does not say, the alternating series bound is often quicker when the terms of the Taylor series alternate in sign and decrease in size; Lagrange works for any function with the needed derivative bound.

Explain why a power series converges only at its centre, on an interval around the centre, or for every real x

resources.calculatorNote: Radius and interval work is done by hand: limits, inequalities and series tests. A calculator does not decide whether a series converges at an endpoint.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
A power series Σ aₙ(x − c)ⁿ converges only at x = c, or on an interval centred at c, or for every real x.
Use the ratio test on the whole term: the series converges when |x − c| < R, the radius of convergence.
The ratio test says nothing at x = c ± R. Test each endpoint separately with another test.
Differentiating or integrating term by term keeps the radius, but the endpoints can change, so test them again.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Power series are BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: Is the radius of convergence the length of the interval?
faqs.answer: No. The radius is the distance from the centre to each endpoint. The interval is 2R long.

faqs.question: Why can't I use the ratio test at the endpoints?
faqs.answer: At x = c ± R the ratio test limit is exactly 1, and a limit of 1 gives no conclusion. Use the p-series test, the alternating series test, the nth term test or a comparison instead.

resources.description: Build Taylor and Maclaurin series from derivatives, learn the series for eˣ, sin x, cos x and 1/(1 − x), and read derivatives and sums back from a series.
prerequisites: Taylor polynomials and the coefficient f⁽ⁿ⁾(c)/n! (Topic 10.11)

The Taylor series for f about c is Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(c)(x − c)ⁿ/n!. A Taylor polynomial is one of its partial sums. A Maclaurin series has c = 0.
Know four series: eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n!, sin x = Σ (−1)ⁿx^(2n+1)/(2n+1)!, cos x = Σ (−1)ⁿx^(2n)/(2n)! (all real x), and 1/(1 − x) = Σ xⁿ for −1 < x < 1.
Work backwards too: the coefficient of (x − c)ⁿ times n! is f⁽ⁿ⁾(c).
Give the general term when asked, and state where the series converges.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Taylor and Maclaurin series are BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a Taylor series and a Maclaurin series?
faqs.answer: A Maclaurin series is a Taylor series centred at x = 0. Every Maclaurin series is a Taylor series; a Taylor series about any other centre uses powers of (x − c).

faqs.question: Which series should I memorise?
faqs.answer: The series for eˣ, sin x, cos x and 1/(1 − x), with their intervals of convergence. Many other series in this unit are built from these four.

The main tools are: rewriting as a/(1 − r), substituting for x, multiplying by a power of x, and differentiating or integrating term by term.

faqs.answer: No. Power series are BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: Is a series built this way really the Taylor series of the function?
faqs.answer: Yes. If a power series has a positive radius of convergence and adds up to f(x) on that interval, it is the Taylor series of f there. So you can read f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) from its coefficients.

faqs.question: Do I always need the general term?
faqs.answer: Often a question asks for the first few nonzero terms and the general term. Give both when asked. The general term is also what you need for the ratio test and the endpoint checks.

prerequisites: The definition of a convergent series as the limit of its partial sums (Topic 10.1)

keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
A geometric series has a constant ratio r between each term and the one before it.
If |r| < 1, the series converges and its sum is (first term)/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 (and the first term is not 0), it diverges.
The nth partial sum is Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1, where a is the first term.
When the series does not start at n = 0, use the actual first term, not the coefficient in front.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Geometric series are BC-only content, like the rest of Unit 10.

faqs.question: Does a/(1 − r) work if the series starts at n = 1 or n = 2?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided a means the first term actually added. Work it out by substituting the starting index into the formula for the terms.

faqs.question: Is a series with r = −1 convergent, since its terms just switch sign?
faqs.answer: No. With r = −1 the partial sums alternate between a and 0, so they have no limit. A geometric series converges only when |r| < 1 (strictly).

faqs.question: If the terms go to 0, does the series converge?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Terms approaching 0 are needed for convergence but are not enough. Worked example 3 builds a series whose terms approach 0 while its partial sums grow without bound.

faqs.question: Is the nth term test the same as checking whether the sequence converges?
faqs.answer: No. The test looks at the limit of the terms aₙ. A sequence can converge (for example to 3/4) while the series built from it diverges.

faqs.question: Do I need to know the sum of a convergent p-series?

faqs.question: Is ∑ 1/2ⁿ a p-series?
faqs.answer: No. In a p-series the variable n is in the base and the power is fixed. In ∑ 1/2ⁿ the power is the variable, so it is a geometric series with ratio 1/2.

resources.description: Use the direct comparison test and the limit comparison test with p-series and geometric benchmarks, learn which comparisons give no conclusion, and write complete justifications.
prerequisites: Limits at infinity of rational and root expressions (Topic 1.15)
Geometric series (Topic 10.2)
The nth term test for divergence (Topic 10.3)
Harmonic series and p-series (Topic 10.5)
learningObjectives: State the direct comparison test and the limit comparison test with all their conditions
Choose a p-series or geometric benchmark by keeping the dominant terms
Use a direct comparison, with an inequality that holds for every n from some point on, to decide convergence
Use the limit comparison test, finding the limit of aₙ/bₙ and interpreting it
Recognise when a comparison gives no conclusion and switch to a better comparison or test
resources.calculatorNote: Comparison tests are a no-calculator skill. Limits are found by algebra, by dividing by the highest power.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
Both comparison tests need series with positive (or non-negative) terms.
Direct comparison: smaller than a convergent series converges; bigger than a divergent series diverges. The other two directions tell you nothing.
Limit comparison: if aₙ/bₙ → L with 0 < L < ∞, the two series both converge or both diverge.
Pick the benchmark bₙ by keeping only the dominant terms of the numerator and the denominator.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Series are BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: Which comparison test should I try first?
faqs.answer: If an easy inequality points the right way (for example a bounded sine on top, or dropping a positive term from the denominator of a convergent-looking series), use direct comparison. If the inequality points the wrong way or is messy, use limit comparison.

faqs.question: Can I use a comparison test on a series with negative terms?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Both tests are for series whose terms are positive (at least from some point on). For series with mixed signs you will use the alternating series test (Topic 10.7) or compare the absolute values (Topic 10.9).

resources.description: Learn the alternating series test: its two conditions, why the partial sums settle down, how to show terms decrease, and how to write a full justification.
prerequisites: Limits of sequences, including limits at infinity and L'Hospital's Rule (Topics 1.15 and 4.7)
Using the sign of a derivative to decide where a function decreases (Topic 5.3)
Partial sums and the meaning of convergence of a series (Topic 10.1)
The nth term test for divergence (Topic 10.3)
learningObjectives: Recognise an alternating series, including one written with cos(nπ)
State the two conditions of the alternating series test and check each one
Show that a sequence of terms is decreasing, from some point on, by algebra or by a derivative
Explain why the test can show convergence but never divergence
Write a complete justification that names the test and verifies its conditions
resources.calculatorNote: Series tests are no-calculator reasoning. A calculator can help you list a few terms to see a pattern, but it cannot prove that terms decrease or tend to 0.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
An alternating series has terms whose signs switch every time: (−1)ⁿ aₙ or (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ aₙ with every aₙ > 0.
Alternating series test: if aₙ decreases (at least from some n on) and lim aₙ = 0, the series converges.
The test can only show convergence. If a condition fails, it tells you nothing; try another test.
If lim aₙ ≠ 0, the series diverges by the nth term test, not by the alternating series test.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Infinite series, including the alternating series test, are BC-only content.

faqs.question: Do the terms have to decrease from the very first term?
faqs.answer: No. Changing or removing finitely many terms does not affect convergence, so it is enough that aₙ₊₁ ≤ aₙ for all n from some point on. Say where the decrease starts.

faqs.question: Does the alternating series test tell me the sum?
faqs.answer: No. It only tells you that the sum exists. Estimating the sum, and bounding the error, comes in Topic 10.10.

resources.title: Ratio Test for Convergence: Study Guide (Calculus BC 10.8)
resources.description: Learn the ratio test: where it comes from, how to simplify ratios with powers and factorials, what L < 1, L > 1 and L = 1 mean, and when to pick another test.
prerequisites: Geometric series and when they converge (Topic 10.2)
The nth term test for divergence (Topic 10.3)
Harmonic series and p-series (Topic 10.5)
Comparison and limit comparison tests (Topic 10.6)
Limits at infinity of rational expressions (Topic 1.15)
learningObjectives: State the ratio test and the meaning of each possible value of the limit L
Simplify aₙ₊₁/aₙ when the terms contain powers such as 3ⁿ and factorials such as n!
Use the ratio test to decide whether a series of numbers converges or diverges, and justify the conclusion
Recognise when the ratio test gives no conclusion and choose another test
Explain the link between the ratio test and geometric series
resources.calculatorNote: Ratio-test limits are found by algebra. A calculator can list a few ratios to suggest the limit, but the justification must use the exact limit.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
Find L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|. If L < 1 the series converges; if L > 1 (or L = ∞) it diverges; if L = 1 the test gives no conclusion.
The ratio test works best when terms contain powers like 5ⁿ or factorials like n!.
Use (n + 1)! = (n + 1) · n! to cancel factorials.
For terms built only from powers of n, such as 1/n² or n/(n³ + 1), L = 1 always: use a p-series or comparison test instead.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Infinite series, including the ratio test, are BC-only content.

faqs.question: Why are there absolute value bars in the ratio test?
faqs.answer: They let the test handle terms with any signs. When L < 1, the series of absolute values converges, which is a stronger result called absolute convergence (Topic 10.9). For series with positive terms, the bars change nothing.

faqs.question: What should I do when L = 1?
faqs.answer: Use a different test. Series with L = 1 can converge (Σ 1/n²) or diverge (Σ 1/n), so the ratio test says nothing about them.

resources.description: Learn to classify a series as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent or divergent, why absolute convergence implies convergence, and why it lets you reorder terms safely.
prerequisites: The nth term test for divergence (Topic 10.3)
The integral test, p-series and the harmonic series (Topics 10.4 and 10.5)
The comparison and limit comparison tests (Topic 10.6)
The alternating series test (Topic 10.7) and the ratio test (Topic 10.8)
learningObjectives: Define absolute convergence, conditional convergence and divergence in terms of Σ aₙ and Σ |aₙ|
Classify a series by testing Σ |aₙ| first and then, if needed, Σ aₙ itself

Use absolute convergence to handle series whose signs do not simply alternate
Explain why only an absolutely convergent series can be regrouped or reordered without changing its sum
resources.calculatorNote: Classifying a series is a no-calculator skill. Show each test and check its conditions in writing; a calculator adds nothing to the justification.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
Absolutely convergent: Σ |aₙ| converges. Conditionally convergent: Σ aₙ converges but Σ |aₙ| diverges. Otherwise the series diverges.
If Σ |aₙ| converges, then Σ aₙ converges. The reverse is false.
Test Σ |aₙ| first. If it diverges, check Σ aₙ itself, usually with the alternating series test.
Only an absolutely convergent series keeps the same sum when its terms are regrouped or reordered.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Absolute and conditional convergence are BC-only content, like the rest of the series tests in Unit 10.

faqs.question: If Σ |aₙ| diverges, does Σ aₙ diverge?
faqs.answer: Not always. Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n converges even though Σ 1/n diverges. When Σ |aₙ| diverges you must test Σ aₙ separately.

faqs.question: Which tests can I use on Σ |aₙ|?
faqs.answer: Any test for series of positive terms that you have learned: p-series, geometric series, comparison, limit comparison, integral and ratio tests.

faqs.answer: No. Integration by parts is BC-only content. AB students can skip this page; BC students need it for indefinite and definite integrals.

faqs.question: Why don't I add + C when I find v?
faqs.answer: Any constant you add to v cancels out in uv − ∫v du, so it is safe to leave it out. Add a single + C at the very end of an indefinite integral.

faqs.question: Is the tabular method required?
faqs.answer: No. It is an optional shortcut for repeated integration by parts when one factor differentiates to zero. The ordinary formula always works.

resources.title: Approximating Solutions Using Euler’s Method: Study Guide (Calculus BC 7.5)
resources.description: Build Euler’s method from tangent lines, run it in a clear table, see how step size changes accuracy, and use concavity to decide whether an estimate is too high or too low.
prerequisites: Tangent lines and local linear approximation (Topic 4.6)
Writing and reading differential equations (Topic 7.1)
Verifying a solution by differentiating (Topic 7.2)
Slope fields and particular solutions (Topics 7.3 and 7.4)
Second derivatives and concavity (Unit 5)
learningObjectives: Explain Euler’s method as a chain of short tangent-line steps that follow a slope field
Carry out Euler’s method by hand for a given step size and number of steps, recording each step in a table
Use a negative step to approximate a value to the left of the starting point
Describe how a smaller step size usually changes the size of the error
Use the sign of the second derivative to decide whether an Euler estimate is an overestimate or an underestimate
Interpret an Euler estimate in context, with units
resources.calculatorNote: Worked example 1 and the backward step are no-calculator. Worked example 2 allows a calculator for square roots; keep full calculator values between steps and round only the final answer to 3 decimal places.
keyPoints: BC only: Euler’s method is not part of Calculus AB.
Euler’s method approximates a solution by taking short tangent-line steps: new y = old y + (step size) × (slope at the old point).
Always use the slope at the point you are stepping from, then update both x and y before the next step.
A smaller step size usually gives a better estimate, but Euler’s method is still an approximation.
If the solutions are concave up where the steps run, Euler underestimates; if concave down, it overestimates.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need Euler’s method?
faqs.answer: No. Topic 7.5 is BC-only. AB students can skip this page; BC students may be asked to carry out the method and to judge the estimate.

faqs.question: Do I have to memorise a formula?
faqs.answer: It helps to know yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h · f(xₙ, yₙ), but it is better to understand each step as a tangent-line approximation. Then you can rebuild the formula whenever you need it.

faqs.question: How should I round?
faqs.answer: Keep exact values or full calculator values from step to step. Round only the final answer, usually to 3 decimal places when a calculator is allowed.

resources.title: Logistic Models with Differential Equations: Study Guide (Calculus BC 7.9)
resources.description: Write a logistic differential equation from a sentence, then read it without solving: the carrying capacity, the long-run limit, and the value where growth is fastest.
prerequisites: Writing differential equations from verbal descriptions (Topic 7.1)
Reasoning with slope fields and constant solutions (Topic 7.4)
Exponential models, dy/dt = ky (Topic 7.8)
Maximum of a quadratic and concavity from the second derivative (Unit 5)
learningObjectives: Turn a statement about joint proportionality into the logistic equation dy/dt = ky(a − y), and recognise the equation in other algebraic forms
Read the carrying capacity and the constant solutions straight from the equation
Use the initial condition to decide whether a solution rises, falls or stays constant, and find its limit as t → ∞
Find the value of the quantity when it is changing fastest, and the greatest rate
Use the second derivative to describe the concavity of a logistic solution
Explain the meaning of each constant and each answer in context, with units
resources.calculatorNote: Everything except the optional solution formula is done by hand. Where a calculator is used, give final decimals to 3 decimal places.
keyPoints: BC only: logistic models are not part of Calculus AB.
Logistic growth: the rate is jointly proportional to y and to (a − y), so dy/dt = ky(a − y) with k > 0. The number a is the carrying capacity.
For any starting value y(0) > 0, the solution tends to a as t → ∞. If y(0) = 0 it stays at 0.
dy/dt is largest when y = a/2, halfway to the carrying capacity. That is also where the solution curve changes concavity.
You can answer all of these from the equation and the initial condition, without solving it.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need logistic models?
faqs.answer: No. Topic 7.9 is BC-only. AB students stop at exponential models (Topic 7.8).

faqs.question: Do I need to solve the logistic equation?
faqs.answer: Not for this topic. You must be able to interpret the equation and the initial condition: the limit, the value where growth is fastest and the shape of the graph. The solution formula is shown here only as optional background.

faqs.question: What if the equation is written as dP/dt = 0.3P − 0.0006P²?
faqs.answer: Factor it: 0.0006P(500 − P). Now it is in the form kP(a − P), so the carrying capacity is 500.

resources.title: The Arc Length of a Smooth, Planar Curve and Distance Traveled: Revision Notes (Calculus BC 8.13)
resources.description: One-page recap of arc length: where the integral comes from, the dx and dy forms, the smoothness condition, distance traveled along a path, and the mistakes that cost marks.
learningObjectives: Recall the arc length integral for y = f(x) and for x = g(y), with its condition
Spot the common errors in arc length setups before making them
resources.calculatorNote: Set up by hand; evaluate with a graphing calculator unless 1 + (f′)² simplifies. Give decimals to 3 decimal places.
keyPoints: BC only.
L = ∫ from a to b of √(1 + (f′(x))²) dx, for f′ continuous on [a, b].
Check: L ≥ b − a and L ≥ the straight-line distance between the end points.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: The Arc Length of a Smooth, Planar Curve and Distance Traveled: Study Guide (Calculus BC 8.13)
resources.description: Build the arc length integral from straight-line pieces, use it for curves y = f(x) and x = g(y), and find the distance traveled along a curved path, by hand and with a calculator.
prerequisites: The distance formula and Pythagoras' theorem
Derivatives, including the chain rule (Units 2 and 3)
The Mean Value Theorem (Topic 5.1)
Riemann sums and the definite integral (Topics 6.2 to 6.6)
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and substitution (Topics 6.7 and 6.9)
learningObjectives: Explain how the arc length integral comes from adding the lengths of many short straight segments
Write a definite integral for the length of a smooth curve y = f(x) on an interval, or x = g(y) on a y-interval
Find an exact arc length by hand when 1 + (f′(x))² simplifies to something you can integrate
Use a graphing calculator to evaluate an arc length integral and round correctly
Use arc length to find the distance traveled along a curved path, and check the answer against the straight-line distance
resources.calculatorNote: Set up every arc length integral by hand. Most of them cannot be evaluated exactly, so use a graphing calculator for the value and give decimals to 3 decimal places. By-hand questions use functions chosen so that 1 + (f′(x))² simplifies.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
For a smooth curve y = f(x) from x = a to x = b, the length is L = ∫ from a to b of √(1 + (f′(x))²) dx.
Smooth means f′ is continuous on [a, b]. Split the interval at any corner.
The integrand is at least 1, so the length is at least b − a, and never less than the straight-line distance between the end points.
The distance traveled by a point moving along the curve from one end to the other, without turning back, is the arc length.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Arc length is BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: Will I have to find arc lengths without a calculator?
faqs.answer: Only for specially chosen curves where 1 + (f′(x))² becomes a perfect square or a simple expression. Most arc length integrals have no elementary antiderivative, so you set them up by hand and evaluate them with a calculator.

faqs.question: Is arc length the same as the total distance from Topic 8.2?
faqs.answer: Both are distances traveled, but for different motions. Topic 8.2 integrates speed |v(t)| for motion along a straight line. Arc length measures the length of a curved path in the plane, using the slope f′(x).

resources.title: Defining and Differentiating Parametric Equations: Study Guide (Calculus BC 9.1)
resources.description: What a parametric curve is, how to find dy/dx from dx/dt and dy/dt, and how to use it for tangent lines, horizontal and vertical tangents, and a path in context.
prerequisites: Derivatives of powers, sin x, cos x, eˣ and ln x (Topics 2.5–2.7)
The chain rule (Topic 3.1)
Writing the equation of a tangent line from a point and a slope (Topics 2.1 and 4.6)
learningObjectives: Describe a curve given by x = f(t) and y = g(t), including the points it passes through and its direction of travel
Find dy/dx for a parametric curve by dividing dy/dt by dx/dt, and explain why this works using the chain rule
Find the slope and the equation of a tangent line at a given value of t or at a given point on the curve
Locate horizontal and vertical tangents, and recognise when dx/dt and dy/dt are both zero and the formula gives no answer

resources.calculatorNote: Derivatives are found by hand: this is a no-calculator skill. Where a calculator is allowed, you may use it to evaluate a slope at a decimal value of t or to solve dx/dt = 0 or dy/dt = 0 numerically. Angles are in radians.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
A parametric curve gives both coordinates as functions of a third variable: x = f(t), y = g(t).
dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0. The result is the slope of the tangent line to the curve.
Horizontal tangent: dy/dt = 0 and dx/dt ≠ 0. Vertical tangent: dx/dt = 0 and dy/dt ≠ 0.
dy/dx is usually a function of t, so find the value of t first when you are given a point (x, y).

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Parametric equations are BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: Is dy/dx the same as the velocity?
faqs.answer: No. dy/dx is the slope of the path. Velocity needs both dx/dt and dy/dt, and is covered in Topics 9.4 to 9.6.

faqs.question: What if dx/dt and dy/dt are both 0?
faqs.answer: Then dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) is the undefined form 0/0, so the formula alone tells you nothing about the tangent there. You need more work, such as simplifying first or looking at the graph.

resources.title: Second Derivatives of Parametric Equations: Study Guide (Calculus BC 9.2)
resources.description: How to find d²y/dx² for a parametric curve by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t and dividing by dx/dt, and how to use it for concavity and tangent-line estimates.
prerequisites: dy/dx for a parametric curve (Topic 9.1)
The quotient rule and the chain rule (Topics 2.9 and 3.1)
Second derivatives and concavity (Topics 3.6 and 5.6)
Tangent-line approximation (Topic 4.6)
learningObjectives: Explain why d²y/dx² is not d²y/dt² divided by d²x/dt² for a parametric curve
Find d²y/dx² by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t and dividing by dx/dt
Evaluate d²y/dx² at a value of t and state the concavity of the curve there
Find the values of t for which a parametric curve is concave up or concave down, taking the sign of dx/dt into account
Decide whether a tangent-line approximation to a parametric curve is an overestimate or an underestimate
resources.calculatorNote: Second derivatives are found by hand: this is a no-calculator skill. Where a calculator is allowed, you may use it to evaluate expressions at a decimal value of t, but show the setup. Angles are in radians.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
d²y/dx² = [d/dt (dy/dx)] ÷ (dx/dt). Differentiate the slope with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt again.
d²y/dx² is not (d²y/dt²) ÷ (d²x/dt²). That shortcut gives wrong answers.
d²y/dx² > 0 means concave up; d²y/dx² < 0 means concave down. When dx/dt < 0, the sign of d/dt (dy/dx) is the opposite of the concavity.
Concave down: the tangent line lies above the curve nearby, so a tangent-line estimate is too big. Concave up: too small.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Parametric second derivatives are BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: Why do I divide by dx/dt a second time?
faqs.answer: dy/dx is a function of t, but d²y/dx² asks how it changes with x. The chain rule converts a t-derivative into an x-derivative by dividing by dx/dt, exactly as in Topic 9.1.

faqs.question: Do I need the formula (x′y″ − y′x″)/(x′)³?
faqs.answer: No. It is an optional check that gives the same answer. The method of differentiating dy/dx and dividing by dx/dt always works and is easier to remember.

resources.title: Finding Arc Lengths of Curves Given by Parametric Equations: Study Guide (Calculus BC 9.3)
resources.description: Build the parametric arc length integral from Pythagoras, check when it applies, and use it for exact lengths by hand and calculator lengths in context.
prerequisites: Derivatives of parametric equations, dx/dt and dy/dt (Topic 9.1)

Length = ∫ from a to b of √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt, for a smooth curve traced exactly once for a ≤ t ≤ b.
The formula is Pythagoras on tiny pieces of the curve, added up by a definite integral.
If the curve is traced more than once, the integral counts the repeated part again.
An arc length is never shorter than the straight-line distance between its end points. Use that as a check.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Parametric arc length is BC-only content, like the rest of Unit 9.

faqs.question: Do I need to find an antiderivative?
faqs.answer: Only when the expression under the square root simplifies to a perfect square. Most of the time you set up the integral and evaluate it with a calculator.

faqs.question: How is this different from the arc length formula in Topic 8.13?
faqs.answer: It is the same idea. If you take x = t and y = f(t), the parametric formula becomes the Topic 8.13 formula ∫ √(1 + (f′(x))²) dx.

Tell apart the vector r″(t) and the scalar d²y/dx²
resources.calculatorNote: Derivatives are found by hand; this is a no-calculator skill. A calculator may be used to give decimal values where allowed (3 decimal places, radian mode).
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
A vector-valued function r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩ takes a number t and returns a vector.
Differentiate each component: r′(t) = ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ and r″(t) = ⟨x″(t), y″(t)⟩.
r′(t) points along the tangent to the curve, in the direction of increasing t; the tangent slope is y′(t)/x′(t).
r″(t) is a vector. It is not the same thing as d²y/dx².

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Vector-valued functions are BC-only content, like the rest of Unit 9.

faqs.question: Is ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩ the same as x(t) i + y(t) j?
faqs.answer: Yes. They are two notations for the same vector. Use whichever the question uses.

faqs.question: Is a vector-valued function different from a pair of parametric equations?
faqs.answer: It describes the same curve. The vector form packs the two equations into one object, so you can talk about the position vector and its derivative as single arrows.

Each component gets its own constant. Find each one from the initial condition.
Position at a new time = position at a known time + the definite integral of velocity between the two times.
From acceleration, integrate twice: use the starting velocity first, then the starting position.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Vector-valued functions are BC-only content. AB students meet the same idea for motion along a line in Topic 8.2.

faqs.question: Is a parametric problem different from a vector problem?
faqs.answer: No. Being told dx/dt and dy/dt is the same as being told the velocity vector ⟨dx/dt, dy/dt⟩. You integrate each one separately in both cases.

faqs.question: Why is the answer to a definite integral of a vector a vector, not a number?
faqs.answer: Each component gives its own number, so you get one number per component. Together they form the net change vector, for example ⟨16, 4⟩.

resources.description: Solve planar motion problems: velocity, speed and acceleration from derivatives, direction of motion, and displacement, position and total distance from integrals.
prerequisites: Vector-valued functions and their derivatives (Topic 9.4)

learningObjectives: Find the velocity vector, acceleration vector and speed of a particle moving in the plane
Read the direction of motion from the signs of dx/dt and dy/dt, and decide when a particle is at rest
Decide whether the speed is increasing or decreasing at a given time, with a reason
Use the definite integral of velocity to find displacement and position

resources.calculatorNote: Derivatives and simple integrals by hand. Total distance usually needs a graphing calculator; give decimals to 3 decimal places and keep more digits in working.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
Velocity v(t) = ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ and acceleration a(t) = ⟨x″(t), y″(t)⟩ are vectors; speed √((x′)² + (y′)²) is a number.
The particle is at rest only when x′ and y′ are both 0 at the same time.
Displacement = ∫ from a to b of v(t) dt (a vector). Total distance = ∫ from a to b of speed dt (a number).
Speed is increasing when x′x″ + y′y″ > 0 and decreasing when it is < 0.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Motion in the plane is BC-only content. AB students study motion along a line in Topics 4.2 and 8.2.

faqs.question: Is total distance travelled the same as arc length?
faqs.answer: It uses the same integral, ∫ √((x′)² + (y′)²) dt. If the particle goes over part of its path twice, the distance counts that part twice, while the length of the curve as a shape does not.

faqs.question: Can I decide whether speed is increasing just by looking at the acceleration vector?
faqs.answer: Not from its size alone. You need to compare its direction with the velocity, which is what the sign of x′x″ + y′y″ does. You can also differentiate the speed directly.

resources.description: Learn what polar coordinates mean, convert between polar and rectangular form, and find dr/dθ, dx/dθ, dy/dθ, dy/dx and d²y/dx² for a polar curve r = f(θ).
prerequisites: Derivatives of parametric curves, dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt) (Topic 9.1)
Second derivatives of parametric curves (Topic 9.2)

learningObjectives: Plot points given in polar coordinates, including points with a negative r, and convert between polar and rectangular coordinates and equations
Treat a polar curve r = f(θ) as a parametric curve with x = f(θ) cos θ and y = f(θ) sin θ
Find dr/dθ, dx/dθ and dy/dθ and say what each one tells you about a point moving along the curve
Find dy/dx and d²y/dx² for a polar curve, write tangent lines and decide concavity
Locate horizontal and vertical tangents, checking that the other derivative is not zero
resources.calculatorNote: Derivatives at exact angles by hand. On calculator questions, set the calculator to radians and give decimals to 3 decimal places, keeping more digits in working.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
A polar point (r, θ) is r units from the pole along the ray at angle θ. Convert with x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ and r² = x² + y².
A polar curve r = f(θ) is a parametric curve with parameter θ: x = f(θ) cos θ, y = f(θ) sin θ.
dy/dx = (dy/dθ) ÷ (dx/dθ), where dx/dθ = f′(θ) cos θ − f(θ) sin θ and dy/dθ = f′(θ) sin θ + f(θ) cos θ.
dr/dθ is not the slope. It tells you whether the point is moving away from the pole (r and dr/dθ with the same sign) or towards it (opposite signs).

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Polar coordinates are BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise the dy/dx formula for polar curves?
faqs.answer: It helps, but you can always rebuild it: write x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, differentiate each with the product rule, then divide dy/dθ by dx/dθ.

faqs.question: Can r be negative?
faqs.answer: Yes. A negative r means you go |r| units in the direction opposite to the ray at angle θ. So (−2, π/4) and (2, 5π/4) are the same point.

learningObjectives: Explain why the area of a polar region is ½ ∫ r² dθ, using sectors and a Riemann sum
Find the area of a region bounded by a polar curve and two rays
Choose limits of integration that trace a loop, petal or closed curve exactly once, using zeros of r, symmetry and a sketch

resources.calculatorNote: Exact areas by hand using power-reducing identities. On calculator questions, use radian mode, write the integral first, and give decimals to 3 decimal places.
keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
The region swept out by r = f(θ) from θ = α to θ = β has area ½ ∫ from α to β of r² dθ.
The formula comes from thin sectors, each of area about ½ r² Δθ, not from thin rectangles.
Choose α and β so that the region is traced exactly once. Zeros of r often mark the ends of a petal or loop.
Square r before integrating, and use sin²θ = ½(1 − cos 2θ) or cos²θ = ½(1 + cos 2θ) to integrate by hand.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Polar area is BC-only content. AB students can skip this page.

faqs.question: What if r is negative on part of the interval?
faqs.answer: The formula uses r², which is never negative, so it still gives the area that is swept out. But the points with negative r are on the opposite side of the pole, so use a sketch to make sure the region you are measuring is the one you want.

faqs.question: Why can't I just integrate from 0 to 2π every time?
faqs.answer: Because many curves are traced more than once, or have loops inside loops, on 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. The circle r = 6 cos θ is traced twice, so 0 to 2π doubles its area.

resources.description: Find areas between two polar curves: locate where the curves meet, including at the pole, decide which curve is outer, and split regions such as the area inside both curves.
prerequisites: Polar coordinates and converting between polar and rectangular form (Topic 9.7)
Area of a region bounded by a single polar curve, ½ ∫ r² dθ (Topic 9.8)

Find every point where two polar curves meet, including meetings at the pole that solving r₁ = r₂ can miss
Decide which curve is the outer boundary on each interval of θ, and justify the decision with a test angle
Set up and evaluate the area of a region inside one polar curve and outside another

keyPoints: BC only: this topic is not part of Calculus AB.
Area between two polar curves = ½ ∫ from α to β of (R² − r²) dθ, where R is the outer curve and r is the inner curve on [α, β].
Square each radius first, then subtract. ½ ∫ (R − r)² dθ is a different, wrong quantity.
Find the limits by solving r₁(θ) = r₂(θ), then check the pole separately: two curves can both pass through it at different angles.
For a region inside both curves, split at the intersection angle and use the nearer curve to the pole on each piece.

faqs.question: Do Calculus AB students need this?
faqs.answer: No. Polar area is BC-only content. AB students find areas between curves in rectangular coordinates only (Topic 8.4).

faqs.question: Why is the formula not ½ ∫ (R − r)² dθ?
faqs.answer: Each thin slice is a big sector minus a small sector. Their areas are ½R² dθ and ½r² dθ, so the slice has area ½(R² − r²) dθ. Squaring the gap R − r measures something else.

faqs.question: Do I always need a sketch?
faqs.answer: In practice, yes. The sketch tells you which curve is outer, where the region starts and stops, and whether you need to split it. A quick test angle then confirms what the sketch shows.

Parametric, vector and polar curves all describe a point by one variable; derivatives with respect to that variable give slope, velocity and concavity.
Integrals of velocity give displacement and position; integrals of speed give distance travelled, which is arc length for a path traced once.
Polar area uses ½ ∫ r² dθ, and between two curves ½ ∫ (R² − r²) dθ, with limits from where the curves meet.

keyPoints: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number, N_A). It lets you count particles by weighing them.
Molar mass M (g mol⁻¹) is numerically equal to the average mass of one particle in atomic mass units.
n = m / M converts grams to moles; N = n × N_A converts moles to particles.

faqs.question: Is molar mass the same as relative formula mass?
faqs.answer: They have the same number. Relative formula mass has no unit; molar mass is the mass of one mole and has the unit g mol⁻¹. For water both are 18.02, but only molar mass is 18.02 g mol⁻¹.

faqs.question: Why are particle numbers so large?
faqs.answer: Atoms are tiny: one carbon atom has a mass of about 2 × 10⁻²³ g. Any sample you can weigh therefore holds roughly 10²² particles or more.

If peak heights are scaled so the tallest is 100, divide each height by the total of all heights to get fractions.
The average always lies between the lightest and heaviest isotope, closest to the most abundant one.

faqs.question: Why is the x-axis labelled m/z and not just mass?
faqs.answer: The instrument separates ions by mass divided by charge (m/z). In this course every ion has a charge of +1, so m/z has the same number as the isotope's mass in amu.

faqs.question: Why does no atom have the average atomic mass?
faqs.answer: For an element with two or more isotopes, each atom is one particular isotope. The average is a property of a large natural sample, so it usually falls between the isotope masses and matches none of them.

resources.title: Elemental Composition of Pure Substances: Study Guide (Chemistry 1.3)
resources.description: Learn how molecules and formula units differ, why a pure compound always has the same mass ratio of elements, and how to turn mass data into an empirical formula.
prerequisites: Converting a mass into moles with n = m / M
Calculating molar mass from a formula
learningObjectives: Tell apart substances made of separate molecules and substances described by a formula unit
Use the law of definite proportions to predict or check the mass of an element in a pure sample
Calculate the percentage by mass of each element in a compound from its formula
Work out an empirical formula from percentage composition or from measured masses
Explain why mass composition gives the empirical formula but not, on its own, the molecular formula
resources.calculatorNote: Use the molar masses from the periodic table you are given; keep at least four significant figures in mole ratios before you decide on whole numbers
keyPoints: Some pure substances are made of separate molecules (H₂O); others are atoms or ions held in a fixed ratio, described by a formula unit (NaCl).
Law of definite proportions: every pure sample of a compound has the same mass ratio of its elements. Water is always 11.19% hydrogen by mass.
The empirical formula is the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms. Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has the empirical formula CH₂O.
To find an empirical formula: grams of each element → moles → divide by the smallest → whole numbers.
Mass composition fixes the atom ratio only, so different compounds can share one empirical formula.

faqs.question: Is the empirical formula always different from the molecular formula?
faqs.answer: No. For water (H₂O) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) the two are the same, because the subscripts already have no common factor. They differ for compounds such as glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, empirical formula CH₂O).

faqs.question: Why do I assume a 100 g sample when I am given percentages?
faqs.answer: It makes each percentage equal to a mass in grams. 40.0% carbon becomes 40.0 g of carbon. Any sample size gives the same ratio, so 100 g is just the easiest choice.

faqs.question: Does the law of definite proportions work for mixtures?
faqs.answer: No. A mixture such as salt water can have any proportion of its parts. The law applies only to a pure compound. Mixtures are the subject of Topic 1.4.

resources.title: Composition of Mixtures: Study Guide (Chemistry 1.4)
resources.description: Learn how pure substances and mixtures differ at the particle level, and how elemental analysis by mass reveals the purity of a sample and the make-up of a mixture.
prerequisites: Converting between mass and moles with n = m / M
Mass percent of an element in a pure compound
learningObjectives: Describe the difference between a pure substance and a mixture in terms of the particles they contain
Explain why a pure compound always has the same mass percent of each element, while a mixture can have a range of values

Find the amounts of two components in a mixture when both contain the analysed element
Use elemental analysis data to find relative numbers of atoms and decide whether a sample is pure
resources.calculatorNote: Use the molar masses from the periodic table you are given; keep unrounded mass fractions until the final step
keyPoints: A pure substance contains particles of one type only; a mixture contains two or more types in proportions that can vary.
A pure compound has a fixed mass percent of each element. A mixture's mass percent depends on how much of each component it holds.
If an impurity contains none of the analysed element, purity = (measured mass of element ÷ mass fraction of element in the pure compound) ÷ sample mass.
For a two-component mixture, write one equation for total mass and one for the analysed element, then solve, usually in moles.
An atom ratio that does not match the expected formula, or a mass percent that changes from sample to sample, is evidence of a mixture.

faqs.question: Can a mixture have a chemical formula?
faqs.answer: No. A formula describes one type of particle in fixed proportions. A mixture can only be described by its components and how much of each it contains, for example 38% NaCl and 62% KCl by mass.

faqs.question: Is a sample that looks uniform always pure?
faqs.answer: No. Salt dissolved in water looks the same everywhere but contains two types of particle. Only the particle-level make-up, or data such as elemental analysis, tells you whether a sample is pure.

resources.title: Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration: Study Guide (Chemistry 1.5)
resources.description: Learn what an atom is made of, how Coulomb's law explains electron attraction, and how to write ground-state electron configurations for atoms and ions using the Aufbau principle.
prerequisites: Protons, neutrons and electrons, atomic number and mass number
Reading the periodic table by period (row) and group (column)
learningObjectives: Describe an atom as a positive nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by negative electrons
Use Coulomb's law as a proportion to compare the attraction between charged particles
Write full and noble-gas ground-state electron configurations for atoms using the Aufbau filling order and the periodic table
Write electron configurations for cations and anions, removing electrons from the highest shell first
Identify core and valence electrons from a configuration
Explain qualitatively, using distance and effective nuclear charge, why some electrons need more energy to remove than others
resources.calculatorNote: Coulomb's law is used here only as a ratio, so no constants are needed; a calculator helps with squares and fractions
keyPoints: An atom is a tiny positive nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by negative electrons held by electrostatic attraction.
Coulomb's law: the force between two charges is proportional to q₁q₂ / r². Bigger charges attract more strongly; greater distance weakens the attraction sharply.
Electrons fill subshells in order of increasing energy (Aufbau): 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s … The periodic table shows this order block by block.
Cations lose electrons from the highest shell (largest n) first, so transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d.
An electron is harder to remove when it is closer to the nucleus and feels a larger effective nuclear charge.

faqs.question: Do I need to know quantum numbers for this topic?
faqs.answer: No. The course exam does not test the assignment of quantum numbers to electrons. You need shells, subshells, configurations and the Coulomb's law reasoning behind them.

faqs.question: What about chromium and copper?
faqs.answer: Their real configurations break the simple filling order (Cr is [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ and Cu is [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰). Writing configurations for these exceptions is not assessed on the exam, but it is useful to know they exist.

resources.title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy: Study Guide (Chemistry 1.6)
resources.description: Learn how a photoelectron spectrum shows the subshells of an atom or ion: peak position gives binding energy, peak height gives electron count, and Coulomb's law explains both.
prerequisites: Writing ground-state electron configurations for atoms and ions up to calcium
Coulomb's law as a proportion, and the idea of shielding by core electrons
learningObjectives: Explain what the position and the height of each peak in a photoelectron spectrum tell you
Turn a photoelectron spectrum into a ground-state electron configuration and identify the atom or ion
Predict the spectrum of an atom or ion from its electron configuration

resources.calculatorNote: Binding energies are given in MJ mol⁻¹ (1 MJ mol⁻¹ = 1000 kJ mol⁻¹). All spectra on this page use illustrative values chosen to show the real pattern; they are not measured data
keyPoints: Photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) measures how much energy it takes to remove electrons from each subshell of an atom or ion.
Each peak is one subshell. Its position is the binding energy; its height is (ideally) proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
Peaks at higher binding energy belong to electrons closer to the nucleus or feeling a larger effective nuclear charge, as Coulomb's law predicts.
Separate 2s and 2p (and 3s and 3p) peaks are evidence that shells are split into subshells.

faqs.question: Why does the binding energy axis often run backwards?
faqs.answer: Many spectra plot binding energy increasing to the left, and often on a log scale. Always read the axis labels before you read the peaks.

faqs.question: Is a PES peak the same as an ionization energy?
faqs.answer: The lowest-energy peak is close to the first ionization energy. The other peaks are not successive ionization energies: each one is the energy to remove a single electron from a different subshell of the neutral atom.

keyPoints: Across a period: Z_eff up, same shell, so radius down and ionization energy and electronegativity up.

resources.title: Periodic Trends: Study Guide (Chemistry 1.7)
resources.description: Explain trends in atomic and ionic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity using Coulomb's law, shielding and effective nuclear charge.
prerequisites: Writing ground-state electron configurations for atoms and ions (Topic 1.5)
Coulomb's law: attraction grows with charge and falls with distance (Topic 1.5)
Linking photoelectron spectra to shells and subshells (Topic 1.6)
learningObjectives: Explain why elements in the same group have similar properties, using their outer electron configurations
Use Coulomb's law, the shell model, shielding and effective nuclear charge to explain trends across a period and down a group
Explain trends in atomic radius, ionic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity
Explain the dips in first ionization energy at groups 13 and 16
Estimate a missing value for an element from the values of its neighbours on the periodic table
resources.calculatorNote: Only simple averaging is needed. Ionization energies are in kJ mol⁻¹; electronegativities (Pauling scale) have no unit
keyPoints: Every trend comes from one idea: Coulomb's law. Outer electrons are held more strongly when the effective nuclear charge is larger and when they are closer to the nucleus.
Across a period, nuclear charge rises but shielding by core electrons stays about the same, so atoms get smaller and hold their electrons more tightly.
Down a group, each new shell puts the outer electrons farther from the nucleus, so atoms get larger and hold their outer electrons less tightly.
First ionization energy dips at groups 13 and 16: a new, higher-energy p subshell starts, and then the first paired p electron feels extra repulsion.
You can estimate a missing value by using the trend between neighbouring elements in the same group or period.

faqs.question: Do I have to give a numerical effective nuclear charge?
faqs.answer: No. The course treats trends qualitatively. A simple estimate (nuclear charge minus core electrons) is a useful way to compare atoms in the same period, but you explain trends in words using Coulomb's law.

faqs.question: What is the difference between electron affinity and electronegativity?
faqs.answer: Electron affinity is a measured energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron. Electronegativity describes how strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons in a covalent bond, on a scale with no unit.

resources.description: Learn how valence electrons explain reactivity trends, why elements in one group form similar compounds, and how to predict ion charges and ionic formulas from the periodic table.
prerequisites: Writing ground-state electron configurations for main-group elements
Coulomb's law, shielding and effective nuclear charge as used for periodic trends
Successive ionization energies and what a large jump means
learningObjectives: Explain how the attraction between nuclei and valence electrons decides whether two elements are likely to bond
Explain reactivity trends down a group of metals and down a group of nonmetals using Coulomb's law
Predict the typical charge of a main-group ion from its position in the periodic table
Write the formula of an ionic compound from ion charges and check that the charges balance
Predict the formula of a compound from the formula of an analogous compound of an element in the same group
resources.calculatorNote: Only simple ratios are needed. Ionization energies are given in kJ mol⁻¹ and rounded to whole numbers
keyPoints: Whether two elements bond, and how, depends on how strongly each nucleus attracts valence electrons.
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they form compounds with the same type of formula (NaCl, KCl; MgO, CaO).
Main-group metals lose all their valence electrons: group 1 forms +1, group 2 forms +2, aluminium forms +3.
Nonmetals in groups 15, 16 and 17 gain electrons to form −3, −2 and −1 ions.
An ionic formula uses the smallest whole-number ratio of ions that gives a total charge of zero.

faqs.question: Why does magnesium stop at Mg²⁺ and not go on to Mg³⁺?
faqs.answer: Mg has two valence electrons. A third electron would have to come from the inner shell, which is much closer to the nucleus and far less shielded, so it costs about five times as much energy as the second.

faqs.question: Do I need to predict charges for transition metals?
faqs.answer: Position is a much weaker guide for transition metals, because many form more than one ion (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, for example). Questions normally give the charge, often as a Roman numeral in the name.

resources.title: Types of Chemical Bonds: Study Guide (Chemistry 2.1)
resources.description: Learn how electronegativity decides whether a bond is nonpolar covalent, polar covalent or ionic, why bonding is a continuum, and how properties reveal ionic and metallic bonding.
prerequisites: Electronegativity trends across a period and down a group (Topic 1.7)
Valence electrons and typical ion charges of main-group elements (Topic 1.8)
Coulomb's law: attraction grows with charge and falls with distance
learningObjectives: Explain electronegativity trends with the shell model, shielding and Coulomb's law
Classify a bond as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent or ionic using electronegativity and the types of element involved
Identify the atom that carries the partial negative charge in a polar bond and rank single bonds by bond dipole
Explain why ionic and covalent bonding form a continuum and why properties are the best evidence of bond type
Describe metallic bonding as metal cations surrounded by delocalized valence electrons
Make and justify a claim about the bonding in a substance from its properties
resources.calculatorNote: Only subtraction is needed. Electronegativities are Pauling values, which have no unit; on the exam you are normally expected to reason from periodic-table position
keyPoints: Electronegativity rises across a period and falls down a group, for the same Coulomb's law reasons as ionization energy.
Atoms with similar electronegativity share electrons equally: a nonpolar covalent bond. C–H bonds count as nonpolar.
With unequal electronegativity the sharing is unequal: the more electronegative atom becomes partially negative (δ−). For single bonds, a bigger difference means a bigger bond dipole.
Ionic and covalent are two ends of a continuum. Metal + nonmetal is usually ionic, two nonmetals covalent, but a compound's properties are the best evidence.
In a metal, the valence electrons are delocalized: they belong to the whole solid, not to any one atom.

faqs.question: Is there a fixed electronegativity difference where bonds become ionic?
faqs.answer: No. Some books quote a rough guide of about 1.7 to 2.0, but there is no sharp line. Hydrogen fluoride has a difference of 1.78 and is still made of covalent molecules. Use the elements involved and, above all, the properties.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorize electronegativity values?
faqs.answer: No. You need the trends and the reasons for them. If a question needs numbers, it gives them. Know that fluorine is the most electronegative element and that oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine are also high.
