resources.title: Intramolecular Force and Potential Energy: Study Guide (Chemistry 2.2)
resources.description: Read and sketch potential energy curves for bonds, find bond length and bond energy, and explain how atom size, bond order and ion charge and size control bond strength.
prerequisites: Covalent, ionic and metallic bonding (Topic 2.1)
Coulomb's law as a proportion: attraction grows with charge and falls with distance (Topic 1.5)
Atomic and ionic radius trends (Topic 1.7)
learningObjectives: Explain the shape of a potential energy curve using attractions and repulsions between the nuclei and electrons of two atoms
Read the equilibrium bond length and the bond energy from a potential energy graph
Sketch potential energy curves with labelled axes, units and a sensible scale, and compare two bonds on one graph
Explain how atom size and bond order affect covalent bond length and bond energy
Use Coulomb's law to compare the strength of attraction between different cations and anions
resources.calculatorNote: Coulomb's law is used only as a ratio, so no constants are needed. Bond energies are in kJ mol⁻¹ and distances in picometres (1 pm = 10⁻¹² m); N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
keyPoints: A graph of potential energy against internuclear distance shows why atoms bond: the energy is lowest at one particular separation.
The distance at the minimum is the bond length. The depth of the minimum below zero is the bond energy, the energy needed to pull the atoms apart.
Larger atoms form longer bonds, which are usually weaker. Higher bond order (double, triple) gives shorter, stronger bonds.
Between ions, Coulomb's law rules: larger charges and smaller ions give stronger attraction.
Breaking a bond always needs energy; forming a bond always releases it.

faqs.question: Why is the potential energy negative when atoms are bonded?
faqs.answer: Zero is chosen to be the energy of the two atoms when they are far apart and not interacting. A bonded pair is more stable than that, so its energy is below zero.

faqs.question: Is a double bond twice as strong as a single bond?
faqs.answer: No. A C=C bond (614 kJ mol⁻¹) is stronger than a C–C bond (347 kJ mol⁻¹) but less than twice as strong. The second pair of electrons is shared less effectively than the first.

resources.title: Structure of Ionic Solids: Study Guide (Chemistry 2.3)
resources.description: Learn how cations and anions pack into a repeating 3-D array, how to draw a particulate model that respects Coulomb's law and ion sizes, and why ion charge and radius matter.
prerequisites: Predicting ion charges and ionic formulas from the periodic table
Coulomb's law: larger charges and shorter distances give stronger attraction
Ionic radius trends: cations are smaller than their atoms, anions are larger
learningObjectives: Describe an ionic solid as a repeating three-dimensional array of cations and anions, not a set of molecules
Draw a particulate model of an ionic solid with alternating charges, sensible relative sizes and the correct ion ratio
Use Coulomb's law to compare the strength of attraction in different ionic solids from ion charges and radii
Evaluate a student's particulate model and correct its errors
Link the particulate model to high melting points, brittleness and electrical conductivity
resources.calculatorNote: Only ratios are needed. Ionic radii are effective six-coordinate values in picometres (pm); other tables give slightly different numbers but the same trends
keyPoints: An ionic solid is a repeating 3-D array of cations and anions. There are no separate molecules.
Each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge, which maximizes attraction and keeps like charges apart.
A good particulate model alternates charges, draws relative ion sizes sensibly and shows the ratio given by the formula.
By Coulomb's law, larger ion charges and smaller ions (shorter distance between centres) give stronger attraction.
You do not need to know or name specific crystal structures for the exam.

faqs.question: Is NaCl a molecule?
faqs.answer: No. Solid sodium chloride is a continuous array of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The formula NaCl gives the ratio of ions (1 : 1), called a formula unit, not a separate particle.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn crystal structures such as the rock-salt or cesium chloride structure?
faqs.answer: No. The course states that specific crystal structures are not assessed. You need a model that alternates charges, uses sensible sizes and keeps the correct ratio.

faqs.question: Why are cations usually drawn smaller than anions?
faqs.answer: A cation has lost its outer electrons, so it is smaller than its atom; an anion has gained electrons, so it is larger. In most common salts, such as NaCl, KBr and MgO, the cation is the smaller ion.

resources.title: Structure of Metals and Alloys: Study Guide (Chemistry 2.4)
resources.description: Learn the electron-sea model of a metal, how interstitial and substitutional alloys differ, and how to draw and interpret particulate models of steel, brass and other alloys.
prerequisites: Valence electrons and the charges of metal ions
Atomic radius trends across a period and down a group
Converting mass percent to amount in moles
learningObjectives: Represent a metallic solid as an array of positive ion cores in a sea of delocalized valence electrons
Classify an alloy as interstitial or substitutional from the relative sizes of its atoms
Draw particulate models of a pure metal, a substitutional alloy and an interstitial alloy
Convert an alloy's mass composition into an atom ratio and show it in a model
Connect the particulate model of metals and alloys to conductivity, malleability and hardness
resources.calculatorNote: Molar masses: C 12.01, Fe 55.85, Ni 58.69, Cu 63.55, Zn 65.38 g mol⁻¹. Radii in picometres (pm); keep unrounded values until the final step
keyPoints: A metal is modelled as a regular array of positive ion cores surrounded by a sea of delocalized valence electrons.
The attraction between the cores and the electron sea holds the metal together; no electron belongs to one atom.
Interstitial alloys form when much smaller atoms fill the gaps between larger metal atoms, as carbon does in steel.
Substitutional alloys form when atoms of similar size replace some host atoms, as zinc does for copper in brass.
Alloys keep the electron sea, so they still conduct; interstitial atoms make the lattice more rigid.

faqs.question: Is an alloy a compound?
faqs.answer: No. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, and its composition can vary. Brass, for example, can contain different proportions of zinc. A compound has a fixed formula.

faqs.question: If the metal is made of positive ions, why is it not charged?
faqs.answer: Each atom gives its valence electrons to the shared sea. The total negative charge of the sea equals the total positive charge of the cores, so the metal is neutral overall.

faqs.question: Do I need to name crystal structures for metals?
faqs.answer: No. You need a model that shows the regular array of cores, the delocalized electrons and, for an alloy, where the second kind of atom sits.

resources.title: Lewis Diagrams: Study Guide (Chemistry 2.5)
resources.description: Learn a reliable step-by-step method for drawing Lewis diagrams of molecules and polyatomic ions, including multiple bonds, incomplete octets and expanded octets.
prerequisites: Finding the number of valence electrons of a main-group element from the periodic table
Telling covalent bonding from ionic bonding (Topic 2.1)
Electronegativity trends across a period and down a group
learningObjectives: Count the total valence electrons in a molecule or polyatomic ion, adjusting for the ion's charge
Choose a sensible skeleton, placing the least electronegative atom in the centre and hydrogen on the outside
Build a Lewis diagram step by step, using double or triple bonds when the central atom is short of an octet
Recognise when a valid Lewis diagram has fewer or more than eight electrons around the central atom
Check a finished Lewis diagram by recounting its electrons and reading its bonding pattern
resources.calculatorNote: Only whole-number electron counts are needed
keyPoints: A Lewis diagram shows every valence electron: shared pairs as lines, lone pairs as pairs of dots.
Start by counting valence electrons. Add one for each negative charge on an ion; subtract one for each positive charge.
Put the least electronegative atom in the centre. Hydrogen and fluorine are always on the outside.
Fill the outer atoms' octets first, then put leftover electrons on the central atom. If the central atom is still short, turn lone pairs into double or triple bonds.
Boron and beryllium can end with fewer than eight electrons; atoms from period 3 onwards can hold more than eight.

faqs.question: Does a Lewis diagram show the shape of the molecule?
faqs.answer: No. It shows which atoms are joined and where the electrons are. You use it as the starting point for predicting shape with VSEPR in Topic 2.7, but the angles on the page mean nothing.

faqs.question: Can I draw lone pairs on any side of an atom?
faqs.answer: Yes. Any side is fine as long as each atom shows the right number of lone pairs and bonds, and the total electron count is correct.

resources.title: Resonance and Formal Charge: Study Guide (Chemistry 2.6)
resources.description: Learn when one Lewis diagram is not enough, how resonance predicts equal bond lengths, and how to use formal charge and the octet rule to choose the best Lewis diagram.
prerequisites: Drawing Lewis diagrams for molecules and polyatomic ions (Topic 2.5)
Electronegativity trends across a period and down a group
learningObjectives: Draw all the equivalent resonance structures for a molecule or ion and explain what the real structure is like
Calculate the average bond order from a set of resonance structures and use it to predict bond lengths
Calculate the formal charge on every atom in a Lewis diagram and check that they add up to the overall charge

resources.calculatorNote: Formal charges are whole numbers; average bond orders are simple fractions
keyPoints: When two or more equivalent Lewis diagrams can be drawn, the real structure is a resonance hybrid: a blend of them, not a switch between them.
Resonance makes the bonds involved identical. Their bond order is the average, such as 1.5 in the formate ion.
Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½ × bonding electrons. The formal charges add up to the overall charge.
The best diagram gives C, N, O and F an octet, keeps formal charges near zero, and puts any negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom.
Species with an odd number of valence electrons, such as NO₂, cannot give every atom an octet: a limitation of the Lewis model.

faqs.question: Does a molecule with resonance flip between its structures?
faqs.answer: No. The molecule has one structure all the time. The separate resonance diagrams are a limitation of drawing electrons as fixed pairs; the real electron arrangement is in between.

faqs.question: Is formal charge the real charge on an atom?
faqs.answer: No. It is bookkeeping that assumes every bond is shared exactly equally. Real charges depend on electronegativity. Formal charge is still a useful guide for choosing between diagrams.

keyPoints: Electron domains (bonds and lone pairs) around an atom repel each other and spread out as far apart as possible. This is VSEPR.
A single, double or triple bond counts as one domain. Lone pairs count as domains but are not part of the shape you name.
2, 3 and 4 domains mean sp (180°), sp² (120°) and sp³ (109.5°). Lone pairs and multiple bonds squeeze the angles slightly.
Every bond has one sigma bond; a double bond adds one pi bond and a triple bond adds two. Pi bonds are weaker and block rotation.
A molecule has a dipole moment when its bond dipoles do not cancel, which depends on both bond polarity and shape.

faqs.question: What is the difference between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry?
faqs.answer: Electron-domain geometry describes where all the domains point, lone pairs included. Molecular geometry describes only where the atoms are. They are the same when the central atom has no lone pairs.

faqs.question: Do I need to give a hybridization for atoms with five or six domains?
faqs.answer: No. For more than four electron domains you only need the shape. Hybridization that involves d orbitals is outside the course.

resources.title: Intermolecular and Interparticle Forces: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.1)
resources.description: Learn the forces that act between molecules and ions, from London dispersion to hydrogen bonding and ion–dipole forces, and how molecular structure sets their relative strength.
prerequisites: Bond polarity and electronegativity (Topic 2.1)

learningObjectives: Tell intermolecular forces (between particles) apart from the bonds inside a molecule
Explain London dispersion forces using temporary dipoles, and predict how electron count, molecular shape and contact area change their strength
Identify dipole–dipole, dipole–induced dipole, hydrogen bonding and ion–dipole forces, and show how the partial charges must line up

Identify the strongest force acting between two different chemical species, including within and between large biomolecules
resources.calculatorNote: No calculation is needed; boiling points are quoted to the nearest degree as evidence
keyPoints: Intermolecular forces act between particles. They are Coulombic attractions between partial or full charges, and they are much weaker than covalent bonds.
London dispersion forces act between all molecules. They grow with the number of electrons (polarizability) and with the contact area between molecules.
A polar molecule adds dipole–dipole forces (with another polar molecule) or dipole–induced dipole forces (with a nonpolar one) on top of dispersion forces.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F in one molecule and a lone pair on N, O or F in another molecule or another part of the same molecule.
Ion–dipole forces, between an ion and a polar molecule, are usually stronger than dipole–dipole forces. Partial charges must point the right way.
For large molecules, dispersion forces are often the strongest net intermolecular force, even when the molecules are polar.

faqs.question: Are London dispersion forces the same as van der Waals forces?
faqs.answer: No. Van der Waals forces is a wider name that usually also covers dipole–dipole and dipole–induced dipole forces. Use the specific name of the force you mean.

faqs.question: Is a hydrogen bond a covalent bond?
faqs.answer: No. It is an intermolecular attraction between an H atom on one molecule and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule (or another part of the same large molecule). It is stronger than most other intermolecular forces but much weaker than a covalent bond.

resources.title: Solubility: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.10)
resources.description: Learn why substances with similar intermolecular forces mix, how ions dissolve in water, why long-chain alcohols are less soluble, and where the like-dissolves-like model falls short.
prerequisites: Types and relative strengths of intermolecular forces, including ion–dipole forces (Topic 3.1)
Deciding whether a molecule is polar from its shape and bond dipoles (Topic 2.7)
Separating mixtures using intermolecular forces (Topic 3.9)
learningObjectives: Describe dissolving as replacing solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions with solute–solvent attractions
Predict whether a substance is more soluble in water or in a nonpolar solvent such as hexane, and justify the prediction with intermolecular forces
Draw a particulate model of ions dissolved in water with the water molecules oriented correctly

resources.calculatorNote: The solubility data are read from a chart; no calculation beyond comparing values is needed
keyPoints: Substances with similar intermolecular interactions tend to dissolve in, or mix with, one another (like dissolves like).
Dissolving swaps solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions for solute–solvent attractions. It happens readily when the new attractions are comparable to the old ones.
Ionic compounds dissolve in water through ion–dipole attractions: the δ− oxygen ends of water molecules face cations and the δ+ hydrogen ends face anions.
Nonpolar substances do not dissolve well in water because water would lose strong hydrogen bonds and gain only weak dispersion attractions.
A longer hydrocarbon chain makes a molecule less soluble in water and more soluble in nonpolar solvents.

faqs.question: What is the difference between soluble and miscible?
faqs.answer: Soluble describes a substance, often a solid, that dissolves in a solvent, usually up to some limit. Miscible describes two liquids that mix in any proportions to form one phase. Liquids that form two layers are immiscible.

faqs.question: Do all ionic compounds dissolve in water?
faqs.answer: No. Many do, but some, such as calcium carbonate and silver chloride, dissolve only in tiny amounts. The course expects you to know that all sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble in water.

resources.title: Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.11)
resources.description: Learn how each region of the electromagnetic spectrum matches one kind of change in a molecule: microwaves change rotation, infrared changes vibration, and UV or visible light moves electrons.
prerequisites: Electrons in atoms occupy quantized energy levels (Topics 1.5 and 1.6)
Covalent bonds and molecular shape (Unit 2)

learningObjectives: Place the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength, frequency and photon energy

resources.calculatorNote: Energies per mole in the tables use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Region boundaries are approximate
keyPoints: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per photon: radio < microwave < infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-ray < gamma.
Molecules have quantized rotational, vibrational and electronic energy levels. The gaps grow in that order.
Microwave photons change rotation, infrared photons change vibration, and ultraviolet or visible photons move electrons between energy levels.
A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches a gap, so the region a substance absorbs in tells you which kind of transition happened.

faqs.question: Do I need to calculate photon energies in this topic?
faqs.answer: Not yet. Here you link spectral regions to transitions and compare energies qualitatively. Topic 3.12 adds the equations c = λν and E = hν so you can calculate them.

faqs.question: Does every molecule absorb infrared radiation?
faqs.answer: No. As background beyond the course: a vibration absorbs infrared only if it changes the molecule's dipole moment. N₂ and O₂ absorb almost no infrared, while CO₂ and H₂O do, which is why they are greenhouse gases.

prerequisites: The regions of the electromagnetic spectrum and the transitions they cause (Topic 3.11)
Scientific notation, unit prefixes (nm, μm, kJ) and significant figures
The mole and Avogadro's number (Topic 1.1)
learningObjectives: Explain that absorbing or emitting a photon changes the energy of an atom or molecule by exactly the photon's energy
Use c = λν to convert between wavelength and frequency

resources.calculatorNote: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Convert nm to m before calculating; keep unrounded values until the final step
keyPoints: When an atom or molecule absorbs a photon, its energy rises by exactly the photon's energy; when it emits a photon, its energy falls by exactly that amount.
Wavelength and frequency are linked by c = λν: as one goes up, the other goes down.
Photon energy is E = hν, or E = hc/λ. Higher frequency and shorter wavelength both mean more energy per photon.
Multiply energy per photon by N_A to get energy per mole of photons, which you can compare with bond energies in kJ mol⁻¹.

faqs.question: Is frequency measured in hertz or s⁻¹?
faqs.answer: Both are the same unit: 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹. Write s⁻¹ when you want the units to cancel clearly in E = hν, because h is in J s.

faqs.question: Do I need to learn the values of h and c?
faqs.answer: The values are given on the equation sheet in the exam. You do need to know which equation uses which constant, and to convert units such as nm to m before you use them.

resources.title: Beer-Lambert Law: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.13)
resources.description: Learn how absorbance depends on molar absorptivity, path length and concentration, how to use a calibration curve, and how lab errors change a calculated concentration.
prerequisites: Molarity and dilution calculations (Topic 3.7)
Absorption of photons by molecules and ions (Topics 3.11 and 3.12)

learningObjectives: Use A = εbc to calculate absorbance, molar absorptivity, path length or concentration, with units
Explain why absorbance is proportional to path length and to concentration in terms of the number of absorbing particles in the light beam
Explain why a spectrophotometer is set to the wavelength of maximum absorbance

resources.calculatorNote: Absorbance has no unit; ε in M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, b in cm, c in M (mol L⁻¹). Keep unrounded values until the final step
keyPoints: The Beer-Lambert law is A = εbc: absorbance equals molar absorptivity × path length × concentration.
ε measures how strongly one species absorbs light of one wavelength. It changes with the species and the wavelength, not with concentration.
Path length and concentration both set how many absorbing particles the light meets, so A is proportional to each.
With the same cuvette and wavelength, A is proportional to c alone: a calibration line through the origin with gradient εb.
Set the instrument to the wavelength of maximum absorbance for the greatest sensitivity.

faqs.question: Does absorbance have a unit?
faqs.answer: No. Absorbance is a ratio of light intensities, so it has no unit. That is why ε has the unit M⁻¹ cm⁻¹: the units of ε × b × c must cancel.

faqs.question: Why do we use a blank?
faqs.answer: The blank (cuvette plus solvent only) is set to A = 0. Any light lost to the cuvette walls or the solvent is then not counted, so the reading measures only the species you are studying.

resources.title: Properties of Solids: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.2)
resources.description: Learn how the particles in a solid and the forces between them explain boiling point, vapor pressure, melting point, hardness and conductivity in ionic, covalent network, molecular and metallic solids.
prerequisites: The five intermolecular and interparticle forces (Topic 3.1)
Particulate models of ionic solids, metals and alloys (Topics 2.3 and 2.4)
learningObjectives: Explain why boiling point and vapor pressure track the strength of intermolecular forces directly, while melting point does so less reliably
Describe the particles and forces in ionic, covalent network, molecular and metallic solids

resources.calculatorNote: No calculation is needed; data are quoted as evidence
keyPoints: Vaporizing a substance overcomes its interparticle forces completely, so stronger forces mean a lower vapor pressure and a higher boiling point.
Melting only rearranges the particles, so melting points also depend on how well the particles pack, and can break the pattern.
Ionic solids: high melting point, low vapor pressure, brittle, conduct only when molten or dissolved.
Covalent network solids (diamond, graphite, SiO₂, SiC): very high melting points; 3D networks are hard, but graphite's layers slide.
Molecular solids: low melting points and no conductivity, because only weak intermolecular forces hold the molecules together.
Metallic solids: conduct heat and electricity and are malleable and ductile; interstitial alloys are more rigid but still conduct.

faqs.question: Why is melting point a less reliable guide to intermolecular forces than boiling point?
faqs.answer: Boiling separates the particles completely, so it measures the full strength of the attractions. Melting only loosens a regular arrangement into a disordered one, so the melting point also depends on how neatly the particles fit together in the solid.

faqs.question: Graphite conducts electricity. Does that make it a metal?
faqs.answer: No. Graphite is a covalent network solid made only of carbon atoms. Its conductivity comes from electrons that can move along each carbon layer, but its bonding, softness and other properties are not metallic.

resources.title: Solids, Liquids, and Gases: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.3)
resources.description: Learn how particles are arranged and how they move in crystalline and amorphous solids, liquids and gases, and how to draw particulate models that show the differences.
prerequisites: Intermolecular forces: dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding
The four main types of solid (ionic, metallic, covalent network, molecular)
Converting between mass, moles and volume using density and molar mass
learningObjectives: Describe the arrangement and motion of particles in crystalline solids, amorphous solids, liquids and gases
Draw particulate models of the same substance in each phase, keeping particle size and identity fixed

keyPoints: In a solid, particles touch and vibrate about fixed positions; they do not move past one another.
A crystalline solid has a regular, repeating 3-D arrangement; an amorphous solid has no long-range order.
In a liquid, particles still touch but keep moving, colliding and sliding past one another.
Solid and liquid phases of a substance have similar molar volumes because particles are in contact in both.
Gas particles are far apart and in constant motion, so a gas has no fixed shape or volume.
A phase change moves whole particles apart or together; the particles themselves do not change.

faqs.question: Is glass a solid or a very slow liquid?
faqs.answer: Glass is an amorphous solid. Its particles have no regular pattern, like a liquid, but they do not move past one another, like any solid.

faqs.question: Do I need to read phase diagrams for this topic?
faqs.answer: No. Interpreting phase diagrams is not assessed in this course. You need particulate models of each phase and the reasons behind them.

faqs.question: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
faqs.answer: Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules in ice in an open, regular pattern with gaps. This is unusual: for most substances the solid is slightly denser than the liquid.

faqs.question: Why must temperature be in kelvin?
faqs.answer: The gas laws are proportional to absolute temperature, which is zero at −273.15 °C. Doubling a Celsius temperature does not double the average kinetic energy of the particles; doubling a kelvin temperature does.

faqs.question: Which value of R should I use?
faqs.answer: Match R to your units. With pressure in atm and volume in L, use 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. With torr, use 62.36 L torr mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. In energy calculations, use 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

faqs.question: Does a heavier gas exert a larger partial pressure?
faqs.answer: No. At a given temperature and volume, partial pressure depends only on the number of moles of that gas, not on its molar mass.

prerequisites: The ideal gas law PV = nRT and partial pressures (Topic 3.4)

learningObjectives: State the assumptions of the kinetic molecular theory and use them to explain gas pressure
Explain, at the particle level, why pressure changes when temperature, volume or amount of gas changes

resources.calculatorNote: Most comparisons are ratios, so no constants are needed. Use temperatures in kelvin (K = °C + 273). R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ appears only in background values
keyPoints: The kinetic molecular theory (KMT) explains gas behaviour with moving particles: pressure is the result of particles hitting the container walls.
The Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles. Double the kelvin temperature and you double the average kinetic energy.
At the same temperature, every gas has the same average kinetic energy, so lighter particles move faster on average (KE = ½mv²).
A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the spread of particle speeds or energies. Heating moves the peak to the right, lowers it and widens the curve; the area stays the same.
Particles in solids and liquids are also in constant, random motion; KMT just describes gases most simply.

faqs.question: If the average kinetic energy is the same, why are the speeds different?
faqs.answer: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed together (KE = ½mv²). A heavier particle needs a lower speed to carry the same kinetic energy.

faqs.question: Do all particles in a gas move at the same speed?
faqs.answer: No. Collisions constantly swap energy between particles, so at any moment there is a wide range of speeds. Temperature tells you only the average kinetic energy.

resources.title: Deviation from Ideal Gas Law: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.6)
resources.description: Explain why real gases depart from PV = nRT: attractions between particles lower the pressure near condensation, and particle volume raises it at very high pressure.
prerequisites: The ideal gas law PV = nRT (Topic 3.4)
The assumptions of the kinetic molecular theory (Topic 3.5)
Types and relative strengths of intermolecular forces (Topic 3.1)
learningObjectives: Identify which assumptions of the kinetic molecular theory fail for real gases
Explain why attractions between gas particles make the measured pressure lower than the ideal value
Explain why the volume of the particles makes the measured volume or pressure higher than the ideal value at very high pressure
Predict the conditions, and the kinds of gas, that give the largest and smallest deviations from ideal behaviour
Compare a measured value with an ideal-gas prediction and justify which effect is dominant
Interpret a graph or table of PV/nRT against pressure
resources.calculatorNote: R = 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. All measured values for gases X and Y are invented for practice, not real data
keyPoints: PV = nRT assumes gas particles have no volume and do not attract each other. Real particles do both, so real gases deviate.

Attractions pull particles back from the walls, so the measured pressure is lower than the ideal value. This matters most near condensation: low temperature, high pressure, strong intermolecular forces.
The particles' own volume makes the measured volume (or pressure) higher than the ideal value. This matters most at very high pressure.
The ratio PV/nRT is 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 when attractions dominate and above 1 when particle volume dominates.
Gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure, especially small particles with weak intermolecular forces, such as helium.

faqs.question: If real gases are not ideal, why use PV = nRT at all?
faqs.answer: At ordinary temperatures and pressures, most gases are within a few per cent of ideal behaviour, so PV = nRT gives good answers. You only need to worry near condensation or at very high pressure.

faqs.question: Do the two effects ever cancel out?
faqs.answer: Yes. At one particular pressure for a given gas and temperature, the effect of attractions and the effect of particle volume can balance, so PV/nRT happens to equal 1. The gas is still not ideal: both effects are present.

keyPoints: A solution is a homogeneous mixture: its properties are the same everywhere in the sample. Solutions can be solids, liquids or gases.
In a heterogeneous mixture the properties depend on where you take the sample.
Molarity M = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution. The unit is mol L⁻¹, written M.
An ionic solute gives each ion its own concentration: 0.25 M CaCl₂ is 0.25 M Ca²⁺ and 0.50 M Cl⁻.
Diluting or mixing changes the volume, not the moles of solute already present: n = M × V before and after.

faqs.question: Is molarity per litre of water or per litre of solution?
faqs.answer: Per litre of solution. Dissolving a solid usually changes the volume a little, so you dissolve it first and then make the whole solution up to the final volume.

faqs.question: Will I need molality or percent by mass?
faqs.answer: Not for calculations in this course. Molarity is the concentration unit you calculate with. Other units may appear in a lab context, but you will not be asked to calculate molality, percent by mass or percent by volume.

resources.title: Separation of Solutions and Mixtures: Study Guide (Chemistry 3.9)
resources.description: Learn why filtration cannot separate a solution, and how chromatography and distillation use differences in intermolecular forces to separate the parts of a mixture.
prerequisites: Types and relative strengths of intermolecular forces (Topic 3.1)
Vapor pressure and boiling point linked to intermolecular forces (Topic 3.2)

learningObjectives: Explain why filtration can remove an undissolved solid but cannot separate the parts of a solution
Describe the mobile phase and stationary phase in paper, thin-layer and column chromatography

keyPoints: Filtration only removes particles bigger than the filter's pores. Dissolved ions and molecules pass straight through, so a solution cannot be separated by filtering.
Solutions are separated by using differences in the intermolecular forces of their components.
In chromatography, each component is pulled between a stationary phase and a moving solvent (the mobile phase). The component held more strongly by the stationary phase moves more slowly.
Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front. On a polar stationary phase, a lower Rf means a more polar component.
In distillation, the component with weaker intermolecular forces has the higher vapor pressure, so it boils off first.

faqs.question: Do I need to remember the formula for Rf?
faqs.answer: It is worth knowing, because it turns a chromatogram into numbers you can compare. The key skill is the reasoning: which component is attracted more strongly to the stationary phase, and why.

faqs.question: Can distillation always give two pure liquids?
faqs.answer: Not always. Some mixtures, such as ethanol and water, reach a fixed composition that boils without changing. Simple distillation also gives only a partial separation when the boiling points are close.

resources.title: Introduction for Reactions: Study Guide (Chemistry 4.1)
resources.description: Learn how to tell a physical change from a chemical change, what counts as evidence of a reaction, why that evidence is only a clue, and how to predict what an experiment will show.
prerequisites: The difference between elements, compounds and mixtures (Unit 1)
Solids, liquids, gases and solutions at the particle level (Unit 3)
learningObjectives: Define physical and chemical changes in terms of whether the composition of the substances changes
Recognise phase changes and the making or separating of mixtures as physical changes
Name the four common signs of a chemical change: heat or light, a gas, a precipitate and a colour change

keyPoints: A physical change alters properties such as state or shape, but the substances keep the same composition.
Phase changes, dissolving to make a mixture and separating a mixture (filtering, distilling) are common physical changes.
A chemical change makes new substances: atoms are rearranged into new combinations, usually with a different composition.
Heat or light, a gas, a precipitate or a colour change are possible evidence of a chemical change. Each can also happen without a reaction.
The deciding question is always: has a new substance formed? Test it by identifying the product or trying to recover the starting material.

faqs.question: Is dissolving salt in water a physical or a chemical change?
faqs.answer: Usually it is called physical, because you can get the salt back by evaporating the water. The ionic bonds in the solid do break, though, so a reasonable argument can be made either way. Topic 4.4 looks at this case in detail.

faqs.question: If I see bubbles, has a reaction happened?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Boiling water and opening a fizzy drink both give bubbles with no new substance. Bubbles are evidence only if the gas is a new substance, for example carbon dioxide made from a carbonate and an acid.

Choose the form of equation that suits the question being asked
resources.calculatorNote: Balancing uses whole-number coefficients. One optional mass check uses molar masses H 1.008, C 12.01, O 16.00, Na 22.99 g mol⁻¹
keyPoints: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, and the same total charge. That is how it shows mass and charge are conserved.
Physical changes have equations too: H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), or KNO₃(s) → K⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) when a salt dissolves.
In a complete ionic equation, write soluble ionic compounds and strong acids as separate ions. Keep solids, liquids, gases, weak acids and molecular substances together.
Spectator ions appear unchanged on both sides. Cancel them to get the net ionic equation, which shows only what actually reacts.
All sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble in water. Other solubility information is given in the question or shown by a precipitate.

faqs.question: Should I write H⁺(aq) or H₃O⁺(aq)?
faqs.answer: Either is accepted in this course. H₃O⁺ (hydronium) is the preferred form, but H⁺ makes equations shorter and is the same thing in water. Be consistent within one answer.

faqs.question: Do I need to memorise a full table of solubility rules?
faqs.answer: No. You need to know that all sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble. Anything else will be given to you, or you can deduce it from an observation such as a precipitate forming.

resources.title: Representations of Reactions: Study Guide (Chemistry 4.3)
resources.description: Learn to turn balanced equations into consistent particle diagrams, and to read before-and-after diagrams back into equations, for reactions, solutions and physical changes.
prerequisites: Balancing chemical equations and writing net ionic equations (Topic 4.2)

learningObjectives: Draw a particle diagram that matches a balanced equation, keeping every atom and the reacting ratio
Read a before-and-after particle diagram and write the balanced equation it shows
Show substances in the right state, with dissolved ionic compounds as separate ions in the formula ratio
Represent a physical process, such as a phase change or dissolving, without breaking molecules apart

resources.calculatorNote: Only whole-number particle counts and simple ratios are needed
keyPoints: A particle diagram is an equation drawn at the scale of atoms. Each circle is one atom or ion; joined circles are one molecule or polyatomic ion.
Every atom in the 'before' box must appear in the 'after' box, in the same total number. Particles are rearranged, never created or lost.
The numbers of particles that react and form must be in the ratio of the coefficients. Unreacted particles stay in the picture unchanged.
Soluble ionic compounds in water are drawn as separate ions in their formula ratio; molecular solutes stay as whole molecules.
In a physical change such as boiling, the same molecules appear before and after; only their spacing and arrangement change.

faqs.question: Do I have to draw the water molecules in a solution diagram?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most questions say water is omitted for clarity. Draw the dissolved particles spread through the container and state in a key or label that water is not shown.

faqs.question: Does the number of particles in the box have to equal the coefficients?
faqs.answer: No. The box can hold any numbers, as long as the particles that react and form are in the coefficient ratio. Six SO₂ reacting with three O₂ is the same 2 : 1 ratio as the equation 2 SO₂ + O₂ → 2 SO₃.

prerequisites: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding (Topic 2.1)
Intermolecular forces, including ion–dipole attractions (Topic 3.1)

learningObjectives: Tell chemical bonds apart from intermolecular attractions, and say which kind changes in a given process
Classify a process as chemical or physical by what happens to bonds at the particle level
Explain why macroscopic signs such as a gas, a colour change or heat are evidence, not proof, of a chemical change

resources.calculatorNote: Only simple comparisons of given values are needed
keyPoints: A chemical process breaks and/or forms chemical bonds (covalent, ionic or metallic), so new substances appear.
A physical process changes only the attractions between particles, as in melting, boiling and dissolving sugar. The particles keep their identity.
What you see (gas, colour change, heat) is evidence, not proof. Boiling makes a gas and iodine changes colour when it sublimes, yet both are physical.
Breaking chemical bonds usually needs far more energy than overcoming intermolecular attractions: for water, more than 20 times as much.
Dissolving a salt breaks ionic bonds and forms ion–dipole attractions, so it can be argued either way. Give your reasoning, not just a label.

faqs.question: Is dissolving salt a physical or a chemical change?
faqs.answer: Both arguments are acceptable if you support them. Physical: the same ions are present and evaporating the water gives back the salt. Chemical: ionic bonds in the lattice break and new ion–dipole interactions form. State which view you take and why.

faqs.question: Does a reversible change have to be physical?
faqs.answer: No. Many chemical reactions can be reversed, and some physical changes are hard to reverse. Decide by asking whether chemical bonds break or form, not by asking whether the change can be undone.

resources.title: Stoichiometry: Study Guide (Chemistry 4.5)
resources.description: Use balanced equations as mole ratios to calculate amounts of reactants and products, find the limiting reactant, and combine stoichiometry with gas and solution data.
prerequisites: Converting between mass, moles and particles (Topic 1.1)

The ideal gas law PV = nRT and molarity M = n / V
learningObjectives: Explain why conservation of atoms lets you calculate product amounts from reactant amounts, and the reverse
Use the coefficients of a balanced equation as mole ratios in multi-step calculations

resources.calculatorNote: Use the molar masses you are given and R = 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; convert °C to K and mL to L; round only at the end
keyPoints: Coefficients in a balanced equation are mole ratios, never mass ratios.
Every stoichiometry problem runs: given quantity → moles of A → mole ratio → moles of B → wanted quantity.
The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first. Find it by comparing moles divided by coefficients, not grams.
Gases enter and leave through n = PV / RT; solutions through n = M × V (V in litres).
Adding more of the excess reactant does not make more product; adding more of the limiting reactant does, until it stops being limiting.

faqs.question: Why can't I compare masses to find the limiting reactant?
faqs.answer: Reactions happen particle by particle, and equal masses of different substances hold different numbers of particles. You must turn each mass into moles and then take the coefficients into account.

faqs.question: Do I always need the balanced equation?
faqs.answer: Yes. The mole ratio comes only from the coefficients of a correctly balanced equation. An unbalanced equation gives wrong ratios and wrong answers.

resources.description: Learn how a titration measures the amount of an unknown substance, how the equivalence point differs from the endpoint, and how to find the equivalence point from amounts.
prerequisites: Molarity and moles in solution, n = M × V
Stoichiometry with mole ratios (Topic 4.5)
Writing balanced and net ionic equations (Topics 4.1 and 4.2)
learningObjectives: Describe what a titration measures and the roles of the analyte, the titrant and the indicator
Distinguish the equivalence point from the endpoint of a titration
Identify the equivalence point from the amounts of titrant and analyte, using the mole ratio of a reaction that goes to completion

Represent titration data on a graph with suitable scale and units, and read the equivalence point from it
resources.calculatorNote: Burette volumes are read to 0.01 mL, so keep 4 significant figures where the data allow; convert mL to L before using n = M × V
keyPoints: A titration finds the amount of an analyte by reacting it with a titrant of known concentration.
The equivalence point is reached when the titrant added has exactly used up the analyte, in the mole ratio of the equation.
The endpoint is the observable change (such as a colour change) that signals the equivalence point. A good method makes the two very close.
At equivalence: n(titrant) = M × V, then the mole ratio gives n(analyte).
M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ works only for a 1:1 reaction. Always use the balanced equation.

faqs.question: Is the equivalence point always at pH 7?
faqs.answer: No. It is at pH 7 for a strong acid with a strong base at 25 °C, but not for titrations involving weak acids or bases. You will study those in Unit 8. In this topic the equivalence point is defined by amounts, not by pH.

faqs.question: Do titrations have to be acid–base reactions?
faqs.answer: No. Any reaction that is fast, goes to completion and has a known equation can be used, including redox and precipitation reactions.

resources.title: Types of Chemical Reactions: Study Guide (Chemistry 4.7)
resources.description: Learn to sort reactions into acid-base, oxidation-reduction and precipitation, using proton transfer, oxidation numbers and a short list of always-soluble salts as evidence.
prerequisites: Writing net ionic equations and spotting spectator ions (Topic 4.2)
Ion charges and formulas of common polyatomic ions
learningObjectives: Assign oxidation numbers to every atom in a molecule, ion or ionic compound
Recognise a redox reaction from a change in oxidation numbers and say which species is oxidised and which is reduced
Recognise combustion as a kind of redox reaction and predict the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon
Recognise an acid-base reaction as the transfer of a proton (H⁺) from one species to another
Recognise a precipitation reaction and use the rule that all sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble to decide which product is the solid
resources.calculatorNote: Oxidation numbers and electron counts are whole numbers or simple fractions; no calculator is needed
keyPoints: The course sorts reactions into three types by what moves: protons (acid-base), electrons (redox), or ions coming together into a solid (precipitation).
A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes. The species whose oxidation number rises is oxidised; the one whose oxidation number falls is reduced.
Electrons always move from the species oxidised to the species reduced, and the numbers lost and gained are equal.
Combustion is redox with oxygen gas. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives only carbon dioxide and water.
All sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts dissolve in water, so in a precipitation reaction the solid is never one of these.

faqs.question: Can a reaction belong to more than one type?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but for this course decide by the evidence. Check oxidation numbers first: if any change, it is redox. If none change, look for a proton passed between species (acid-base) or aqueous ions joining into an ionic solid (precipitation).

faqs.question: Do I need to learn a full table of solubility rules?
faqs.answer: No. The course expects you to know that sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are always soluble. Any other solubility information you need will be given in the question.

resources.description: Learn the Brønsted-Lowry model: acids donate protons, bases accept them, water can do both, and conjugate acid-base pairs let you compare the strengths of acids and bases.
prerequisites: Recognising an acid-base reaction as a proton transfer (Topic 4.7)
Formulas and charges of common polyatomic ions
learningObjectives: Identify the Brønsted-Lowry acid and base in a proton-transfer reaction
Write the conjugate acid or conjugate base of a species and pick out both conjugate pairs in an equation
Explain how water can accept a proton from some species and donate a proton to others
Recognise amphiprotic species and write equations for both of their roles

resources.calculatorNote: Counting particles in a model and simple percentages only
keyPoints: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a Brønsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
A conjugate acid-base pair differs by exactly one H⁺. Removing H⁺ lowers the charge by 1; adding H⁺ raises it by 1.
Every proton-transfer reaction has two conjugate pairs: acid with its conjugate base, and base with its conjugate acid.
Water can act as a base (accepting H⁺ to become H₃O⁺) or as an acid (donating H⁺ to become OH⁻).
The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base. A strong acid ionises fully, so its conjugate base hardly accepts protons at all.

faqs.question: Are H⁺(aq) and H₃O⁺(aq) different things?
faqs.answer: No. A bare proton does not exist on its own in water; it is attached to water molecules. H₃O⁺(aq) shows this. Many equations write H⁺(aq) for short. Both mean the same thing.

faqs.question: Do I need the Lewis definition of acids and bases?
faqs.answer: No. The course uses the Brønsted-Lowry model and focuses on reactions in water. The Lewis model is not assessed.

resources.description: Learn how to split a redox reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balance each one in acidic solution, and combine them so electrons lost equal electrons gained.
prerequisites: Assigning oxidation numbers and spotting the species oxidized and reduced (Topic 4.7)

learningObjectives: Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions for a redox reaction, with electrons shown

In acidic solution, balance a half-reaction in this order: other atoms, then O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with e⁻.
Multiply the half-reactions so that electrons lost equal electrons gained, then add them and cancel everything that appears on both sides.
A balanced redox equation must balance both atoms and total charge, and it never shows free electrons.
The coefficients of the balanced equation are the mole ratios you use in stoichiometry and titration.

faqs.question: Do I need the terms oxidizing agent and reducing agent?
faqs.answer: The course framework says the meaning of these two terms is not assessed on the exam. You will meet them in textbooks, but on the exam you only need to say which species is oxidized and which is reduced.

faqs.question: Why can't I just balance a redox equation by inspection?
faqs.answer: For simple cases you sometimes can. But an equation can have the same atoms on both sides and still have different total charges. The half-reaction method balances atoms and electrons together, so the charge always comes out right.

resources.title: Reaction Rates: Study Guide (Chemistry 5.1)
resources.description: Learn what a reaction rate measures, how coefficients link the rates of different species, how rates are measured in the lab, and why concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts change them.
prerequisites: Balancing chemical equations and using mole ratios (Unit 4)
Molarity as moles of solute per litre of solution (Topic 3.7)
Reading the slope of a straight line on a graph
learningObjectives: Define the rate of a reaction as the change in amount or concentration of a species per unit time, with a positive value and correct units
Use the coefficients of a balanced equation to convert the rate of one species into the rate of another, and into the rate of reaction
Calculate an average rate from experimental data and explain how an instantaneous rate is found from a tangent
Describe lab measurements that can follow a reaction over time, such as gas volume, mass loss and colour
Explain, at the particle level, how concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts change the rate of a reaction
resources.calculatorNote: Molar masses: C 12.01, O 16.00 g mol⁻¹. Keep unrounded values until the final step; rates usually to 2–3 significant figures
keyPoints: A reaction rate is how fast reactants are turned into products: the change in concentration (or amount) per unit time, usually in M s⁻¹.
Reactants are used up, so their rate of disappearance is −Δ[reactant]/Δt. Products form, so their rate of formation is +Δ[product]/Δt. Both are positive numbers.
Coefficients set the ratio of rates. In 3 A → B + 2 C, A disappears three times as fast as B forms.
Rates usually fall as a reaction goes on, because reactant concentrations fall. An average rate covers an interval; an instantaneous rate is the slope of the tangent at one moment.
Higher concentration, higher temperature, larger surface area and a catalyst all make a reaction faster.

faqs.question: Why is the rate of a reactant written with a minus sign?
faqs.answer: Its concentration goes down, so Δ[reactant] is negative. The minus sign turns this into a positive rate, because a rate is always reported as a positive number.

faqs.question: Does a faster reaction make more product?
faqs.answer: No. Rate tells you how quickly product forms, not how much forms in the end. The final amount depends on the amounts of reactants (stoichiometry) and, for reversible reactions, on equilibrium.

resources.title: Multistep Reaction Energy Profile: Study Guide (Chemistry 5.10)
resources.description: Learn how to read and draw the energy profile of a reaction with several elementary steps: one hump per step, intermediates in the valleys, each step's activation energy and the overall ΔH.
prerequisites: Energy profile of a single elementary step: transition state, activation energy and ΔH (Topic 5.6)
Intermediates and the rate-limiting step in a mechanism (Topics 5.7 and 5.8)

learningObjectives: Explain how the energy profile of a multistep reaction is built from the profiles of its elementary steps
Identify transition states, intermediates, the number of steps and the number of intermediates on a profile
Read the activation energy of each step and the overall energy change from a profile

resources.calculatorNote: Energies in kJ mol⁻¹; every value is found by adding or subtracting heights on the profile
keyPoints: A multistep profile is the single-step profiles joined end to end: one hump (transition state) for each elementary step.
Intermediates sit in the valleys between humps. For steps in a chain, the number of intermediates is one less than the number of steps.
Each step's activation energy is measured from the valley where that step starts up to its own peak, not from the reactants.
The step with the largest activation energy is normally the slowest, so it is the rate-limiting step.
The overall ΔH is products minus reactants. It equals the sum of the steps' ΔH values and does not depend on how many steps there are.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an intermediate and a transition state on a profile?
faqs.answer: An intermediate is at a valley (a local minimum): it is a real species that lasts long enough to collide again, and it can in principle be detected. A transition state is at a peak (a maximum): an arrangement of atoms partway between bonds breaking and forming, which cannot be isolated.

faqs.question: Does the profile tell me how long the reaction takes?
faqs.answer: Not directly. The horizontal axis is the reaction coordinate, the progress of bond rearrangements, not time. A taller barrier means a smaller fraction of collisions succeed, so that step is slower, but the profile has no time scale.

prerequisites: Collision model and activation energy (Topics 5.5 and 5.6)

learningObjectives: Explain, at the particle level, the two ways a catalyst can raise the rate of a reaction

resources.calculatorNote: Energies are in kJ mol⁻¹ and rates in M s⁻¹; the numbers are small enough to check by hand
keyPoints: A catalyst raises the rate by making more collisions effective, usually by opening a new reaction path with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst is used up in one step of the mechanism and made again in a later step, so its overall concentration does not change.
An intermediate is the opposite: it is made in one step and used up in a later one.
Because a catalyst is often consumed in the rate-determining step, it can appear in the rate law.
A catalyst does not change ΔH: the reactants and products sit at the same energies on both profiles.

faqs.question: If a catalyst is not used up, why does it appear in the mechanism at all?
faqs.answer: It takes part in the reaction. It is used up in one elementary step and given back in a later one. Only the overall equation hides it, because it cancels when you add the steps.

faqs.question: Does a catalyst give the particles more energy?
faqs.answer: No. At a fixed temperature the spread of collision energies is the same. The catalyst lowers the energy barrier, so a larger fraction of the same collisions can get over it.

faqs.question: Can I write the rate law straight from the balanced equation?
faqs.answer: Not for an overall reaction. The orders must be measured. They often differ from the coefficients, because most reactions happen in several steps. Topic 5.4 shows the one case where you can: a single elementary step.

faqs.question: Why use initial rates?
faqs.answer: At the very start you know exactly what the concentrations are, because you mixed them. Products have not built up and reactants have hardly been used, so nothing else is changing the rate.

faqs.question: Do I have to memorise the three integrated rate laws?
faqs.answer: No. All three, and t½ = 0.693/k, are on the formula sheet in the exam. You do need to know which graph each one makes straight and what the slope means.

faqs.question: Where does 0.693 come from?
faqs.answer: It is ln 2, rounded to three significant figures. Half-life is the time for [A] to fall to half, and ln(1/2) = −0.693.

faqs.question: Can I plot absorbance instead of concentration?
faqs.answer: Yes, if absorbance is directly proportional to concentration (Beer's law). The same plot will be straight and the slope gives the same k for a first-order reaction.

faqs.question: How do I know if a reaction is elementary?
faqs.answer: In this course you are usually told that a step is elementary. You can never prove it from the balanced equation alone. An experimental rate law that differs from the one the equation predicts shows the reaction is not a single step.

faqs.question: Is molecularity the same as order?
faqs.answer: For an elementary step, the overall order equals the molecularity. But order is also used for overall reactions, where it is found by experiment and can be zero or a fraction. Molecularity only applies to elementary steps and is always 1, 2 or 3.

resources.description: Learn why only some collisions lead to reaction, how energy and orientation decide success, and how the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution explains the effect of temperature on rate.
prerequisites: Writing the rate law of an elementary reaction from its equation (Topic 5.4)

learningObjectives: Explain why reactant particles must collide before any bonds can break and form

keyPoints: Particles must collide before bonds can break and new bonds can form. No collision, no reaction.
A collision succeeds only if it has enough energy (at least the activation energy, Eₐ) and a suitable orientation. In most reactions only a small fraction of collisions succeed.
Higher concentration means more collisions per second, so a faster rate. The fraction of collisions that succeed stays the same.
The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows how particle energies are spread out. The area under the curve beyond Eₐ shows the fraction of particles with enough energy.

At a higher temperature the curve flattens and shifts right, so a larger fraction of collisions reach Eₐ. This, much more than the small rise in collision frequency, is why rate rises with temperature.

faqs.question: Does a higher temperature lower the activation energy?
faqs.answer: No. Eₐ is set by the reaction itself. A higher temperature gives more particles enough energy to reach Eₐ; the barrier stays the same height. (A catalyst, which you meet later in this unit, is what provides a route with a lower barrier.)

faqs.question: Why does the area under a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve stay the same when the temperature changes?
faqs.answer: The area represents the total number of particles in the sample. Heating the sample does not add particles; it only spreads their energies out, so the curve gets lower and wider.

Eₐ(reverse) = Eₐ(forward) − ΔH.
k = A e^(−Eₐ/RT): higher T, larger k; larger Eₐ, smaller k and more temperature-sensitive.

resources.title: Reaction Energy Profile: Study Guide (Chemistry 5.6)
resources.description: Learn to draw and read the energy profile of an elementary reaction: reaction coordinate, transition state, forward and reverse activation energy, overall energy change and the Arrhenius idea.
prerequisites: The collision model and Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions (Topic 5.5)
Bond breaking needs energy; bond forming releases energy
learningObjectives: Describe an elementary reaction as bonds breaking and forming along a reaction coordinate
Draw a labelled energy profile for an elementary reaction, showing reactants, transition state and products
Read the forward activation energy, reverse activation energy and overall energy change from a profile, and calculate any one from the other two
Describe the transition state as the highest-energy arrangement, with bonds partly broken and partly formed
Explain, using the Arrhenius equation qualitatively, why rate rises with temperature and why a larger activation energy makes a reaction more sensitive to temperature
resources.calculatorNote: Profile calculations are additions and subtractions in kJ mol⁻¹. Arrhenius values in Worked example 3 are background only
keyPoints: An energy profile plots energy against the reaction coordinate: reactants, up to a single peak (the transition state), down to products.
Forward activation energy = energy of transition state − energy of reactants. Overall energy change ΔH = energy of products − energy of reactants.
Reverse activation energy = energy of transition state − energy of products, so Eₐ(reverse) = Eₐ(forward) − ΔH.
The transition state is the highest-energy arrangement of atoms, with old bonds partly broken and new bonds partly formed. It cannot be isolated.
Arrhenius equation: k = A e^(−Eₐ/RT). Higher temperature gives a larger k; a larger Eₐ gives a smaller k that is more sensitive to temperature. You will not be asked to calculate with it.

faqs.question: Is the transition state the same as an intermediate?
faqs.answer: No. A transition state sits at the top of a peak and lasts only as long as one molecular vibration; it cannot be isolated. An intermediate sits in a dip between two peaks in a multistep reaction and has a real, if short, lifetime. A single elementary step has a transition state but no intermediate.

faqs.question: Does a negative ΔH make a reaction fast?
faqs.answer: No. Speed depends on the activation energy, not on ΔH. A strongly exothermic reaction can still be very slow if its peak is high.

resources.title: Introduction to Reaction Mechanisms: Study Guide (Chemistry 5.7)
resources.description: Learn what a reaction mechanism is, how to spot reactants, products, intermediates and catalysts in its steps, how the steps add up to the overall equation, and how intermediates give evidence.
prerequisites: Elementary reactions and molecularity (Topic 5.4)
The collision model and reaction energy profiles (Topics 5.5 and 5.6)
Balancing chemical equations
learningObjectives: Describe a reaction mechanism as a sequence of elementary steps
Identify the reactants, products, intermediates and catalysts in a proposed mechanism
Add the elementary steps of a mechanism, cancelling species, to check that they give the overall balanced equation
Explain why an intermediate exists only while the reaction is running

keyPoints: A reaction mechanism is a series of elementary steps. The balanced equation shows only the overall change.
When you add the steps and cancel anything that appears on both sides, you must get the overall balanced equation.
An intermediate is made in one step and used up in a later step. It is not in the overall equation and is present only while the reaction runs.
A catalyst is used up in one step and given back in a later step. It is also not in the overall equation.
Detecting an intermediate that only one proposed mechanism predicts is evidence for that mechanism.

faqs.question: Is an intermediate the same as a transition state?
faqs.answer: No. A transition state exists only at the top of an energy barrier during a single collision and cannot be isolated. An intermediate is a real species that is formed in one step and lasts long enough to take part in a later step.

faqs.question: If a mechanism adds up to the right equation, is it correct?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Adding up correctly is a test every mechanism must pass, but different mechanisms can add up to the same equation. You need further evidence, such as a detected intermediate or the rate law (Topic 5.8).

resources.title: Reaction Mechanism and Rate Law: Study Guide (Chemistry 5.8)
resources.description: Learn why the slowest step sets the pace of a reaction, how to write the rate law from a mechanism whose first step is rate limiting, and how to test proposed mechanisms against an experimental rate law.
prerequisites: Rate laws, reaction order and units of k (Topics 5.2 and 5.3)
Writing the rate law of an elementary step from its coefficients (Topic 5.4)
Reaction mechanisms, intermediates and catalysts (Topic 5.7)
learningObjectives: Explain why the slowest elementary step limits the rate of the whole reaction
Write the rate law for a reaction from a mechanism in which the first step is the slow, rate-limiting step
Use the rate law from a mechanism to predict how the rate changes when concentrations change, and give the units of k

Explain why a rate law can support a mechanism but cannot prove it
resources.calculatorNote: Concentrations in mol L⁻¹ (M), rates in M s⁻¹; give answers to the significant figures of the data
keyPoints: A reaction cannot go faster than its slowest elementary step. That step is the rate-limiting (rate-determining) step.
When the first step is the slow step, the rate law of the whole reaction is the rate law of that step: each reactant in it is raised to its coefficient in the step.
The rate law comes from the slow step, not from the overall equation, so reactants used only in later fast steps do not appear in it.
An intermediate never appears in a final rate law. A catalyst can, if it takes part in the slow step.
A mechanism that adds up correctly and predicts the experimental rate law is consistent with the evidence, but it is not proven.

faqs.question: Why can I use the coefficients of the slow step but not those of the overall equation?
faqs.answer: The slow step is an elementary step, so its coefficients show the particles that actually collide. The overall equation is a summary of several steps, so its coefficients say nothing about collisions.

faqs.question: What if the slow step is not the first step?
faqs.answer: Then the slow step usually contains an intermediate, which cannot appear in the final rate law. You need an approximation to replace it; that is Topic 5.9, the pre-equilibrium approximation.

resources.description: Learn how to find the rate law of a mechanism whose first step is a fast equilibrium: set forward and reverse rates equal, solve for the intermediate and substitute it out.
prerequisites: Writing the rate law of an elementary step from its molecularity (Topic 5.4)
Identifying intermediates and the rate-limiting step in a mechanism (Topics 5.7 and 5.8)

learningObjectives: Explain why the rate law of the slow step cannot be the final answer when it contains an intermediate
Use the idea that a fast reversible step has equal forward and reverse rates to write the intermediate's concentration in terms of reactants

resources.calculatorNote: Concentrations in M (mol L⁻¹), time in s; keep unrounded values until the final step
keyPoints: If the first step is slow, its rate law is the overall rate law (Topic 5.8). If a later step is slow, its rate law usually contains an intermediate, so more work is needed.
A fast reversible first step reaches equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate, so k₁[reactants] = k₋₁[intermediate].
Solve that equation for the intermediate and substitute it into the slow step's rate law. The final rate law contains only species you can control, never an intermediate.
The overall rate constant is a combination such as k = k₂k₁ / k₋₁, and orders can be fractions such as ½.
A mechanism that gives the experimental rate law is consistent with the data. It is not proven.

faqs.question: Why can't an intermediate appear in the final rate law?
faqs.answer: An intermediate exists only while the reaction runs, usually at a tiny concentration. You cannot weigh it out or set its concentration, so a rate law that depends on it cannot be tested against experiments. The rate law must use species you add, such as reactants or a catalyst.

faqs.question: Does 'equilibrium' here mean the whole reaction has stopped?
faqs.answer: No. Only the fast first step is close to balance: it goes forward and backward much faster than the slow step drains the intermediate. The overall reaction keeps going at the rate of the slow step.

resources.title: Endothermic and Exothermic Processes: Study Guide (Chemistry 6.1)
resources.description: Decide whether a heating, phase change, reaction or dissolving process is endothermic or exothermic, and justify the claim from temperature data and particle interactions.
prerequisites: Breaking a chemical bond needs energy; forming one releases energy (Topic 2.2)
Intermolecular and interparticle forces (Topic 3.1)
A particle view of solutions and dissolving (Topics 3.7 to 3.10)
learningObjectives: Define the system and the surroundings for a process and say which way energy moves between them
Use a temperature rise or fall in the surroundings to classify a process as exothermic or endothermic
Classify heating and cooling, phase changes and chemical reactions as endothermic or exothermic, and explain why

resources.calculatorNote: Only temperature differences are found. ΔT = T(final) − T(initial); quote it to the same decimal place as the thermometer readings
keyPoints: Exothermic: the system loses energy to the surroundings. Endothermic: the system gains energy from the surroundings.
The thermometer usually sits in the surroundings. If the water warms up, the process inside it is exothermic; if the water cools, the process is endothermic.
Melting, boiling and sublimation are endothermic; freezing, condensing and deposition are exothermic.
Energy lost by the system equals energy gained by the surroundings. It can move as heat or as work.
Dissolving is exothermic when the new solute–solvent attractions are stronger overall than the attractions broken, and endothermic when they are weaker.

faqs.question: Does an endothermic reaction 'give out cold'?
faqs.answer: No. Cold is not a substance and nothing called cold moves. An endothermic process takes energy in, so the water, air or skin that supplied the energy is left with less and its temperature falls.

faqs.question: Can the same event be exothermic and endothermic?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you change the system. Burning gas under a pan is exothermic for the gas and its products. The water in the pan gains that energy, so heating the water is endothermic for the water. Always say which system you mean.

resources.title: Heat Transfer and Thermal Equilibrium: Study Guide (Chemistry 6.3)
resources.description: Explain heat transfer through particle collisions: why energy moves from a warmer body to a cooler one, and why it stops at thermal equilibrium when the temperatures are equal.
prerequisites: Kinetic molecular theory: KE = ½mv² and Kelvin temperature is proportional to average kinetic energy (Topic 3.5)
System, surroundings and conservation of energy (Topic 6.1)
learningObjectives: Link the temperature of a body to the average kinetic energy of its particles
Explain, at the particle level, how collisions transfer energy from a warmer body to a cooler one

resources.calculatorNote: Convert to kelvin with T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15 before comparing average kinetic energies; temperature differences are the same in °C and K
keyPoints: The particles of a warmer body have a greater average kinetic energy than the particles of a cooler body.
When two bodies touch, their particles collide. On average, energy passes from the faster particles to the slower ones, so energy moves from the warmer body to the cooler one. This is heat transfer.
Heat transfer continues until both bodies have the same average kinetic energy, and so the same temperature. This is thermal equilibrium.
At thermal equilibrium the particles still move and collide, but the energy passed each way is equal, so there is no net transfer.
Average kinetic energy is proportional to the Kelvin temperature, so always compare temperatures in kelvin.

faqs.question: Is heat the same thing as temperature?
faqs.answer: No. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles in a body. Heat is energy that moves from one body to another because their temperatures differ. A body has a temperature; it does not 'contain' heat.

faqs.question: Does cold move from an ice cube into my drink?
faqs.answer: No. Only energy moves. Particles in the drink collide with particles of the ice and pass energy to them, so the drink loses energy and its temperature falls.

resources.calculatorNote: Specific heat capacity of water and dilute solutions: 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K. Keep unrounded values until the end; the temperature change usually limits the significant figures
keyPoints: q = mcΔT gives the heat absorbed (q positive) or released (q negative) by a substance that changes temperature without changing phase. ΔT = T(final) − T(initial).
Specific heat capacity c (J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) is the energy needed to warm 1 g by 1 °C. Molar heat capacity (J mol⁻¹ °C⁻¹) is the energy to warm 1 mol by 1 °C: multiply c by the molar mass.
The same energy gives a much larger temperature change in a substance with a small c. Water has an unusually large c (4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹).
Energy is conserved (first law of thermodynamics). In an insulated calorimeter, the heat released by one part equals the heat absorbed by the rest: q(lost) + q(gained) = 0.
If the mixture in a dissolution calorimeter warms, dissolving released energy (exothermic); if it cools, dissolving absorbed energy (endothermic).

faqs.question: Do I use °C or K for ΔT?
faqs.answer: Either. A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size, so a change of 5.0 °C is a change of 5.0 K. You only need kelvin when you use a temperature itself, not a difference, for example in the gas laws or kinetic energy ratios.

faqs.question: Why is the q of the reaction the opposite sign of the q of the water?
faqs.answer: Energy is conserved. If the water in a calorimeter gains 1200 J, that energy came from the process inside it, which therefore lost 1200 J. Gain is positive and loss is negative, so the two values have opposite signs.

prerequisites: Endothermic and exothermic processes, and energy diagrams for phase changes (Topics 6.1 and 6.2)

learningObjectives: Explain why a system gains energy when it melts or boils and loses energy when it freezes or condenses
Explain why the temperature of a pure substance stays constant while it changes phase
Calculate the energy absorbed or released in a phase change from the amount in moles and the molar enthalpy of the change

resources.calculatorNote: Water: ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ at 0 °C, ΔH_vap = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 100 °C, c(liquid) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, c(ice) = 2.09 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Convert J to kJ before adding steps; round only at the end
keyPoints: Melting and boiling need energy (endothermic); freezing and condensing release the same amount (exothermic).
For a phase change, q = n × ΔH, where n is in moles and ΔH is the molar enthalpy of the change in kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔH_freezing = −ΔH_fusion and ΔH_condensation = −ΔH_vaporization.
While a pure substance changes phase, its temperature stays constant: the energy goes into overcoming attractions, not into faster motion.
On a heating curve, flat sections are phase changes and sloping sections are one phase warming up.

faqs.question: Why is a burn from steam worse than a burn from boiling water at the same temperature?
faqs.answer: Steam at 100 °C first condenses on your skin, releasing 40.7 kJ for every mole, and then the water cools. Water at 100 °C only cools. Per gram, condensing releases about five times more energy than cooling the water all the way from 100 °C to 0 °C.

faqs.question: Is ΔH_vap the same at every temperature?
faqs.answer: No, it changes a little with temperature, which is why a data table states the temperature (often the normal boiling point). In this course, use the value you are given for the conditions in the question.

Doubling the equation doubles ΔH; reversing the equation changes its sign.

Only the limiting reactant sets how much reaction happens, and so how much heat is transferred.

faqs.question: What does kJ mol⁻¹ mean when the equation has several substances?
faqs.answer: It means kJ per mole of reaction: the energy for the amounts in the balanced equation as written. For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, one mole of reaction uses 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ and makes 2 mol H₂O.

faqs.question: Is enthalpy change the same thing as energy change?
faqs.answer: For the reactions in this course, carried out at constant pressure, you can treat ΔH as the heat, and so the energy, transferred by the reaction. The fine difference between enthalpy and internal energy is not assessed.

resources.description: Estimate the enthalpy change of a gas-phase reaction from average bond enthalpies: count the bonds broken and formed, find the difference, and explain why the answer is only an estimate.

learningObjectives: Explain why breaking a bond needs energy and forming a bond releases energy

Estimate ΔH for a reaction as the energy needed to break bonds minus the energy released forming bonds
