keyPoints: With no government policy, flexible wages and prices bring the economy back to full-employment output (Yf) in the long run, and unemployment returns to the natural rate.
Recessionary gap: unemployment is high, nominal wages fall, SRAS shifts right, the price level falls and output rises to Yf.
Inflationary gap: labour is scarce, nominal wages rise, SRAS shifts left, the price level rises and output falls back to Yf.
After an AD shock, only the price level is different in the long run. After a temporary SRAS shock, the economy returns to its starting point.
A shift of LRAS means full-employment output has changed. A rightward shift is economic growth.

faqs.question: Does self-adjustment move the AD curve?
faqs.answer: No. Self-adjustment works through input prices, mainly nominal wages, so it shifts the SRAS curve. AD moves only if something changes spending, such as government policy.

faqs.question: Why do governments not just wait for self-adjustment?
faqs.answer: Because it can be slow, especially when wages have to fall. Unemployment stays above the natural rate while the economy waits. Fiscal policy (Topic 3.8) is one way to close a gap faster.

keyPoints: Fiscal policy is the government's use of spending and taxes/transfers to reach goals such as full employment and stable prices.
Government spending is part of AD, so it shifts AD directly. Taxes and transfers change disposable income first, so they shift AD indirectly.
Recessionary gap: expansionary policy (spend more, cut taxes, raise transfers). Inflationary gap: contractionary policy (the opposite).
Change needed = output gap ÷ multiplier. The spending multiplier is larger than the tax multiplier, so a smaller change in spending than in taxes does the job.
Discretionary fiscal policy works with lags: it takes time to recognise a problem, decide on a policy and put it into action.

faqs.question: Is a central bank cutting interest rates fiscal policy?
faqs.answer: No. Fiscal policy is set by the government through spending and taxes. Changes made by the central bank, such as interest rate changes, are monetary policy (Unit 4).

faqs.question: Why is the needed spending change smaller than the gap?
faqs.answer: Because of the multiplier. Each valda of new government spending becomes income that is partly spent again, so AD rises by more than the first change.

resources.description: Learn what automatic stabilizers are, how tax revenue and transfer payments change on their own as real GDP rises and falls, and why this makes recessions and booms milder.
prerequisites: The tax multiplier and how disposable income affects consumption (Topic 3.2)
Expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy, and the lags in discretionary policy (Topic 3.8)
learningObjectives: Define an automatic stabilizer and tell it apart from discretionary fiscal policy

resources.calculatorNote: Only multiplication and subtraction are needed. All data are fictional, in billions of valdas (VD) at base-year prices unless stated.
keyPoints: Automatic stabilizers are parts of the tax and transfer system that change by themselves as real GDP changes, with no new government decision.
In a recession, tax revenue falls and transfer payments rise, so disposable income and consumption fall by less than they otherwise would.
In an expansion, tax revenue rises and transfer payments fall, so consumption rises by less and the economy is less likely to overheat.
They make the shift in AD smaller in both directions. They moderate the business cycle; they do not remove it or restore full employment on their own.
Because no new law is needed, they avoid the decision and implementation lags of discretionary fiscal policy.

faqs.question: If tax revenue falls in a recession, has the government cut taxes?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. With tax rates unchanged, revenue falls because incomes, spending and profits fall. That automatic fall is the stabilizer at work. A cut in tax rates would be a new, discretionary decision.

faqs.question: Do automatic stabilizers shift AD to the right in a recession?
faqs.answer: They make the leftward shift smaller than it would otherwise be. Compared with an economy without them, AD ends up further to the right, so real GDP and the price level fall by less.

faqs.question: Do I need to calculate a multiplier that includes a tax rate?
faqs.answer: No. You need to define automatic stabilizers and explain how they moderate the business cycle. The calculations on this page only use multiplication and subtraction to make the idea concrete.

faqs.question: Why does a bond's price fall when interest rates rise?
faqs.answer: An existing bond pays a fixed amount of interest. When new bonds pay more, nobody will pay the full original price for the old one. Its price falls until a buyer earns the new, higher rate on it.

faqs.question: Is a stock a loan to the company?
faqs.answer: No. A bond is a loan: the issuer promises to repay with interest. A stock is part-ownership of the company. Stockholders are not promised any repayment; they share in profits and in changes in the company's value.

Explain how lenders and borrowers set a nominal interest rate from the real rate they expect and the inflation they expect
Explain how a change in expected inflation affects the nominal rate, and how unexpected inflation changes the real rate actually earned
Calculate a nominal rate from an expected real rate and expected inflation
Calculate a real interest rate in hindsight from a nominal rate and the actual inflation rate, including from price index data
resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Round inflation rates to 2 decimal places before subtracting them from a nominal rate.
keyPoints: The nominal interest rate is the rate written on a loan, not adjusted for inflation.
The real interest rate measures the return in purchasing power: the nominal rate minus inflation.
When a loan is agreed: nominal rate = expected real rate + expected inflation.
In hindsight: real rate = nominal rate − actual inflation rate.
If inflation turns out higher than expected, the real rate is lower than expected, and borrowers gain at lenders' expense.

faqs.question: Can a real interest rate be negative?
faqs.answer: Yes. If inflation is higher than the nominal rate, the real rate is negative. A lender is repaid more valdas than she lent, but they buy less than the valdas she gave up.

faqs.question: Is the real rate exactly the nominal rate minus inflation?
faqs.answer: The course uses this subtraction, and it is very close when rates are small. A more exact method divides instead of subtracting, but you are not asked to use it.

resources.description: Learn what counts as money, its three functions, and how to calculate M1, M2 and the monetary base from data, including how everyday transactions change each measure.
prerequisites: Liquidity and the opportunity cost of holding money (Topic 4.1)

learningObjectives: Define money as any asset that people accept as a means of payment
Identify which function of money (medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value) an example shows

resources.calculatorNote: Only addition and subtraction are needed. All data are fictional, in billions of valdas (VD).
keyPoints: Money is any asset people accept as a means of payment.
Money has three functions: medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
M1 = currency in circulation + demand (checkable) deposits.
M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits + retail money market funds.
Monetary base = currency in circulation + bank reserves. Reserves are in the base but not in M1 or M2.

faqs.question: Is a credit card money?
faqs.answer: No. A credit card lets you borrow for a short time. You pay the debt later with money, usually from a demand deposit. Unused credit limits are not counted in M1 or M2.

faqs.question: Does depositing cash in a checking account change M1?
faqs.answer: No. Currency in circulation falls and demand deposits rise by the same amount, so M1 is unchanged. The money is only changing form.

prerequisites: M1, M2 and the monetary base (Topic 4.3)

resources.calculatorNote: Only multiplication, division and reciprocals are needed. Write the required reserve ratio as a decimal (10% = 0.1). All data are fictional, in millions of valdas (VD).
keyPoints: Assets = liabilities + owners' equity. Demand deposits are a bank's liability; reserves and loans are its assets.
Required reserves = required reserve ratio × demand deposits. Excess reserves = total reserves − required reserves.
A single bank can lend at most its excess reserves.
Maximum money multiplier = 1 ÷ required reserve ratio.
Maximum change in the money supply = initial excess reserves × money multiplier. Excess reserves held by banks and extra currency held by the public make the real change smaller.

faqs.question: Why does a cash deposit not count as new money straight away?
faqs.answer: Cash in circulation and demand deposits are both in M1. When cash is deposited, currency falls and deposits rise by the same amount, so M1 is unchanged. New money appears only when banks lend out the excess reserves the deposit creates.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the money multiplier and the expenditure multiplier?
faqs.answer: The money multiplier links reserves to the money supply and depends on the required reserve ratio. The expenditure multiplier (Topic 3.2) links a change in spending to a change in real GDP and depends on the MPC. They are different ideas.

prerequisites: Bonds and the inverse link between bond prices and interest rates (Topic 4.1)

learningObjectives: Define the money market, money demand and money supply, and draw a correctly labelled money market graph
Explain why the quantity of money demanded falls as the nominal interest rate rises, and why the money supply curve is vertical

resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Money amounts are in billions of valdas (VD bn); interest rates are in per cent a year.
keyPoints: The price of holding money is the nominal interest rate you give up by not holding bonds.
Money demand (MD) slopes down: a higher nominal interest rate means people want to hold less money.
Money supply (MS) is vertical: the central bank fixes it, whatever the interest rate.
Equilibrium is where MD crosses MS. A surplus of money pushes the rate down; a shortage pushes it up.
A higher price level or higher real GDP shifts MD right and raises the interest rate; a bigger money supply lowers it.

faqs.question: Which interest rate goes on the money market graph?
faqs.answer: The nominal interest rate. The loanable funds market (Topic 4.7) uses the real interest rate. Label the axis carefully, because the wrong rate costs the graph point.

faqs.question: Why does the money supply curve not slope upwards like a normal supply curve?
faqs.answer: Banks and households do not decide how much money exists in response to the interest rate in this model. Given the monetary base set by the central bank, the quantity of money is fixed, so the curve is vertical.

resources.title: Monetary Policy: Study Guide (Macroeconomics 4.6)
resources.description: Learn the tools of monetary policy in limited-reserve and ample-reserve banking systems, how open market operations change the money supply, and how policy moves interest rates, output and prices.
prerequisites: The money market and the equilibrium nominal interest rate (Topic 4.5)
Balance sheets, required and excess reserves, and the money multiplier (Topic 4.4)
Recessionary and inflationary output gaps in the AD–AS model (Unit 3)
learningObjectives: Define monetary policy, the policy rate, and expansionary and contractionary monetary policy
Describe the tools of monetary policy and explain how their use differs between banking systems with limited reserves and with ample reserves
Calculate the effect of an open market operation on reserves, the monetary base and the maximum change in the money supply
Use the reserve market, money market and AD–AS models to explain the short-run effects of a monetary policy action
Choose the monetary policy that would close a recessionary or inflationary output gap
Explain why monetary policy works with lags
resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Money amounts are in billions of valdas (VD bn). The maximum money multiplier is 1 ÷ required reserve ratio.
keyPoints: Monetary policy is a central bank's use of interest rates and the money supply to pursue goals such as stable prices and full employment.
Tools: open market operations, the required reserve ratio, the discount rate and administered rates such as interest on reserves.
With limited reserves, the central bank moves interest rates by changing the quantity of reserves. With ample reserves, it moves them by changing its administered rates.
An open market purchase raises reserves and the monetary base; with limited reserves the money supply rises by more, because of the money multiplier.
Expansionary policy lowers interest rates, raising investment, consumption, AD, real output and the price level. Contractionary policy does the opposite.

faqs.question: Is monetary policy the same as fiscal policy?
faqs.answer: No. Fiscal policy is government spending and taxes (Topic 3.8). Monetary policy is carried out by the central bank through interest rates and the money supply.

faqs.question: Which graph should I draw for a monetary policy question?
faqs.answer: Whichever the question asks for. The money market, the reserve market and the AD–AS model can all show the short-run effects. If it asks about the interest rate, use the money market or reserve market; if it asks about output and prices, use AD–AS.

prerequisites: Nominal and real interest rates (Topic 4.2)

learningObjectives: Describe the loanable funds market as the meeting place of savers and borrowers, and draw a correctly labelled graph of it

keyPoints: Savers supply loanable funds and borrowers demand them; the price is the real interest rate.

National saving = private saving (Y − T − C) + public saving (T − G). In a closed economy, investment = national saving.

faqs.question: Why does the loanable funds graph use the real interest rate and not the nominal rate?
faqs.answer: Savers and borrowers care about purchasing power. A saver wants to know how many more goods the money will buy when it is repaid, and a firm compares the real return on a machine with the real cost of borrowing.

faqs.question: Should a government deficit shift demand or supply of loanable funds?
faqs.answer: Either is a sound model. Showing the government as an extra borrower shifts demand right; showing the deficit as lower public saving shifts supply left. Both raise the real interest rate and reduce private investment. Pick one, label it and explain it.

prerequisites: Fiscal policy tools and the spending and tax multipliers (Topics 3.2 and 3.8)

faqs.question: Why would a country use both policies instead of just one?
faqs.answer: Each policy has limits and side effects. Using both lets each move be smaller, and the mix lets policymakers influence the interest rate as well as AD. For example, a central bank can stop a government spending rise from pushing interest rates up.

faqs.question: Is this topic about crowding out?
faqs.answer: Not yet. Here you only need the short-run effects on AD, output, the price level and interest rates. How higher interest rates can reduce private investment over time is Topic 5.5, Crowding Out.

resources.description: Learn how the short-run and long-run Phillips curves show the link between inflation and unemployment, and how demand shocks, supply shocks and changes in the natural rate move the economy.
prerequisites: The natural rate of unemployment (Topic 2.3)
Inflation rates (Topic 2.4)

keyPoints: The short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) slopes downward: in the short run, lower unemployment comes with higher inflation.
The long-run Phillips curve (LRPC) is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment: there is no long-run trade-off.

faqs.question: Can the economy be off the short-run Phillips curve?
faqs.answer: No. The economy is always somewhere on its current SRPC. When something seems to push it off, the SRPC itself has shifted.

faqs.question: Which axis is which?
faqs.answer: The inflation rate goes on the vertical axis and the unemployment rate on the horizontal axis. Both are percentages.

learningObjectives: Explain, with an AD–AS graph, why inflation that lasts is caused by money growth that is too fast for too long
Explain why a sustained fall in the money supply leads to deflation
State the equation of exchange (MV = PY) and the quantity theory of money in your own words

resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Keep unrounded values until the final step; round percentages to 2 decimal places.
keyPoints: Inflation that lasts is a monetary event: it happens when the money supply grows too fast for a long time.
Equation of exchange: M × V = P × Y, where P × Y is nominal GDP.
Quantity theory: velocity is stable and real output is set by real resources, so in the long run a change in M changes P by the same percentage.
At full employment, money does not change real output in the long run. It only changes prices.
Growth form: % change in M + % change in V ≈ inflation rate + % change in real output.

faqs.question: Does printing money ever raise real GDP?
faqs.answer: In the short run it can, because AD rises before wages and other input prices adjust. In the long run, once they adjust, output returns to full employment and only the price level is higher.

faqs.question: What is velocity?
faqs.answer: Velocity is the number of times an average unit of money is spent on final goods and services in a year. It equals nominal GDP divided by the money supply.

faqs.question: Is the quantity theory exact?
faqs.answer: The equation of exchange is always true, because velocity is defined to make it true. The quantity theory adds two assumptions, stable velocity and output fixed by real resources, that hold best in the long run.

resources.description: Learn how to calculate a government budget surplus or deficit, how deficits add to the national debt, and why interest on the debt is a burden that uses funds with other possible uses.
prerequisites: Government purchases and transfer payments (Topics 2.1 and 3.8)

learningObjectives: Define a budget surplus, a budget deficit and a balanced budget

resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Work in VD billion and round to VD 0.01 billion.
keyPoints: Budget balance = tax revenue − (government purchases + transfer payments), with interest on the debt counted as spending.
A positive balance is a surplus; a negative balance is a deficit.
The deficit is a flow for one year; the national debt is the stock built up from past deficits minus surpluses.
A deficit adds to the debt. Only a surplus reduces it.
Interest on the debt must be paid every year, which uses funds that could go to other uses and, if borrowed, makes the debt grow faster.

faqs.question: If the deficit gets smaller, does the national debt fall?
faqs.answer: No. Any deficit, however small, adds to the debt. The debt rises more slowly, but it still rises. The debt falls only when the government runs a surplus.

faqs.question: Is interest on the debt part of G?
faqs.answer: No. G counts government purchases of goods and services. Interest, like a transfer payment, buys no good or service, so it is not in G. It is still government spending in the budget, so it counts when you work out the deficit.

resources.description: Learn how deficit-financed fiscal policy raises the real interest rate in the loanable funds market, crowds out interest-sensitive private spending and can slow long-run growth.
prerequisites: Budget deficits and the national debt (Topic 5.4)

resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Interest rates are real rates in percent; loanable funds are in VD billion.
keyPoints: Crowding out: government borrowing pushes up the real interest rate and so reduces interest-sensitive private spending.
A budget deficit is usually financed by borrowing, which increases the demand for loanable funds.
In the loanable funds graph the demand curve shifts right, the real interest rate rises and private investment falls.
In the short run, crowding out makes the net rise in aggregate demand smaller than the multiplier predicts.
In the long run, less private investment means less physical capital and slower economic growth.

faqs.question: Is crowding out the same as the government spending the money instead of firms?
faqs.answer: Not exactly. Crowding out works through the price of borrowing. Extra government borrowing raises the real interest rate, and firms and households then choose to borrow and spend less on interest-sensitive items.

faqs.question: Can I show government borrowing as a shift of the supply of loanable funds instead?
faqs.answer: Yes. A deficit is negative public saving, so it lowers national saving and shifts supply left. The real interest rate rises and private investment falls either way. Pick one method, label it, and stay consistent.

prerequisites: Real and nominal GDP and the GDP deflator (Topic 2.6)

resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Round growth rates to 2 decimal places and money per person to VD 0.01.
keyPoints: Economic growth is measured by the growth rate of real GDP per capita over time.
Real GDP per capita = real GDP ÷ population; growth rate = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
Labour productivity = real output ÷ number of employed workers.
Productivity depends on physical capital per worker, human capital per worker and technology.

faqs.question: Why per capita and not just real GDP?
faqs.answer: Real GDP can rise simply because there are more people. Dividing by the population shows whether the average person has more goods and services, which is what growth in living standards means.

faqs.question: Is a recovery from a recession economic growth?
faqs.answer: Not in the long-run sense used here. A recovery moves output back towards full employment, from a point inside the PPC towards the curve. Long-run growth means full-employment output itself rises, so the PPC and LRAS shift.

resources.description: Learn how policies that raise productivity or labour force participation lift real GDP per capita, what supply-side fiscal policy is, and how to show its short-run and long-run effects.
prerequisites: Economic growth as growth in real GDP per capita, and its determinants (Topic 5.6)

learningObjectives: Explain how a policy that raises labour productivity raises real GDP per capita and long-run growth
Explain how a policy that raises labour force participation raises real GDP per capita, even with productivity unchanged
Explain why public investment in infrastructure, education and research shifts the LRAS curve and the PPC outward
Define supply-side fiscal policy and give examples that work through incentives to work, save, invest and innovate
Use an AD–AS graph to show the short-run and long-run effects of a supply-side fiscal policy
Identify the trade-offs of growth policies, including present consumption and crowding out
resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Round percentages to 2 decimal places and money to the nearest valda.
keyPoints: Real GDP per capita = output per worker × share of the population that is employed. Policy can raise either part.
Policies that raise productivity: education and training, public infrastructure, support for research and new technology, incentives to invest in capital.
Policies that raise labour force participation (for example, childcare support or lower taxes on extra work) raise output per person even if output per worker is unchanged.
Supply-side fiscal policies change taxes and government spending to change incentives to work, save, invest and innovate, so they shift AS and potential output.
Most growth policies also shift AD in the short run; their lasting effect is a rightward shift of LRAS (an outward shift of the PPC).

faqs.question: Is every expansionary fiscal policy a growth policy?
faqs.answer: No. A rise in spending or a tax cut that only raises AD changes output in the short run. If the economy is at full employment, the long-run result is a higher price level, not more output. A policy raises long-run growth only if it raises the economy's capacity.

faqs.question: What happens to the price level after a supply-side policy?
faqs.answer: It depends on the sizes of the shifts. AD shifts right, which pushes prices up; SRAS and LRAS shift right, which pushes prices down. Without numbers, say the price level could rise, fall or stay the same, but real output rises.

resources.title: Balance of Payments Accounts: Study Guide (Macroeconomics 6.1)
resources.description: Learn what the current account and the capital and financial account record, how credits and debits work, how to calculate both balances, and why they always add up to zero.
prerequisites: Net exports as a component of GDP (Topic 2.1)
What a financial asset is: stocks, bonds and bank deposits (Topic 4.1)
learningObjectives: Define the balance of payments (BOP), the current account (CA) and the capital and financial account (CFA)
List what the current account records: net exports, net income from abroad and net unilateral transfers
Classify an international transaction as a credit or a debit and place it in the correct account

resources.calculatorNote: Only addition and subtraction are needed. Write every balance with its sign: + for a surplus, − for a deficit.
keyPoints: The balance of payments records all of a country's international transactions over a period. It has two parts: the current account (CA) and the capital and financial account (CFA).
CA = net exports + net income from abroad + net unilateral transfers.
CFA = foreign purchases of domestic assets − domestic purchases of foreign assets. A CFA surplus is a net financial capital inflow.
Money flowing into the country is a credit (+); money flowing out is a debit (−).
Total credits equal total debits, so CA + CFA = 0. A CA deficit is matched by a CFA surplus of the same size.

faqs.question: Is the balance of trade the same as the current account?
faqs.answer: No. The balance of trade is net exports of goods and services. It is one part of the current account, which also includes net income from abroad and net unilateral transfers.

faqs.question: If the BOP always balances, how can a country have a 'deficit'?
faqs.answer: The BOP as a whole sums to zero, but each account can be in surplus or deficit. A country can run a current account deficit, as long as it has a capital and financial account surplus of the same size.

keyPoints: Demand for a currency: from buyers of that country's goods, services and assets. Downward sloping.
Supply of a currency: from that country's residents paying in other currencies. Upward sloping.
Surplus: rate falls (depreciation). Shortage: rate rises (appreciation).
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: The Foreign Exchange Market: Study Guide (Macroeconomics 6.3)
resources.description: Learn where the demand for and supply of a currency come from, why the curves slope as they do, how the equilibrium exchange rate is set and how surpluses and shortages push the rate back to equilibrium.
prerequisites: Exchange rates, appreciation and depreciation (Topic 6.2)
Supply, demand and market equilibrium (Topics 1.4 to 1.6)
learningObjectives: Describe the foreign exchange market and say who demands and who supplies a currency
Explain why the demand curve for a currency slopes downward and the supply curve slopes upward
Draw a correctly labelled graph of a foreign exchange market and identify the equilibrium exchange rate
Explain, with a graph, how a surplus or shortage of a currency moves a flexible exchange rate back to equilibrium
Link the market for one currency to the market for the other currency
resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Round exchange rates to 4 decimal places and percentages to 2 decimal places.
keyPoints: In the foreign exchange market one currency is traded for another; the price is the exchange rate.
Demand for a currency comes from people who want that country's goods, services and financial assets. It slopes downward.
Supply of a currency comes from that country's residents paying for things in other currencies. It slopes upward.
The equilibrium exchange rate is where the quantity of the currency demanded equals the quantity supplied.
Above equilibrium there is a surplus and the currency depreciates; below it there is a shortage and the currency appreciates.

faqs.question: What goes on the vertical axis of a foreign exchange graph?
faqs.answer: The price of the currency being traded, measured in the other currency. In the market for valdas, that is ostros per valda. The horizontal axis is the quantity of valdas.

faqs.question: Do I need to know what shifts the curves in this topic?
faqs.answer: Not yet. This topic is about movements along the curves and reaching equilibrium. What shifts demand and supply, including fiscal and monetary policy, is Topic 6.4.

resources.description: One-page recap of what shifts currency demand and supply, how fiscal and monetary policy change exchange rates, and the direction mistakes that cost marks.
learningObjectives: Recall the factors that shift currency demand and supply and the direction of each effect
Recall the policy chains from fiscal and monetary policy to the exchange rate
keyPoints: Demand up or supply down: the currency appreciates.
Demand down or supply up: the currency depreciates.
Lower interest rates (expansionary monetary policy): depreciation. Higher real interest rates (contractionary monetary policy or deficit-financed fiscal expansion): appreciation.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Policies, Economic Conditions and the Foreign Exchange Market: Study Guide (Macroeconomics 6.4)
resources.description: Learn what shifts the demand for and supply of a currency, including tastes, incomes, inflation, interest rates, trade barriers and fiscal and monetary policy, and how each shift changes the equilibrium exchange rate.
prerequisites: The foreign exchange market (Topic 6.3)
Fiscal policy (Topic 3.8) and monetary policy (Unit 4)
learningObjectives: List the main factors that shift the demand for a currency and the supply of a currency
Show on a correctly labelled graph how a shift in currency demand or supply changes the equilibrium exchange rate
Trace how expansionary or contractionary fiscal policy can change a country's exchange rate
Trace how expansionary or contractionary monetary policy changes interest rates and the exchange rate
Predict the effect of one event on both currencies, and of two events when the outcome may be uncertain
resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Round exchange rates to 4 decimal places and percentages to 2 decimal places.
keyPoints: Demand for a currency shifts with foreign demand for the country's goods, services and assets (tastes, foreign incomes, relative prices, relative interest rates).
Supply of a currency shifts with residents' demand for foreign goods, services and assets, including the effect of tariffs and quotas on imports.
Higher demand or lower supply makes the currency appreciate; lower demand or higher supply makes it depreciate.
Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates and makes the currency depreciate; contractionary policy does the opposite.
Deficit-financed expansionary fiscal policy raises the real interest rate, which increases demand for the currency, so it appreciates.

faqs.question: Should I shift demand or supply when interest rates change?
faqs.answer: Either shift gives the right direction if your reasoning is right. A higher Valdorian interest rate raises foreign demand for valdas and also cuts Valdorians' supply of valdas for foreign assets. Both make the valda appreciate. Showing the demand shift alone is the usual answer.

faqs.question: Does this topic cover the effect on net exports and aggregate demand?
faqs.answer: No. Here you find the change in the exchange rate. How appreciation or depreciation then changes net exports and aggregate demand is Topic 6.5.

keyPoints: Questions 1–4 are multiple choice; 5–7 need written working or graphs.
Appreciation lowers net exports; depreciation raises them.
Each answer explains why the wrong options are wrong.

resources.title: Changes in the Foreign Exchange Market and Net Exports: Revision Notes (Macroeconomics 6.5)
resources.description: One-page recap of how appreciation and depreciation change export and import prices, net exports and aggregate demand, with the conversion rules and the mistakes that cost marks.
learningObjectives: Recall how a change in a currency's value affects exports, imports, net exports and aggregate demand
Convert prices between two currencies without turning the calculation upside down
keyPoints: Appreciation: X falls, M rises, NX falls, AD shifts left.
Depreciation: X rises, M falls, NX rise, AD shifts right.
One currency's appreciation is the other currency's depreciation.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Changes in the Foreign Exchange Market and Net Exports: Study Guide (Macroeconomics 6.5)
resources.description: Learn how an appreciation or depreciation changes the prices of exports and imports, why it moves net exports in the opposite direction, and how that shifts aggregate demand.
prerequisites: Appreciation, depreciation and the foreign exchange market graph (Topics 6.2 and 6.3)
What shifts the demand for and supply of a currency (Topic 6.4)
Net exports as a component of aggregate demand (Topic 3.1) and the spending multiplier (Topic 3.2)
learningObjectives: Convert the price of a traded good from one currency into another before and after a change in the exchange rate
Explain why an appreciation lowers a country's exports, raises its imports and so lowers its net exports
Explain why a depreciation raises a country's exports, lowers its imports and so raises its net exports
Link a change in net exports to a shift of aggregate demand and its short-run effects on real output, employment and the price level
Show the whole chain on a foreign exchange market graph and an AD–AS graph
resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Exchange rates are given as kestas (KS) per valda (VD). Round money to 2 decimal places.
keyPoints: When a country's currency appreciates, its goods become dearer for foreigners and foreign goods become cheaper at home.
Appreciation: exports fall, imports rise, net exports fall.
Depreciation: exports rise, imports fall, net exports rise.
A change in net exports that is not caused by the price level shifts aggregate demand.
A rise (fall) in AD raises (lowers) real output, employment and the price level in the short run.

faqs.question: Is a strong currency good or bad for a country?
faqs.answer: Neither on its own. An appreciation helps buyers of imports and hurts exporters. For the economy as a whole it lowers net exports and aggregate demand, which is unwelcome in a recession but can help cool an overheating economy.

faqs.question: When one currency appreciates, does the other always depreciate?
faqs.answer: Yes. An exchange rate links two currencies. If the valda buys more kestas, each kesta must buy fewer valdas, so the kesta has depreciated against the valda.

prerequisites: Drawing the loanable funds and foreign exchange market graphs

Explain the effect of capital flows on exchange rates and on loanable funds markets in both countries
Trace changes in saving, borrowing and monetary policy through capital flows to net exports
Use CA + CFA = 0 to link capital flows to the current account
resources.calculatorNote: Real interest rate = nominal interest rate − expected inflation. Exchange rates are written as kestas (KS) per valda (VD).
keyPoints: Questions 1–4 are multiple choice; 5–7 need written working or graphs.
Compare real interest rates, then follow the flow through each market.

resources.description: One-page recap of how real interest rate differences move financial capital between countries, and the knock-on effects on exchange rates, loanable funds, net exports and the balance of payments.
learningObjectives: Recall the direction of capital flows, exchange-rate changes and loanable funds shifts when real interest rates differ
Spot the common errors in multi-market answers before making them
keyPoints: Capital flows towards the relatively higher real interest rate.
Inflow → demand for the currency rises → appreciation → net exports fall.
Inflow → supply of loanable funds rises at home; outflow → supply falls abroad.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Real Interest Rates and International Capital Flows: Study Guide (Macroeconomics 6.6)
resources.description: Learn why financial capital flows towards the country with the relatively higher real interest rate, and how that flow changes loanable funds markets, exchange rates and net exports.
prerequisites: Nominal and real interest rates (Topic 4.2) and the loanable funds market (Topic 4.7)
The balance of payments: current account and capital and financial account (Topic 6.1)
How a currency change affects net exports and aggregate demand (Topic 6.5)
learningObjectives: Compare real interest rates across countries and predict the direction of financial capital flows
Explain how a capital flow shifts the demand for or supply of a currency and changes the exchange rate
Explain how capital inflows and outflows shift the supply of loanable funds and change real interest rates in both countries
Explain how a central bank's short-run influence on the interest rate, or government borrowing, changes net capital inflows
Connect capital flows to net exports and to the balance of payments identity, current account + capital and financial account = 0
resources.calculatorNote: All the arithmetic works on a four-function calculator. Real interest rate = nominal interest rate − expected inflation, in percentage points.
keyPoints: Financial capital flows towards the country with the relatively higher real interest rate.
An inflow raises demand for the country's currency, so it appreciates; the country's net exports then fall.
An inflow adds to the supply of loanable funds at home; an outflow reduces it abroad.
A central bank can change the domestic interest rate in the short run, and so change net capital inflows.
A bigger capital and financial account surplus goes with a bigger current account deficit (CA + CFA = 0).

faqs.question: Why use the real interest rate and not the nominal one?
faqs.answer: Savers care about what their returns will buy. A high nominal rate in a country with high expected inflation can still give a low real return, so the real rate is the fair comparison.

faqs.question: Is financial capital the same as physical capital?
faqs.answer: No. Financial capital here means funds used to buy financial assets such as bonds, shares and bank deposits. Physical capital means machines, buildings and equipment.

resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Drawing Graphs and Writing Cause-and-Effect Explanations: Exam Skills Guide (Macroeconomics)
resources.description: Draw correctly labelled AD-AS, money market, loanable funds, Phillips curve and foreign exchange graphs, link two graphs in one answer, write complete cause-and-effect chains and set out calculations.
prerequisites: You have studied most of the six units of the course, or are revising them
You can draw a supply and demand graph and show a shift of one curve
learningObjectives: Draw the five main graphs of the course with correct axis labels and curve labels, and show a shift with a new curve, an arrow and a labelled new equilibrium
Link two graphs in one answer so that the result of the first graph becomes the cause on the second
Write cause-and-effect chains that name the direction of every variable from the starting change to the final outcome
Set out multiplier, money creation and real-value calculations with a formula, substituted numbers and a labelled answer
Tell identify, explain and calculate questions apart and give each the kind of answer it asks for
resources.calculatorNote: A four-function calculator is enough. All data are fictional, in billions of valdas (VD bn) for Valdoria; the kesta (KS) is the currency of Kestria. Rates are in per cent.
keyPoints: A graph earns credit only when both axes and every curve are labelled, the shift is shown with a new labelled curve, and the new equilibrium values are marked on the axes.
When an answer needs two graphs, the variable that changes on the first graph is the cause on the second: the nominal interest rate links the money market to AD-AS.
A cause-and-effect chain states the direction of every link, for example: interest rate falls, investment rises, AD increases, real GDP and the price level rise.
Calculations need a formula, the numbers substituted and an answer with units; the multiplier you use must match the change (spending, tax or money).
Identify asks for a short answer, explain asks how or why, and calculate asks for working.

faqs.question: Do I need to put numbers on my graphs?
faqs.answer: Only when the question gives numbers or asks you to show a value. Otherwise use labels such as PL₁, PL₂, Y₁ and Y₂ on the axes, with dashed lines from each equilibrium to the axes.

faqs.question: Can a graph replace a written explanation?
faqs.answer: A graph can support an explanation, but when the question says explain, write the chain in words as well. The graph shows the result; the words show the reason.

faqs.question: How long should a cause-and-effect chain be?
faqs.answer: Long enough to reach the variable the question asks about, with no gaps. Most chains have three to five links. Stop when you reach the outcome asked for.

resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Task Verbs and Free-Response Technique: Exam Skills Guide (Macroeconomics)
resources.description: What each free-response task verb asks you to do, how much to write, how to read a multi-part question, plan your time and show work, with original worked examples.
prerequisites: You have studied at least the first three units of the course
You can draw the basic course graphs: AD–AS, the money market, loanable funds and the foreign exchange market
learningObjectives: Say what each free-response task verb requires and how much to write for it
Read a multi-part question so that each part uses the right information and your earlier answers
Plan the 60 minutes of the free-response section across one long and two short questions
Show calculation work so a reader can follow every step from formula to answer
Spot the habits that earn credit and the habits that lose it
resources.calculatorNote: A four-function calculator is enough for every example. Write the formula before the numbers, keep unrounded values until the last step, and round money to VD 0.01 and percentages to 2 decimal places.
keyPoints: The task verb tells you the kind of answer: a short claim, a reason, a number with work, a graph, or a change shown on a graph.
Identify and question words (what, which, will) need a short answer; explain needs the cause, the link and the result.
Read every part before you write: later parts often build on your earlier answers and graphs.
For a calculation, write the formula, substitute the numbers, then give the answer with units.
Most lost credit comes from mislabelled graphs, missing steps in a chain of reasoning and bare numbers with no work.

faqs.question: How long should an answer be?
faqs.answer: As long as the verb needs. For identify, a word or a short phrase is enough. For explain, write the cause, the link and the result, usually one to three sentences. Extra writing can add a wrong statement that cancels a right one.

faqs.question: What if I get an early part wrong?
faqs.answer: Keep going and stay consistent. Use your own earlier answer in later parts and say so, for example 'using my answer to part (B)'. A later part can still show correct economics even if the earlier value was wrong.

faqs.question: Can I use arrows instead of sentences when I explain?
faqs.answer: Yes, graphs and symbols can be part of an explanation. Each link must still be clear: name what changes and in which direction, for example 'money supply rises, so the nominal interest rate falls, so investment rises'.

resources.title: Scarcity: Study Guide (Microeconomics 1.1)
resources.description: Learn what scarcity means in economics, the four factors of production, why most resources are scarce, why shared knowledge may not be, and how scarcity forces choices and trade-offs.
prerequisites: No economics needed: this is the first topic of the course
Basic arithmetic (multiplication and division)
learningObjectives: Explain what economists mean by scarcity and why it forces people and societies to make choices
Name the factors of production (land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship) and classify real resources into them
Explain the causes of scarcity: limited resources with alternative uses set against wants that keep growing
Explain why some resources, such as established knowledge, may not be scarce because they are non-rival
Distinguish scarcity from a shortage, and link scarcity to trade-offs and opportunity cost
resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are needed
keyPoints: Scarcity means there are not enough resources to satisfy everything people want and need.
The factors of production are land, labour, capital (tools, machines, buildings) and entrepreneurship. Money is not a factor of production.
Resources are scarce because they are limited and have other uses, while wants keep growing. Time is scarce for everyone.
Scarcity forces choices, and every choice is a trade-off: the next best option given up is the opportunity cost.
Established knowledge can be used by many people at once without running out (it is non-rival), so it may not be scarce.

faqs.question: Is scarcity the same as a shortage?
faqs.answer: No. A shortage is a temporary gap in one market that can disappear. Scarcity is permanent and affects every resource that is limited relative to wants.

faqs.question: Do rich countries face scarcity?
faqs.answer: Yes. A rich country has more resources, but wants still exceed them, and time is limited. It must still choose between uses.

resources.title: Resource Allocation and Economic Systems: Study Guide (Microeconomics 1.2)
resources.description: Learn the three questions every economy must answer and how command, market and mixed economies answer them, with their coordinating mechanisms, strengths and limits.
prerequisites: Scarcity and the factors of production (Topic 1.1)
Opportunity cost and trade-offs
learningObjectives: State the three basic questions of resource allocation: what, how and for whom to produce
Describe how a command, a market and a mixed economy answer each of the three questions
Identify the main institutions and the coordinating mechanism of each economic system
Compare the economic systems, including their similarities, differences and limitations as models
Explain, with simple cost data, how prices in a market guide the choice of production method
resources.calculatorNote: Only multiplication, addition and subtraction are needed. All prices and quantities are fictional
keyPoints: Because resources are scarce, every society must decide what to produce, how to produce it and who gets the output.
An economic system is a set of institutions (who owns resources, who decides) plus a coordinating mechanism (plans or prices).
Command economy: a central authority owns most resources and answers the three questions through a plan.
Market economy: private owners answer the questions through buying and selling; prices coordinate their choices.
Mixed economy: markets answer most questions, and government answers some. Every real economy is mixed, to different degrees.

faqs.question: Which economic system is best?
faqs.answer: The course asks you to compare systems, not to rank them. Each has strengths and limits, and real economies combine features of both pure models.

faqs.question: Do economic systems change scarcity?
faqs.answer: No. Scarcity exists in every system. The system only changes who makes the choices and how they are coordinated.

resources.title: Production Possibilities Curve: Study Guide (Microeconomics 1.3)
resources.description: Learn how a production possibilities curve shows scarcity, trade-offs and opportunity cost, why it bows outward, and how to tell a shift of the curve from a movement along it.
prerequisites: Scarcity and the idea of opportunity cost (Topic 1.1)

learningObjectives: Define the production possibilities curve (PPC) and state the assumptions behind it
Use a PPC to identify efficient, inefficient and unattainable combinations
Calculate opportunity cost from a PPC table or graph, for constant and increasing opportunity cost
Explain why a PPC is linear or bowed outward
Distinguish a shift of the PPC from a movement along or towards it, and explain what causes each
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use subtraction and division only
keyPoints: A PPC shows every maximum combination of two goods an economy can make with fixed resources and technology, using them fully and efficiently.
On the curve = efficient; inside = inefficient (unused or misused resources); outside = unattainable for now.
Opportunity cost of one more unit of X = units of Y given up ÷ extra units of X gained.
A straight PPC means constant opportunity cost; a PPC bowed outward means increasing opportunity cost.
More or better resources, or better technology, shift the PPC outward (growth). Re-employing idle resources only moves a point towards the curve.

faqs.question: Is a point inside the PPC impossible?
faqs.answer: No. A point inside is easy to reach; it is simply wasteful. The economy could have more of at least one good without giving up any of the other.

faqs.question: Why do we only use two goods?
faqs.answer: Two goods let us draw the trade-off on a flat graph. The second good can stand for 'everything else', so the model still says something about a real economy.

resources.title: Comparative Advantage and Trade: Study Guide (Microeconomics 1.4)
resources.description: Learn the difference between absolute and comparative advantage, how to find each from output or input data, and how specialisation and fair terms of trade let both sides gain.
prerequisites: Opportunity cost (Topic 1.1)
Reading a linear PPC and calculating opportunity cost from it (Topic 1.3)
learningObjectives: Define absolute advantage and comparative advantage and explain how they differ
Identify absolute and comparative advantage from output tables, input tables and PPCs
Explain why producers should specialise by comparative advantage, not absolute advantage
Show how specialisation and trade let each side consume a combination outside its own PPC
Calculate the range of terms of trade that benefits both sides, and test a proposed rate
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use division, multiplication and subtraction only
keyPoints: Absolute advantage: you can produce more of a good than another producer with the same resources (or the same output with fewer resources).
Comparative advantage: you can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
Specialise according to comparative advantage, not absolute advantage. Then trade.
Mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the two producers' opportunity costs.
With trade, each side can consume a combination outside its own PPC, even though its PPC has not moved.

faqs.question: Can one country have a comparative advantage in both goods?
faqs.answer: No. With two goods and two producers, if one has the lower opportunity cost for one good, the other must have the lower opportunity cost for the second good. If the costs are equal, neither has a comparative advantage.

faqs.question: Does trade shift a country's PPC outward?
faqs.answer: No. The PPC shows what a country can produce, and that does not change. Trade lets it consume a combination outside its PPC.

resources.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis: Study Guide (Microeconomics 1.5)
resources.description: Learn how rational decision makers weigh costs and benefits: opportunity cost, explicit and implicit costs, net benefit, and when to use totals instead of marginal steps.
prerequisites: Scarcity and the idea of opportunity cost (Topic 1.1)
Reading values from a table and a simple line graph
learningObjectives: Define opportunity cost and identify the next-best alternative given up in a choice
Tell explicit costs from implicit costs and add them to find the total economic cost of a decision
Explain how total benefit is measured for a consumer (utility) and for a firm (total revenue)

Explain which decisions can be split into marginal steps and which must be judged on totals alone
resources.calculatorNote: All data are fictional. Calculations use addition, subtraction and multiplication only
keyPoints: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up, not the sum of every alternative.
Total economic cost = explicit costs (money paid out) + implicit costs (value of your own resources and income given up).
Total benefit is utility for a consumer and total revenue for a firm.
Net benefit = total benefit − total cost. The rational choice is the option with the largest net benefit.
'How much' decisions can be taken one step at a time using marginal benefit and marginal cost. 'All or nothing' decisions must compare totals.

faqs.question: Is an implicit cost a real cost if no money changes hands?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you use your own time, building or savings, you give up what they could have earned elsewhere. That lost value is part of the economic cost of the decision.

faqs.question: Should I choose the option with the biggest total benefit?
faqs.answer: No. Choose the option where total benefit minus total cost is largest. The biggest total benefit often comes with an even bigger total cost.

resources.title: Marginal Analysis and Consumer Choice: Study Guide (Microeconomics 1.6)
resources.description: Learn how to decide using marginal benefit and marginal cost, why sunk costs do not matter, how diminishing marginal utility works, and how a consumer spends a budget to get the most utility.
prerequisites: Opportunity cost, total benefit and total cost (Topic 1.5)
Reading values from a table and a simple graph
learningObjectives: State the assumptions of the model of rational consumer choice
Define marginal benefit, marginal cost, marginal utility and marginal analysis
Use marginal benefit and marginal cost from a table or graph to decide whether to do more, less or the same of an activity
Explain why sunk costs and benefits already fixed by past choices do not change the best quantity
Calculate total and marginal utility and explain diminishing marginal utility
Find the combination of two goods that maximizes utility by comparing marginal utility per dollar
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use addition, subtraction and division only. All people, prices and utility values are fictional
keyPoints: Marginal means one more unit. Marginal benefit (MB) is the extra benefit of one more unit; marginal cost (MC) is the extra cost.
If MB > MC, do more. If MB < MC, do less. The best quantity is where MB = MC, which is where total net benefit is largest.
Sunk costs, and benefits already fixed by past choices, do not change the best quantity: only what changes at the margin matters.
Marginal utility usually falls as you consume more of a good (diminishing marginal utility), even while total utility still rises.
With a fixed income, utility is maximized when all income is spent and MU ÷ price is equal for the last unit of each good.

faqs.question: What is a util?
faqs.answer: An imaginary unit of satisfaction. Utils let us compare choices with numbers. Only the comparisons matter, not the size of one util.

faqs.question: Do I need indifference curves for this course?
faqs.answer: No. Indifference curves are outside the course. You do need to compare marginal utility divided by price for two goods.

resources.title: Demand: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.1)
resources.description: Learn the law of demand, why demand curves slope down, how market demand is built from individual demand, and how to tell a change in quantity demanded from a shift in demand.
prerequisites: Marginal benefit and diminishing marginal utility (Topic 1.6)

learningObjectives: Explain why markets need clearly defined property rights, and how buyers respond to incentives and constraints

resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction and multiplication are needed. All people, prices and quantities are fictional
keyPoints: Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price in a period, with other influences held constant.
Law of demand: when a good's own price rises, quantity demanded falls (and the reverse). This is a movement along the demand curve.
Demand slopes down because of the substitution effect, the income effect and diminishing marginal utility. The demand curve is a marginal benefit curve.
Market demand = the sum of every buyer's quantity demanded at each price (add horizontally).
A change in any determinant other than own price (income, related prices, tastes, expectations, number of buyers) shifts the whole curve.

faqs.question: Why is price on the vertical axis if quantity depends on price?
faqs.answer: It is a convention in economics. Read the demand curve either way: across from a price to find quantity demanded, or up from a quantity to find the marginal benefit of the last unit.

faqs.question: Does a demand curve have to be a straight line?
faqs.answer: No. Straight lines are used because they are easy to draw and read. What matters is that the curve slopes downward.

resources.title: Supply: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.2)
resources.description: Learn the law of supply, why supply curves slope upward, how market supply is built from individual sellers, and how input costs, technology and other determinants shift supply.
prerequisites: Demand, determinants and shifts versus movements (Topic 2.1)
Marginal cost and increasing opportunity cost (Topics 1.3 and 1.6)
learningObjectives: State the law of supply and show it as a movement along an upward-sloping supply curve
Explain the upward slope using marginal cost and the profit incentive
Build an individual supply schedule from marginal cost data
Build a market supply schedule by adding individual quantities supplied at each price
Identify the determinants of supply and show how each one shifts the supply curve
Explain how sellers respond to changes in incentives, such as taxes and subsidies, and in technology
resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction and multiplication are needed. All farms, prices and quantities are fictional
keyPoints: Supply is the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at each price in a period, with other influences held constant.
Law of supply: when a good's own price rises, quantity supplied rises (and the reverse). This is a movement along the supply curve.
Supply slopes up because extra output costs more to produce (rising marginal cost), so sellers need a higher price to produce more.
Market supply = the sum of every seller's quantity supplied at each price (add horizontally).
Input prices, technology, prices of other goods the seller could make, taxes and subsidies, expectations, number of sellers and natural conditions shift the whole curve.

faqs.question: Is a decrease in supply a shift down?
faqs.answer: No. A decrease in supply shifts the curve to the left, which on the graph also looks like a shift up: sellers need a higher price for each quantity. An increase shifts it right (down).

faqs.question: Is supply the same as the amount actually sold?
faqs.answer: No. Supply shows what sellers would offer at each price. How much is actually sold depends on demand too, which you will see in Topic 2.6.

resources.title: Price Elasticity of Demand: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.3)
resources.description: Learn what price elasticity of demand measures, how to calculate it with the midpoint method, why slope is not elasticity, what makes demand elastic, and how a price change affects total revenue.
prerequisites: The law of demand and reading a demand curve (Topic 2.1)
Calculating a percentage change
learningObjectives: Define price elasticity of demand and explain what its size tells you
Calculate price elasticity of demand from a table, a graph or given percentages, using the midpoint method where needed
Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, unit elastic, perfectly elastic or perfectly inelastic over a price range
Explain why elasticity changes along a straight-line demand curve even though the slope does not
Explain how the availability of substitutes and other factors affect price elasticity of demand
Use the total revenue test to predict how a price change affects total revenue or total expenditure
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use subtraction, addition and division only. Give elasticities to 2 decimal places unless exact. All data are fictional
keyPoints: Price elasticity of demand (PED) = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. Economists usually quote its size and ignore the minus sign.
|PED| > 1 is elastic, |PED| < 1 is inelastic and |PED| = 1 is unit elastic over the price range you measured.
Use the midpoint method: divide each change by the average of the two values, so the answer is the same whether price rises or falls.
Slope is not elasticity. On a straight-line demand curve, demand is elastic above the midpoint, unit elastic at it and inelastic below it.
Total revenue test: if demand is elastic, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; if inelastic, they move in the same direction; if unit elastic, total revenue does not change.

faqs.question: Why is price elasticity of demand negative?
faqs.answer: By the law of demand, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so one percentage change is positive and the other negative. Economists usually drop the sign and compare the size with 1.

faqs.question: Do I always have to use the midpoint method?
faqs.answer: Use it when you are given two prices and two quantities. If a question gives you the percentage changes directly, just divide one by the other.

resources.title: Price Elasticity of Supply: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.4)
resources.description: Learn what price elasticity of supply measures, how to calculate it with the midpoint method, how to classify supply, and why time, spare capacity and the cost of extra inputs make supply more or less elastic.
prerequisites: The law of supply and reading a supply curve (Topic 2.2)
The midpoint method for percentage changes (Topic 2.3)
learningObjectives: Define price elasticity of supply and explain what its size tells you
Calculate price elasticity of supply from a table, a graph or given percentages
Classify supply as elastic, inelastic, unit elastic, perfectly elastic or perfectly inelastic over a price range
Explain how time, spare capacity, the price and availability of extra or alternative inputs, and storage affect price elasticity of supply
Draw supply curves that show different elasticities, including short-run and long-run supply
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use subtraction, addition and division only. Give elasticities to 2 decimal places unless exact. All data are fictional
keyPoints: Price elasticity of supply (PES) = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price. It is positive, because price and quantity supplied move together.
PES > 1 is elastic, PES < 1 is inelastic and PES = 1 is unit elastic over the price range you measured.
Use the midpoint method when you are given two prices and two quantities.
Supply is more elastic when firms have more time, spare capacity, easy access to extra or alternative inputs at a steady price, or stocks they can sell.
Supply is usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run, so the long-run supply curve is flatter through the same point.

faqs.question: Is there a total revenue test for supply?
faqs.answer: No. Along a supply curve a higher price comes with a larger quantity supplied, so sellers' revenue always rises when the price rises. The total revenue test belongs to demand.

faqs.question: What is the most important factor for supply elasticity?
faqs.answer: Time. Given longer, firms can hire, buy machines, build new capacity and new firms can enter, so the quantity supplied responds much more to a price change.

resources.title: Other Elasticities: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.5)
resources.description: Learn how income elasticity and cross-price elasticity of demand are calculated, what their signs and sizes tell you, and how to use them to classify normal, inferior, substitute and complementary goods.
prerequisites: Normal and inferior goods, substitutes and complements as determinants of demand (Topic 2.1)
The midpoint method for percentage changes (Topic 2.3)
learningObjectives: Explain that elasticity can measure the response of quantity to any determinant of demand or supply, not only price
Define and calculate income elasticity of demand, and use its sign to classify a good as normal or inferior
Define and calculate cross-price elasticity of demand, and use its sign to classify two goods as substitutes, complements or unrelated
Use a demand graph to show how a change in income or in the price of a related good shifts demand
Use a known elasticity to predict the percentage change in quantity demanded
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use subtraction, addition, multiplication and division only. Give elasticities to 2 decimal places unless exact. All data are fictional
keyPoints: Any elasticity = percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in the thing that caused it.
Income elasticity of demand (YED) = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income. Positive means a normal good; negative means an inferior good.
Cross-price elasticity of demand (XED) = % change in quantity demanded of good X ÷ % change in the price of good Y. Positive means substitutes; negative means complements; zero means unrelated.
For YED and XED, keep the sign. The sign tells you the type of good; the size tells you how strong the link is.
A change in income or in a related good's price shifts the demand curve. Own-price elasticity is about movements along it.

faqs.question: Why do I keep the minus sign here when I could drop it for price elasticity of demand?
faqs.answer: For price elasticity of demand the sign is always negative, so it carries no news. For income and cross-price elasticity the sign can be positive or negative, and it is the sign that tells you whether a good is normal or inferior, or whether two goods are substitutes or complements.

faqs.question: Can I use the total revenue test with income or cross-price elasticity?
faqs.answer: No. The total revenue test links a change in a good's own price to spending on that good. Income and cross-price elasticities describe shifts of the whole demand curve, so they need a different kind of reasoning.

resources.title: Market Equilibrium and Consumer and Producer Surplus: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.6)
resources.description: Learn how demand and supply set the equilibrium price and quantity, how prices guide resource allocation, and how to measure consumer, producer and total surplus from a graph or a table.
prerequisites: Demand, supply and their determinants (Topics 2.1 and 2.2)
Marginal benefit and marginal cost (Topics 1.5 and 1.6)
Area of a triangle: ½ × base × height
learningObjectives: Define market equilibrium and find the equilibrium price and quantity from a table, a graph or a list of buyers and sellers
Explain how equilibrium price carries information that guides buyers' and sellers' decisions
Define consumer surplus and producer surplus and show them as areas on a supply and demand graph
Calculate consumer, producer and total surplus at equilibrium from a graph or a table
Explain why a perfectly competitive market in equilibrium, with no market failures, maximises total surplus
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use addition, subtraction, multiplication and division only. Surplus areas are triangles: ½ × base × height. All data are fictional
keyPoints: Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The market clears: there is no shortage and no surplus.
The equilibrium price is a signal. It tells buyers how scarce a good is and tells sellers where resources are most wanted.
Consumer surplus = what buyers are willing to pay minus what they pay. On a graph, it is the area below demand and above the price.
Producer surplus = the price sellers receive minus the lowest price they would accept. On a graph, it is the area above supply and below the price.
Total surplus = consumer surplus + producer surplus. With no market failures, it is largest at the competitive equilibrium, so the market is efficient.

faqs.question: Is consumer surplus the same as the money buyers save?
faqs.answer: Not quite. It is the gap between the most a buyer would have paid and the price actually paid. No money changes hands for it. It is a measure of the extra benefit buyers get from trading.

faqs.question: Does the equilibrium price change the size of total surplus?
faqs.answer: The quantity traded decides total surplus. The price only decides how it is split between buyers and sellers. In a competitive market, though, the price is what brings the market to the quantity that makes total surplus largest.

resources.title: Market Disequilibrium and Changes in Equilibrium: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.7)
resources.description: Learn what shortages and surpluses are, how market forces remove them, and how shifts in demand and supply change price, quantity, consumer surplus and producer surplus.
prerequisites: Demand, supply and the difference between a shift and a movement along a curve (Topics 2.1 and 2.2)
Price elasticity of demand and supply (Topics 2.3 and 2.4)
Market equilibrium, consumer surplus and producer surplus (Topic 2.6)
learningObjectives: Define a shortage and a surplus and calculate their size from a table, equations or a graph
Explain how a shortage or surplus pushes price and quantity back towards equilibrium
Predict and show on a graph how a shift in demand or supply changes equilibrium price and quantity
Calculate changes in consumer surplus, producer surplus and total surplus after a shift or at a disequilibrium price
Explain how the price elasticities of demand and supply affect the size of the price and quantity changes
Work out which variable is indeterminate when demand and supply shift at the same time
resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are needed. All markets and data are fictional
keyPoints: A shortage (excess demand) happens when price is below equilibrium: quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. A surplus (excess supply) happens when price is above equilibrium.
In a free competitive market, shortages push the price up and surpluses push it down until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Demand up: price and quantity rise. Demand down: both fall. Supply up: price falls, quantity rises. Supply down: price rises, quantity falls.
When both curves shift at once, you can predict only one of price or quantity; the other depends on the sizes of the shifts.
Shifts change consumer, producer and total surplus. Elasticity decides whether the change shows up mostly in price or mostly in quantity.

faqs.question: Is a shortage the same as scarcity?
faqs.answer: No. Scarcity is permanent: wants are always greater than resources. A shortage is temporary and happens only when the price is below equilibrium. Raise the price to equilibrium and the shortage disappears, but scarcity does not.

faqs.question: Which quantity is actually traded when the market is out of equilibrium?
faqs.answer: The smaller of quantity demanded and quantity supplied. Nobody can force a buyer to buy, or a seller to sell, more than they want at that price.

resources.title: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.8)
resources.description: Learn how price ceilings, price floors, quotas, per-unit taxes and subsidies change price, quantity, consumer and producer surplus, government revenue and deadweight loss.
prerequisites: Shortages, surpluses and changes in equilibrium (Topic 2.7)
Consumer surplus, producer surplus and total surplus (Topic 2.6)
Price elasticity of demand and supply (Topics 2.3 and 2.4)
learningObjectives: Define price ceilings, price floors, quantity controls, per-unit taxes and per-unit subsidies
Tell a binding price control from a non-binding one and predict the shortage or surplus it creates
Show on a graph how a tax or subsidy shifts supply and creates a gap between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep
Calculate the new price, quantity, consumer surplus, producer surplus, tax revenue or subsidy cost, and deadweight loss
Explain why intervention in an efficient competitive market lowers total surplus
Explain how the price elasticities of demand and supply decide who bears a tax or gains from a subsidy
resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are needed. Quantities are in thousands, so surplus values are in thousands of dollars. All markets and data are fictional
keyPoints: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. It binds only below equilibrium, where it causes a shortage. A price floor is a legal minimum price. It binds only above equilibrium, where it causes a surplus.
A per-unit tax on sellers shifts supply up by the tax. Buyers pay more, sellers keep less, quantity falls and the government collects tax × quantity.
A per-unit subsidy to sellers shifts supply down by the subsidy. Buyers pay less, sellers receive more, quantity rises and the government pays subsidy × quantity.
In an efficient competitive market, every one of these policies lowers total surplus. The loss is deadweight loss.
The side of the market that is more inelastic bears more of a tax and gains more of a subsidy.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether a tax is collected from buyers or sellers?
faqs.answer: Not for the outcome. A tax on buyers shifts demand down by the tax instead of shifting supply up. The price buyers pay, the price sellers keep, the quantity and the revenue are the same either way. Elasticities decide who really pays.

faqs.question: If a policy lowers total surplus, why do governments use it?
faqs.answer: Governments may care about who gets the surplus as well as its total size, or they may want to raise revenue. In markets with external costs or benefits (Unit 6), a tax or subsidy can even raise efficiency. This topic deals with markets that are already efficient.

Recall the effects of a tariff and of an import quota
keyPoints: With trade, a small economy's price becomes the world price; the gap between domestic demand and supply is filled by imports or exports.
Trade raises total surplus, but producers lose when a country imports and consumers lose when it exports.
Tariff: price rises by t, imports fall, revenue = t × new imports, deadweight loss = two triangles. Quota: same direction of effects, but no tariff revenue.

resources.title: International Trade and Public Policy: Study Guide (Microeconomics 2.9)
resources.description: Learn how opening a market to trade changes price, quantity and surplus for importers and exporters, and how tariffs and quotas affect price, imports, revenue and total surplus.
prerequisites: Market equilibrium, consumer surplus and producer surplus (Topic 2.6)
How a per-unit tax creates deadweight loss (Topic 2.8)
learningObjectives: Define a tariff and an import quota
Compare the autarky equilibrium with the outcome when a small economy opens to trade at a world price below or above it
Find imports or exports as the gap between domestic quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the world price
Calculate the changes in consumer, producer and total surplus when an economy opens to trade
Show on a graph and calculate how a tariff changes domestic price, quantities, imports, government revenue, surplus and deadweight loss
Explain how an import quota changes domestic production, price, consumer surplus and total surplus, without graphing it
resources.calculatorNote: Areas of triangles and rectangles only. Quantities are in thousand tonnes and prices in dollars per kg, so every surplus is in millions of dollars. All countries and data are fictional
keyPoints: Under autarky (no trade), price is set where domestic demand meets domestic supply. With free trade, a small economy's price becomes the world price.
World price below the autarky price: the country imports Qd − Qs. Consumers gain, producers lose, total surplus rises.
World price above the autarky price: the country exports Qs − Qd. Producers gain, consumers lose, total surplus rises.
A tariff is a tax on imports. It raises the domestic price, raises domestic output, cuts consumption and imports, earns revenue and creates deadweight loss.
An import quota is a limit on the quantity imported. It raises the domestic price and domestic output and lowers consumer and total surplus, but the government earns no tariff revenue.

faqs.question: If trade raises total surplus, why do some groups oppose it?
faqs.answer: Because the gain is not shared evenly. When a country imports, domestic producers lose surplus; when it exports, domestic consumers lose surplus. The winners gain more than the losers lose, but the losers are real.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw a quota on a graph?
faqs.answer: No. Graphing a quota is outside the course. You do need to explain how a quota changes the quantity produced at home, the price, consumer surplus and total surplus.
