resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: The Production Function: Study Guide (Microeconomics 3.1)
resources.description: Learn how a production function links inputs to output, how to calculate total, marginal and average product, and why diminishing marginal returns appear in the short run.
prerequisites: The factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship (Topic 1.1)
Marginal thinking: comparing one more unit with the one before (Topic 1.6)
learningObjectives: Explain what a production function shows and how the short run differs from the long run
Define total product, marginal product and average product and calculate each from a table
Describe how marginal and average product change as a firm adds workers to a fixed input
Explain why diminishing marginal returns occur in the short run and identify where they begin
Use the relationships between the total, marginal and average product curves to read and sketch them
resources.calculatorNote: Only subtraction, addition, multiplication and division are needed. Give averages to 2 decimal places unless exact. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: A production function shows the most output a firm can make from each combination of inputs, with given technology.
Short run: at least one input is fixed. Long run: every input can be changed.
Marginal product (MP) = change in total product ÷ change in the input. Average product (AP) = total product ÷ quantity of the input.
Diminishing marginal returns: in the short run, each extra worker eventually adds less output than the one before, because the fixed input is shared by more people.
When MP is above AP, AP rises; when MP is below AP, AP falls. Total product is at its maximum where MP reaches zero.

faqs.question: Do diminishing marginal returns mean total output is falling?
faqs.answer: No. Total product keeps rising as long as marginal product is positive. It only rises by less with each extra worker. Total product falls only when marginal product is negative.

faqs.question: Is the short run a fixed length of time, such as one year?
faqs.answer: No. The short run is any period in which at least one input cannot be changed. For a food stall it may be a week; for a steel plant it may be several years.

MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points; a change in fixed cost never changes MC.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Short-Run Production Costs: Study Guide (Microeconomics 3.2)
resources.description: Learn how fixed and variable costs make up total cost, how to calculate marginal and average costs, why the cost curves have their shapes, and what shifts them.
prerequisites: Total, marginal and average product, and diminishing marginal returns (Topic 3.1)
learningObjectives: Distinguish fixed costs from variable costs and explain why total fixed cost is the same at every output, including zero
Calculate total, average fixed, average variable, average total and marginal cost from a table
Explain why marginal cost eventually rises, linking it to diminishing marginal returns, and why specialisation can make it fall at first
Draw correctly labelled short-run cost curves, with marginal cost cutting average variable and average total cost at their minimum points
Explain how changes in input prices and productivity shift the cost curves
resources.calculatorNote: Only subtraction, addition, multiplication and division are needed. Give costs to the nearest cent. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: Total cost = total fixed cost + total variable cost. Total fixed cost does not change with output and is still paid at zero output.
Marginal cost = change in total cost ÷ change in output. It equals the change in total variable cost, because fixed cost does not change.
Average fixed, variable and total cost are each total ÷ quantity of output, and ATC = AFC + AVC.
Diminishing marginal returns make marginal cost rise; marginal cost cuts AVC and ATC at their lowest points.
A change in a variable input's price or in productivity shifts MC, AVC and ATC. A change in fixed cost shifts only AFC and ATC.

faqs.question: Why does marginal cost not depend on fixed cost?
faqs.answer: Fixed cost is the same whatever the firm produces, so it does not change when output rises by one unit. Only variable cost changes, so marginal cost is the change in variable cost.

faqs.question: Why is the lowest point of ATC to the right of the lowest point of AVC?
faqs.answer: Past the minimum of AVC, average fixed cost is still falling. For a while that fall outweighs the rise in AVC, so ATC keeps falling until marginal cost reaches it.

keyPoints: Long run: every input can change, so all costs are variable.
Falling LRATC = economies of scale; flat = constant returns to scale; rising = diseconomies of scale.
MES = smallest output at the lowest LRATC. Large MES relative to demand means few firms.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Long-Run Production Costs: Study Guide (Microeconomics 3.3)
resources.description: Learn why all costs are variable in the long run, how returns to scale shape the long-run average total cost curve, and how minimum efficient scale affects how many firms a market can hold.
prerequisites: Fixed, variable, total and average costs in the short run (Topic 3.2)
Diminishing marginal returns when one input is fixed (Topic 3.1)
learningObjectives: Explain why every input, and so every cost, is variable in the long run
Identify increasing, constant and decreasing returns to scale from input and output data
Calculate long-run average total cost from a table and describe the regions of the LRATC curve
Explain the causes of economies and diseconomies of scale, and how they differ from diminishing marginal returns
Find the minimum efficient scale and use it to explain how concentrated a market is likely to be
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use multiplication and division only. Give average costs to 2 decimal places. All data are fictional
keyPoints: In the long run a firm can change every input, including its plant size, so there are no fixed costs: all costs are variable.
Returns to scale compare the change in output with an equal percentage change in all inputs: more than proportional is increasing, equal is constant, less is decreasing.
Long-run average total cost (LRATC) falls with economies of scale, stays flat with constant returns to scale and rises with diseconomies of scale.
Minimum efficient scale (MES) is the smallest output at which LRATC reaches its lowest level.
The larger the MES compared with market demand, the fewer firms the market can hold at the lowest cost, so the market tends to be more concentrated.

faqs.question: How long is the long run?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed number of months. The long run is any period long enough for the firm to change all its inputs. For a market stall it may be weeks; for a steel works it may be years.

faqs.question: Are economies of scale the same as increasing returns to scale?
faqs.answer: They are closely linked. Returns to scale describe inputs and output. Economies of scale describe cost per unit. If input prices stay the same, increasing returns to scale give economies of scale.

learningObjectives: Recall the formulas for accounting profit, economic profit and normal profit

keyPoints: Accounting profit = TR − explicit costs. Economic profit = TR − explicit − implicit costs.
Normal profit: economic profit = 0, so accounting profit just covers implicit costs.
Firms respond to economic profit: profit attracts entry, losses lead to exit.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Types of Profit: Study Guide (Microeconomics 3.4)
resources.description: Learn how accounting profit, economic profit and normal profit differ, which implicit costs accountants leave out, how to calculate each type of profit, and why firms respond to economic profit.
prerequisites: Explicit and implicit costs (Topic 1.5)
Total and average total cost (Topic 3.2)
learningObjectives: Define accounting profit, economic profit and normal profit, and explain how they differ
Identify the implicit costs of running a firm, such as forgone interest, compensation for risk and the owner's time
Calculate a firm's accounting profit and economic profit (or loss) from totals or from per-unit data
Explain why firms respond to economic profit rather than accounting profit, and how they respond
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use addition, subtraction and multiplication only. All data are fictional
keyPoints: Accounting profit = total revenue − explicit costs.
Economic profit = total revenue − explicit costs − implicit costs = accounting profit − implicit costs.
Implicit costs include the owner's forgone wages, forgone interest on the owner's own money, forgone rent on property the owner uses, and compensation for risk.
Normal profit is earned when economic profit is zero: the accounting profit just covers all implicit costs.
Firms respond to economic profit: positive economic profit attracts resources and new firms; economic losses push them out.

faqs.question: Is a firm earning zero economic profit doing badly?
faqs.answer: No. Zero economic profit means normal profit: the owner earns exactly what their time, money and risk could earn in the next-best use. There is no reason to leave.

faqs.question: Can accounting profit be positive while economic profit is negative?
faqs.answer: Yes. This happens whenever accounting profit is smaller than the implicit costs. The books show a profit, but the owner would be better off using their resources elsewhere.

resources.description: One-page recap of profit maximization: the MR = MC rule, how to apply it to whole-unit tables and graphs, MR for price takers and price setters, and the mistakes that cost marks.
learningObjectives: Recall the profit-maximizing rule and how to apply it to tables and graphs
Recall which cost and revenue changes alter the profit-maximizing output
keyPoints: Profit-maximizing output: MR = MC, where MC is rising.
Whole units: produce every unit with MR ≥ MC; stop before the first unit with MC > MR.

resources.title: Profit Maximization: Study Guide (Microeconomics 3.5)
resources.description: Learn the profit-maximizing rule MR = MC, how to find the profit-maximizing output from a table or a graph, and why a firm should not simply maximize revenue or profit per unit.
prerequisites: Marginal cost and how it changes with output (Topic 3.2)
Economic profit, accounting profit and normal profit (Topic 3.4)
Marginal analysis: comparing marginal benefit and marginal cost (Topic 1.6)
learningObjectives: State the profit-maximizing rule and explain why it works using marginal reasoning
Calculate marginal revenue and marginal cost from a table and use them to find the profit-maximizing output
Confirm the profit-maximizing output by comparing total revenue and total cost
Identify the profit-maximizing output on a graph of marginal revenue and marginal cost
Explain why a firm should not maximize total revenue or profit per unit, and why fixed costs do not change the profit-maximizing output
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use addition, subtraction and multiplication only. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: A firm maximizes profit by producing the output where marginal revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC), with MC rising.
With data in whole units, produce every unit whose MR is at least its MC, and stop before the first unit whose MC is greater than its MR.
If MR > MC, producing more raises profit. If MC > MR, producing less raises profit.
The rule holds for every firm. For a firm that takes the market price, MR equals the price. For a firm that must cut its price to sell more, MR is below the price.
Fixed costs do not affect MC, so they do not change the profit-maximizing output. They only change how much profit is made.

faqs.question: Does producing where MR = MC guarantee a profit?
faqs.answer: No. It gives the best result available: the largest profit, or the smallest loss. Whether the firm should produce at all in the short run is the subject of Topic 3.6.

faqs.question: Why compare MR with MC and not price with average cost?
faqs.answer: The output decision is about the next unit. MR and MC tell you how that unit changes revenue and cost, so they tell you how it changes profit. Averages include every earlier unit too.

learningObjectives: Recall the short-run shutdown rule and the long-run entry and exit conditions

resources.title: Short-Run Production and Long-Run Entry or Exit Decisions: Study Guide (Microeconomics 3.6)
resources.description: Learn when a firm should keep producing at a loss or shut down in the short run, using TR versus TVC or price versus AVC, and why firms enter or exit a market in the long run.
prerequisites: Fixed, variable and average costs (Topic 3.2)
Economic profit and normal profit (Topic 3.4)
The profit-maximizing rule MR = MC (Topic 3.5)
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between shutting down in the short run and exiting a market in the long run
Decide whether a firm should produce or shut down by comparing total revenue with total variable cost, or price with average variable cost
Calculate a firm's profit or loss when it produces and when it shuts down
Identify the shutdown point and the break-even point on a cost-curve graph or in a table

resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use addition, subtraction, multiplication and division only. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: In the short run a firm must pay its fixed costs even if it produces nothing. So the shutdown decision ignores fixed costs.
Produce in the short run if total revenue covers total variable cost (price ≥ AVC). Shut down if TR < TVC (price < AVC).
A firm that shuts down loses exactly its total fixed cost. Producing at a loss is better if the loss is smaller than that.
The shutdown point is the minimum of AVC; the break-even point is the minimum of ATC.
In the long run all costs are variable. With no barriers, firms enter a market where they expect economic profit and exit one where they expect economic losses.

faqs.question: Is shutting down the same as leaving the market?
faqs.answer: No. Shutting down is a short-run choice to produce zero output while still holding fixed inputs and paying fixed costs. Exiting is a long-run choice to leave the market, which ends fixed costs as well.

faqs.question: Why would a firm keep producing if it is making a loss?
faqs.answer: Because shutting down would not save its fixed costs. If revenue covers the variable cost, the extra money helps pay part of the fixed cost, so the loss is smaller than if the firm shut down.

resources.title: Perfect Competition: Study Guide (Microeconomics 3.7)
resources.description: Learn how price-taking firms in a perfectly competitive market choose output, calculate economic profit or loss, and reach an efficient long-run equilibrium through entry and exit.
prerequisites: Short-run cost curves: MC, AVC and ATC (Topic 3.2)
Economic profit and the MR = MC rule (Topics 3.4 and 3.5)
Shut-down and entry or exit decisions (Topic 3.6)
learningObjectives: Describe the features of a perfectly competitive market and explain why each firm is a price taker
Draw side-by-side market and firm graphs with the firm's demand curve as P = MR = d
Find the profit-maximising output where MC = MR = P, from a table or a graph
Calculate economic profit or loss as (P − ATC) × q and show it as a rectangle
Explain how short-run profits or losses lead to entry or exit and a long-run equilibrium with zero economic profit
Explain why long-run equilibrium is allocatively and productively efficient, and how prices act as signals
Compare long-run supply in constant-cost, increasing-cost and decreasing-cost industries
resources.calculatorNote: Calculations use multiplication, subtraction and division only. All firms, markets and data are fictional
keyPoints: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: it can sell any amount at the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal and P = MR = d.
The firm maximises profit where MC = MR = P (on the rising part of MC).
Economic profit = (P − ATC) × q. It is positive when P > ATC and negative (a loss) when P < ATC.
Short-run profits attract entry and short-run losses cause exit, until P = minimum ATC and economic profit is zero.
In long-run equilibrium P = MC (allocative efficiency) and P = minimum ATC (productive efficiency).
Long-run supply is horizontal in a constant-cost industry, upward-sloping in an increasing-cost industry and downward-sloping in a decreasing-cost industry.

faqs.question: If economic profit is zero in the long run, why do firms stay in the market?
faqs.answer: Zero economic profit means the firm covers all its costs, including the opportunity cost of the owner's time and money. It earns a normal profit, which is as much as it could earn in its next best use.

faqs.question: Is the firm's demand curve the same as the market demand curve?
faqs.answer: No. Market demand slopes downward. Each firm is so small that it can sell all it wants at the market price, so the demand curve it faces is horizontal at that price.

resources.title: Introduction to Imperfectly Competitive Markets: Study Guide (Microeconomics 4.1)
resources.description: Learn what makes a market imperfectly competitive, why marginal revenue falls below price, why price above marginal cost is inefficient, and how barriers to entry protect profit.
prerequisites: Perfect competition: price-taking firms, P = MR = MC and long-run entry and exit (Topic 3.7)
Total revenue and the total revenue test (Topic 2.3)
Consumer surplus, producer surplus and allocative efficiency (Topic 2.6)
learningObjectives: Name the imperfectly competitive market structures in product markets, and the one in factor markets
Compare perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly by their key characteristics
Explain why a firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve must cut its price to sell more, and why its marginal revenue is therefore below price
Calculate total and marginal revenue from a demand schedule and split a change in revenue into a price effect and a quantity effect
Explain why a price above marginal cost signals an inefficient quantity
Identify high start-up costs, legal barriers and control of a key resource as barriers to entry, and explain how they let imperfect competition last
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use multiplication and subtraction only. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: Imperfectly competitive product markets are monopoly, oligopoly and monopolistic competition; monopsony is the factor-market case.
These firms face a downward-sloping demand curve, so to sell one more unit they must cut the price on every unit. Marginal revenue is therefore below price.
On a graph, the MR curve lies below the demand curve for every imperfectly competitive seller that charges one price to all buyers.
At the quantity these firms choose, price is above marginal cost. Some units that buyers value above their cost are never made, so the outcome is inefficient.
Barriers to entry (high start-up costs, legal barriers, control of a key resource) stop new firms from competing profits away.

faqs.question: Is every firm with some control over price a monopoly?
faqs.answer: No. Monopolistically competitive firms and oligopolists also face downward-sloping demand curves. A monopoly is the special case with a single seller and no close substitutes.

faqs.question: Why is marginal revenue below price but not below zero at first?
faqs.answer: Selling one more unit brings in its price but loses a little on every earlier unit. At first the gain is bigger, so MR is positive but smaller than price. Once the loss on earlier units is bigger, MR turns negative.

resources.title: Monopoly: Study Guide (Microeconomics 4.2)
resources.description: Learn how a monopoly chooses output where MR = MC, reads its price from demand, and how to calculate its profit, consumer surplus, producer surplus and deadweight loss, including natural monopoly.
prerequisites: Marginal revenue below price for a firm with a downward-sloping demand curve (Topic 4.1)
Cost curves (MC, ATC, AVC) and economies of scale (Topics 3.2 and 3.3)
Consumer and producer surplus as areas on a graph (Topic 2.6)
learningObjectives: Explain why a monopoly exists and lasts only when barriers to entry block rivals
Find the profit-maximising quantity where MR = MC and read the price from the demand curve, using a table, an equation or a graph
Draw a correctly labelled monopoly graph showing price, quantity, profit or loss, consumer surplus and deadweight loss
Calculate profit, consumer surplus, producer surplus and deadweight loss for a monopoly, and compare them with the competitive outcome
Explain why a monopoly's price is above marginal cost and why its output is inefficient
Define a natural monopoly and explain why one firm can serve the whole market at lower cost than two or more
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use the four operations only. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: A monopoly is the only seller of a product with no close substitutes. It exists because barriers to entry keep rivals out.
Profit-maximising rule: produce where MR = MC, then go up to the demand curve for the price. The price is above MC.
Profit = (P − ATC) × Q. It can last in the long run because barriers block entry.
Compared with perfect competition, a monopoly charges more, sells less, shrinks consumer surplus and creates a deadweight loss.
A natural monopoly has economies of scale over the whole range of market demand, so one firm can supply the market more cheaply than several.

faqs.question: Does a monopoly charge the highest price it can?
faqs.answer: No. A higher price means selling fewer units. The monopoly picks the quantity where MR = MC and charges the highest price buyers will pay for that quantity, which is read from the demand curve.

faqs.question: Can a monopoly make a loss?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the short run, if the price at its best quantity is below average total cost. It keeps producing if price covers average variable cost; otherwise it shuts down. With no profit possible in the long run, it leaves the market.

resources.description: Learn what price discrimination is, the conditions a firm needs to use it, and how perfect price discrimination changes output, consumer surplus, profit and deadweight loss compared with a single-price monopoly.
prerequisites: The single-price monopoly model: MR = MC, price read from demand (Topic 4.2)
Consumer surplus, producer surplus and deadweight loss as areas on a graph (Unit 2)
Price elasticity of demand (Topic 2.3)
learningObjectives: Define price discrimination and explain why a firm with market power uses it
State the three conditions a firm needs before it can price discriminate
Explain why the group with less elastic demand is charged the higher price
Show on a graph how perfect price discrimination changes output, consumer surplus, profit and deadweight loss compared with a single-price monopoly
Calculate consumer surplus, profit and deadweight loss for a single-price monopolist and a perfectly price-discriminating monopolist
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use multiplication, subtraction and the triangle area ½ × base × height. All data are fictional
keyPoints: Price discrimination means selling the same product to different buyers at different prices, where the difference is not explained by a difference in cost.
A firm needs three things: market power, a way to tell buyers apart by willingness to pay, and a way to stop resale.
When a firm sets a price for each group, the group with less elastic demand pays the higher price.
Under perfect price discrimination every unit sells at the buyer's maximum price, so marginal revenue equals the demand curve.

A perfectly price-discriminating monopolist produces where price equals marginal cost: output is the competitive quantity, deadweight loss is zero, and the firm takes all the surplus, so consumer surplus is zero.

faqs.question: Is perfect price discrimination efficient?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the economist's sense. The last unit sells at a price equal to marginal cost, so every unit worth more to a buyer than it costs to make is produced and there is no deadweight loss. It is not good for consumers: all the surplus goes to the firm.

faqs.question: Is a student discount price discrimination?
faqs.answer: Usually yes. The ticket costs the firm the same to provide, but students (who tend to have more elastic demand) are charged less. The student card lets the firm identify the group and stops others from using the cheaper ticket.

faqs.question: If firms earn zero economic profit in the long run, why do they stay in business?
faqs.answer: Zero economic profit means total revenue covers all costs, including the owners' opportunity costs. The owners earn a normal return, as much as they could earn in their next best use of the money and time.

faqs.question: How is this different from perfect competition in the long run?
faqs.answer: Both end at zero economic profit, because entry is free. But in perfect competition each firm's demand is horizontal, so it is tangent to ATC at its minimum and P = MC. In monopolistic competition demand slopes down, so the tangency is to the left of minimum ATC and P > MC.

prerequisites: Profit maximisation where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (Unit 3)
The monopoly outcome and deadweight loss (Topic 4.2)
Allocative efficiency: price equal to marginal cost
learningObjectives: Describe an oligopoly: few interdependent firms, high barriers to entry and an inefficient outcome
Explain why oligopolists are tempted to collude and form cartels, and why cartels tend to break down
Define a game, a strategy, a payoff matrix, a dominant strategy and a Nash equilibrium

resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction and multiplication are needed. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: An oligopoly has a few firms behind high barriers to entry. Each firm's best choice depends on what its rivals do: the firms are interdependent.
Oligopolists gain by colluding to act like one monopoly, but each member also gains by cheating, so cartels are hard to hold together.
A dominant strategy is best whatever the other player does. A Nash equilibrium is a cell where neither player can do better by changing only its own action.
In a prisoner's dilemma, both players follow their dominant strategies and end up worse off than if they had cooperated.
To change a dominant strategy, a payment or penalty must close the largest payoff gap across the other player's actions.
Even without a working cartel, oligopoly prices are usually higher and quantities lower than in perfect competition.

faqs.question: Is the Nash equilibrium always the best outcome for the players?
faqs.answer: No. It is only stable: no player can gain by changing alone. In a prisoner's dilemma both players would be better off in a different cell.

faqs.question: Does every game have a dominant strategy?
faqs.answer: No. Often a player's best action depends on what the other player does. You can still find a Nash equilibrium by checking best responses.

faqs.question: Which payoff in a cell belongs to which player?
faqs.answer: By convention the first number belongs to the row player and the second to the column player. Always check the question's own key.

resources.title: Introduction to Factor Markets: Study Guide (Microeconomics 5.1)
resources.description: Learn how factor markets work, why labour demand is a derived demand, how to calculate marginal revenue product and marginal resource cost, and why labour demand slopes down and supply slopes up.
prerequisites: Total product, marginal product and diminishing marginal returns (Topic 3.1)
Marginal revenue for a price taker and for a firm with market power (Units 3 and 4)
Demand, supply and market equilibrium (Unit 2)
learningObjectives: Explain how factor markets differ from product markets, and who buys and who sells in each
Name the payment to each factor of production: wages, interest and rent
Explain why the demand for labour is a derived demand that depends on productivity, the output price and the cost of the factor
Calculate marginal revenue product from a table, as the change in total revenue or as marginal product times marginal revenue

resources.calculatorNote: Only subtraction and multiplication are needed. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: In factor markets the roles swap: households sell labour, capital and land, and firms buy them, paying wages, interest and rent.
Labour demand is a derived demand: firms want workers only for the output they make and the revenue that output brings.
Marginal revenue product (MRP) is the extra revenue from one more worker: MRP = ΔTR ÷ ΔL = MP × MR. For a price taker in the output market, MRP = MP × P.
Marginal resource cost (MRC) is the extra cost of one more worker: MRC = ΔTC ÷ ΔL. A firm that pays the market wage has MRC equal to the wage.
Quantity of labour demanded falls as the wage rises (MRP falls as workers are added); quantity supplied rises as the wage rises.

faqs.question: Is marginal revenue product the same as the value of the marginal product?
faqs.answer: Only when the firm sells its output in a perfectly competitive market, because then marginal revenue equals price. A firm with market power must cut its price to sell more, so its MRP is lower than MP × P.

faqs.question: Why is entrepreneurship not in the wage, interest and rent list?
faqs.answer: The course focuses on labour, capital and land in factor markets. The reward to entrepreneurship is profit, which you met in Unit 3.

faqs.question: Is marginal resource cost the same as marginal factor cost?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both names describe the extra cost of hiring one more unit of a factor. You may see either on exam papers and in textbooks.

resources.title: Changes in Factor Demand and Factor Supply: Study Guide (Microeconomics 5.2)
resources.description: Learn what shifts labour demand and labour supply, how a change in output price or productivity moves a firm's MRP curve, and how to find the new wage and employment after one or two shifts.
prerequisites: Marginal revenue product, marginal resource cost and derived demand (Topic 5.1)
Shifts of demand and supply curves and their effect on equilibrium (Unit 2)
learningObjectives: Tell a movement along a labour demand or supply curve (caused by the wage) from a shift (caused by another determinant)
Explain how changes in output price, worker productivity and the prices of other inputs shift labour demand
Explain how immigration, education, working conditions, age distribution, alternative options, preferences for leisure and cultural expectations shift labour supply
Calculate how a change in output price or productivity changes MRP and the number of workers worth hiring
Show on a graph, and calculate from equations, the effect of one or two shifts on the equilibrium wage and quantity of labour
resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are needed. All firms, places and data are fictional
keyPoints: A change in the wage moves the market along the labour demand and supply curves. Any other change shifts a curve.
Labour demand shifts when the output price or worker productivity changes, because MRP = MP × P changes for every worker. Prices of other inputs also matter.
Labour supply shifts with immigration, education and training, working conditions, age distribution, alternative options, preferences for leisure and cultural expectations.
More labour demand raises the wage and employment; more labour supply lowers the wage and raises employment.
When both curves shift, one of the two outcomes (wage or quantity) is indeterminate unless you know the sizes of the shifts.

faqs.question: Does a rise in the wage shift the labour demand curve left?
faqs.answer: No. The wage is on the vertical axis, so a change in it moves the market along the curve. Firms hire fewer workers, but that is a fall in the quantity demanded, not in demand.

faqs.question: Does better technology always reduce the demand for labour?
faqs.answer: No. Technology that makes workers more productive raises MP and so raises labour demand. Machines that replace workers can reduce it, as a cheaper substitute input.

faqs.question: Is immigration a demand shifter or a supply shifter?
faqs.answer: In this topic, treat it as a labour supply shifter: more people are able and willing to work in the market at every wage.

resources.title: Profit-Maximising Behaviour in Perfectly Competitive Factor Markets: Revision Notes (Microeconomics 5.3)
resources.description: One-page recap of hiring in a perfectly competitive labour market: the wage-taking firm, MRP = MRC = wage, MRP versus VMP, and the least-cost and profit-maximising input rules.
learningObjectives: Recall the features of a perfectly competitive labour market and the firm's hiring rule
Recall the formulas for MRP, VMP, the least-cost rule and the profit-maximising rule
keyPoints: The market sets the wage; each firm takes it, so MRC = W and the firm's labour supply is horizontal.
Hire while MRP > W; stop where MRP = MRC = W.

resources.title: Profit-Maximising Behaviour in Perfectly Competitive Factor Markets: Study Guide (Microeconomics 5.3)
resources.description: Learn how a wage-taking firm decides how many workers to hire where MRP equals the wage, how MRP differs from VMP, and how to choose the least-cost and profit-maximising mix of inputs.
prerequisites: Marginal product and diminishing marginal returns (Topic 3.1)
Marginal revenue for price takers and for firms with downward-sloping demand (Topics 3.7 and 4.1)
Marginal revenue product and marginal resource cost as measures (Topic 5.1)
learningObjectives: Describe a perfectly competitive labour market and show on side-by-side graphs how the market sets the wage that each firm takes
Explain why a wage-taking firm keeps hiring while MRP is above the wage and stops where MRP = MRC = wage
Calculate marginal product, MRP and the profit-maximising number of workers from a table
Distinguish MRP from the value of the marginal product (VMP = MP × P) and explain when they are equal
Apply the least-cost rule (MP per dollar equal across inputs) and the profit-maximising rule (MRP = price of each input)
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use the four operations only. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: In a perfectly competitive labour market, market supply and demand set the wage. Each firm is a wage taker: it can hire as many workers as it wants at that wage.
For a wage taker, the marginal resource cost of one more worker is the wage, so its labour supply curve is horizontal at the market wage.
Profit-maximising hiring rule: keep hiring while MRP > wage; stop where MRP = MRC = wage.
MRP = ΔTR ÷ ΔL = MP × MR. If the output market is perfectly competitive, MR = P, so MRP = VMP = MP × P.
Least-cost rule: MP_L ÷ W = MP_K ÷ r. Profit-maximising rule: MRP_L = W and MRP_K = r, so each ratio MRP ÷ input price equals 1.

faqs.question: Can a monopoly be a wage taker?
faqs.answer: Yes. A firm can be the only seller of its product and still be one of many employers hiring a common type of worker. It then sells as a monopoly but hires as a perfect competitor, at the market wage.

faqs.question: Why does the firm hire the worker whose MRP exactly equals the wage?
faqs.answer: That worker adds as much revenue as cost, so profit is the same with or without them. By convention we say the firm hires up to the point where MRP = MRC, so that worker is included.

resources.title: Monopsonistic Markets: Study Guide (Microeconomics 5.4)
resources.description: Learn why a monopsony's marginal resource cost is above the wage, how it hires where MRC = MRP and pays the wage on the supply curve, and how its outcome compares with a competitive labour market.
prerequisites: Marginal revenue product and the hiring rule MRP = MRC (Topic 5.3)
Labour supply slopes upward: more workers offer to work at higher wages (Topic 5.1)
Deadweight loss as lost surplus (Topic 2.8)
learningObjectives: Describe a monopsonistic labour market and explain why the firm is a wage setter facing the upward-sloping market supply of labour
Explain why hiring one more worker costs more than that worker's wage, so MRC lies above the supply curve
Calculate total labour cost and MRC from a supply schedule, and find the monopsony's quantity of labour and wage
Draw a correctly labelled monopsony graph showing S, MRC, MRP, the monopsony wage and employment, and the competitive outcome
Compare the monopsony outcome with a perfectly competitive labour market and explain why it is inefficient
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use the four operations only. All firms, places and data are fictional
keyPoints: A monopsony is the only (or dominant) buyer of a type of labour. It faces the upward-sloping market supply curve, so it must raise the wage to hire more workers.
If it pays everyone the same wage, one more worker costs their own wage plus the raise given to all existing workers. So MRC is greater than the wage.
Hiring rule: hire while MRP > MRC; stop where MRC = MRP. Then go down to the supply curve for the wage.
Compared with a competitive labour market, a monopsony hires fewer workers and pays a lower wage, and the wage is below MRP. The lost output is a deadweight loss.
For a straight-line supply curve, the MRC line starts at the same point on the vertical axis and is twice as steep.

faqs.question: Is a monopsony the same as a monopoly?
faqs.answer: No. A monopoly is a single seller; a monopsony is a single buyer. A firm can be both, either or neither. In this topic the firm is a single buyer of labour.

faqs.question: Why doesn't the monopsony pay the wage where MRC = MRP?
faqs.answer: Because it does not have to. The supply curve shows the lowest wage at which that many workers will work. At the chosen quantity, the firm pays exactly that wage, which is below MRC and MRP.

resources.title: Socially Efficient and Inefficient Market Outcomes: Study Guide (Microeconomics 6.1)
resources.description: Learn what makes a quantity socially efficient (MSB = MSC), why competitive markets reach it, why market power and other failures do not, and how to calculate deadweight loss.
prerequisites: Consumer surplus, producer surplus and total surplus as areas on a graph (Topic 2.6)
Deadweight loss from price controls and taxes (Topic 2.8)
Price and output decisions under perfect competition and monopoly (Topics 3.7 and 4.2)
learningObjectives: Define social efficiency as the quantity where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost
Explain, with a graph, why a perfectly competitive market with no external effects reaches the socially efficient quantity
Explain how rational buyers and sellers who weigh only private benefits and costs, or who use market power, can produce an inefficient quantity
Name the main sources of market inefficiency and say whether each leads to too little or too much output
Calculate deadweight loss for underproduction and overproduction from a table, an equation or a graph
Use cost-benefit analysis to judge whether a policy that moves output towards the efficient quantity is worth its cost
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use the four operations only. All markets and data are fictional
keyPoints: The socially efficient (optimal) quantity is where the marginal social benefit of the last unit equals its marginal social cost (MSB = MSC). Total surplus is then as large as it can be.
A perfectly competitive market reaches this quantity only when buyers and sellers bear all the benefits and costs of their choices, so demand = MSB and supply = MSC.
Rational agents equate private marginal benefit with private marginal cost. When private and social values differ, or a firm has market power, the market quantity is not efficient.
Monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, externalities, asymmetric information and public goods can all move output away from the efficient quantity.
Producing too little or too much both create deadweight loss: the triangle between MSB and MSC from the actual quantity to the efficient one.

faqs.question: Is a socially efficient outcome also a fair outcome?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Efficiency is about making total surplus as large as possible. It says nothing about who receives that surplus. How income is shared is a separate question (Topic 6.5).

faqs.question: Why does producing too much create a loss? Surely more output is good.
faqs.answer: Each unit beyond the efficient quantity costs society more to make than it is worth to anyone. Making it uses resources that would create more value elsewhere, so total surplus falls.

faqs.question: Is deadweight loss the extra profit a monopoly earns?
faqs.answer: No. Extra profit taken from buyers is a transfer: one group loses and another gains. Deadweight loss is surplus that nobody receives, because units worth more than they cost are never made.

keyPoints: Negative externality: too much, price too low. Positive externality: too little.
MSC = MPC + MEC; MSB = MPB + MEB; optimum where MSB = MSC.
Corrective tax = MEC at the optimal quantity; corrective subsidy = MEB at the optimal quantity.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Externalities: Study Guide (Microeconomics 6.2)
resources.description: Learn what positive and negative externalities are, why markets over- or under-produce, how to graph and calculate the deadweight loss, and how taxes, subsidies, regulation and property rights correct it.
prerequisites: The socially efficient quantity (MSB = MSC) and deadweight loss (Topic 6.1)
Effects of a per-unit tax and subsidy on a market (Topic 2.8)
learningObjectives: Define an externality and classify it as positive or negative, in production or in consumption
Explain why externalities arise from poorly defined property rights or high transaction costs, and why rational agents ignore external costs and benefits
Explain how non-excludable benefits give people an incentive to free ride
Draw correctly labelled graphs of negative and positive externalities showing the market quantity, the socially optimal quantity and the deadweight loss
Calculate the market quantity, the socially optimal quantity, the deadweight loss and the corrective tax or subsidy
Explain how taxes, subsidies, regulation, public provision and property rights can correct an externality
resources.calculatorNote: All calculations use the four operations only. All markets and data are fictional
keyPoints: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on a third party who is not part of the trade. MSC = MPC + MEC and MSB = MPB + MEB.
Rational buyers and sellers respond only to private costs and benefits, so a negative externality leads to too much output and a positive externality to too little.
Externalities arise when property rights are not well defined or when bargaining is too costly. Non-excludable benefits invite free riding.
The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSB and MSC from the market quantity to the socially optimal quantity, pointing to where MSB = MSC.

A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost (or a subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit) at the optimal quantity moves the market to the efficient outcome. Regulation, public provision and property rights are other tools.

faqs.question: Is the socially optimal amount of pollution zero?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Cutting pollution to zero would mean giving up goods whose benefit is greater than their full social cost. The optimal quantity is where MSB = MSC, which normally still involves some pollution.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether a corrective subsidy is paid to buyers or to sellers?
faqs.answer: Not for the quantity. Either way the gap between what buyers pay and what sellers receive equals the subsidy, so the market reaches the same quantity. The prices quoted differ, but the outcome is the same.

faqs.question: Is a rise in the price of a good caused by other buyers an externality?
faqs.answer: No. Price changes are passed through the market and are part of how markets work. An externality is an effect on a third party that no market price records, such as noise, pollution or a health benefit.

resources.title: Public and Private Goods: Study Guide (Microeconomics 6.3)
resources.description: Learn how rivalry and excludability sort goods into private goods, public goods and open-access resources, why free riders leave public goods underprovided, and why shared resources get overused.
prerequisites: Marginal social benefit, marginal social cost and the socially optimal quantity (Topic 6.1)
Externalities and the free rider incentive (Topic 6.2)
learningObjectives: Decide whether a good is rival or non-rival, and excludable or non-excludable, and give a reason for each
Classify a good as a private good, a public good or an open-access resource
Explain how the free rider problem stops private markets from providing public goods
Use benefit and cost data to decide whether a public good is worth providing and how a tax can fund it

Explain, with data or a graph, why open-access resources are overused and how policy can limit the overuse
resources.calculatorNote: Only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are needed. All places and data are fictional
keyPoints: Rival: one person's use leaves less for others. Excludable: people who do not pay can be kept out.
Private goods are rival and excludable. Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable.
Non-excludable goods invite free riding, so private firms rarely provide public goods; government usually provides them, paid for by taxes.
Open-access resources are rival but non-excludable, so each user ignores the cost they impose on others and the resource is overused.
Who provides a good does not decide its type: free state schooling is still a private good.

faqs.question: Is a public good the same as a good the government provides?
faqs.answer: No. The type of good depends only on rivalry and excludability. Governments also provide private goods, such as school places, free of charge. Those goods stay private goods.

faqs.question: Why can't a firm just sell a public good?
faqs.answer: It cannot stop people who do not pay from enjoying the good, so most people will wait for others to pay. The firm cannot collect enough revenue to cover its costs.

resources.description: One-page recap of taxes, subsidies, price controls, natural monopoly regulation and antitrust policy across market structures, with the rules for price, output and deadweight loss and the mistakes that cost marks.
learningObjectives: Recall which policies change marginal cost and which change only fixed cost
Recall how price controls and regulation affect output in each market structure
keyPoints: Per-unit tax or subsidy → MC shifts → price and output change. Lump-sum → fixed cost only → price and output unchanged.
Monopoly + ceiling where demand meets MC → efficient output. Competitive market + binding ceiling → less output.
Natural monopoly: P = MC needs a lump-sum subsidy; P = ATC is the fair return.
resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: The Effects of Government Intervention in Different Market Structures: Study Guide (Microeconomics 6.4)
resources.description: See how per-unit and lump-sum taxes and subsidies, price ceilings and floors, natural monopoly regulation and antitrust policy change prices, output, surplus and deadweight loss in different market structures.
prerequisites: Per-unit taxes, subsidies and price controls in a competitive market (Topic 2.8)
Monopoly and natural monopoly graphs (Topic 4.2) and monopsony (Topic 5.4)
Deadweight loss and the socially optimal quantity (Topic 6.1)
learningObjectives: Explain which policies change a firm's marginal cost and which change only its fixed cost
Predict and calculate the effects of per-unit and lump-sum taxes and subsidies on price, output, surplus, deadweight loss and government revenue or cost
Explain how a binding price ceiling or floor affects output differently in perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and monopsony
Compare the unregulated, fair-return and socially optimal prices for a natural monopoly, and explain why the socially optimal price needs a lump-sum subsidy
Explain the aim of antitrust policy and when intervention increases efficiency
resources.calculatorNote: Only the four operations and ½ × base × height are needed. Quantities are in thousands, so money values are in thousands of dollars. All firms and data are fictional
keyPoints: First ask: does the policy change marginal cost (or the price the firm can charge), or only fixed cost?
Per-unit taxes and subsidies shift MC, so they change price and output in every market structure. Lump-sum taxes and subsidies change only fixed cost, so price and output stay the same.

A binding price ceiling always cuts output in perfect competition, but a ceiling set between a monopoly's MC at its unregulated output and its price raises the monopoly's output. A ceiling where demand meets MC gives the efficient quantity.
A natural monopoly priced at MC makes a loss and needs a lump-sum subsidy; a fair-return price (P = ATC) gives zero economic profit but some deadweight loss.
Intervention increases efficiency only when it corrects the incentive that caused the inefficiency.

faqs.question: Why does a lump-sum tax not change a monopoly's price?
faqs.answer: The tax is the same whatever the firm produces, so it does not change marginal cost or marginal revenue. MR = MC at the same quantity as before, so price and output stay put; only profit falls.

faqs.question: Can a price ceiling ever increase output?
faqs.answer: Yes, for a firm with market power. A ceiling below the monopoly price, but above MC at the monopoly's output, means extra units no longer push the price down, so the firm produces more, up to where the ceiling meets MC or demand.

resources.title: Inequality: Study Guide (Microeconomics 6.5)
resources.description: Learn how economists measure income and wealth inequality with poverty rates, Lorenz curves and the Gini coefficient, and why market outcomes, taxes and access to resources create inequality.
prerequisites: Factor markets: a firm hires a factor until its marginal revenue product equals its price (Unit 5)
Market failure and the role of government (Topics 6.1 to 6.4)
learningObjectives: Tell income apart from wealth, and describe how poverty rates and incomes differ between groups and between countries
Read a Lorenz curve and use it, with the Gini coefficient, to compare how unequal two distributions are
Explain how paying each factor the value of its marginal product can lead to unequal incomes
Classify a tax as progressive, regressive or proportional from average tax rates, and explain its effect on inequality
Explain how human capital, social capital, inheritance, discrimination, access to financial markets, mobility and bargaining power cause inequality
resources.calculatorNote: All data are fictional. Calculations need only the four basic operations; give percentages to 2 decimal places where needed
keyPoints: Income is a flow earned over a period; wealth is a stock of assets minus debts. Both can be shared out unequally.
A Lorenz curve that sags farther below the line of equality shows more inequality. The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything).
In competitive markets each factor tends to earn the value of its marginal product, so people who own more productive labour or capital earn more.
A tax is progressive if the average tax rate rises with income, regressive if it falls and proportional if it stays the same.
Other sources of inequality: human capital, social capital, inheritance, discrimination, access to financial markets, mobility and bargaining power.

faqs.question: Do I need to draw a Lorenz curve or calculate a Gini coefficient?
faqs.answer: No. Both are outside the course. You must be able to read a Lorenz curve, say what the Gini coefficient shows, and use them to compare distributions.

faqs.question: If a tax takes more dollars from the rich, is it progressive?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Compare the tax as a percentage of income. If richer people pay more dollars but a smaller percentage of income, the tax is regressive.

prerequisites: You have studied most of the six units of the course, or are revising them
You can draw supply and demand, cost curves and the profit-maximising rule MR = MC
learningObjectives: Draw graphs that earn every label point: axes, curves, equilibrium values, shifts with arrows and correctly shaded areas
Draw side-by-side market and firm graphs (or labour market and firm graphs) with the price or wage carried across
Write cause-and-effect chains that name each link and state the direction of every change

resources.calculatorNote: All countries, firms, markets and data are fictional. Only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are needed
keyPoints: A graph earns credit through its labels: both axes, every curve, the equilibrium price and quantity, an arrow for each shift and a clear label on any shaded area.
For a price-taking firm, draw the market and the firm side by side and carry the market price across as P = MR = d.
A strong explanation is a chain of links, and every link states a direction: rises, falls, shifts left, shifts right.
Show calculation steps: the rule, the numbers put into it and the answer with its unit.
Identify wants a short answer, explain wants the reason why, and calculate wants the working as well as the result.

faqs.question: Do my graphs need to be drawn to scale?
faqs.answer: No. They need to be clear and correctly labelled, with curves sloping the right way and points in the right order. Mark the values the question gives on the axes, and use dashed lines to link each point to its price and quantity.

faqs.question: If I draw a correct graph, do I still need to write an explanation?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the question says explain. A graph can support an explanation, but write the reasoning in words as well. A graph alone often shows what happens without saying why.

faqs.question: How much working should I show in a calculation?
faqs.answer: Enough for a reader to follow you: the formula or rule, the numbers you put into it and the final answer with its unit. A correct number with no working may not earn the point.

resources.title: Task Verbs and Free-Response Technique: Exam Skills Guide (Microeconomics)
resources.description: Learn what each free-response task verb in microeconomics asks for, how much to write, how to plan the section's time and how to set out calculations, with original worked examples.
prerequisites: You have studied most of the six units of the course
You can draw the main market, cost and firm graphs and do simple calculations with a four-function calculator
learningObjectives: Recognise every free-response task verb and say what a complete answer to each one must contain
Match the length and form of an answer to its verb and to the points a part is likely worth
Read a multi-part question so that each part uses the right graph, data and earlier results
Set out calculations with a formula, substituted values, a unit and a clear final answer
Plan time across the one long and two short questions of the free-response section
resources.calculatorNote: All places, firms and data are fictional. Only addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are needed
keyPoints: The verb sets the job: Identify needs only the answer, Explain needs a reason linked to the answer, Calculate needs visible working.
Free response is 3 questions in 60 minutes, including a 10-minute reading period: 1 long question (10 points) and 2 short questions (5 points each).
Graphing tasks carry 30-50% of free-response points, so every graph needs labelled axes, labelled curves and labelled equilibrium values.
A sensible plan for the 50 writing minutes is about 25 minutes on the long question, 11 on each short one and 3 to check.
Most lost credit comes from a direction with no reason, a reason that skips a step, an unlabelled graph or a number with no working.

faqs.question: Do I need full sentences for every part?
faqs.answer: No. Identify and Calculate parts need a word, a value or a short line of working. Explain parts read best as one to three short sentences that link cause to effect.

faqs.question: Can a graph count as part of an explanation?
faqs.answer: Yes, the course allows graphs and symbols in an explanation. Still add a sentence in words, because a reader needs to see which curve moved and why.

faqs.question: What if I cannot do an early part that a later part needs?
faqs.answer: Write a clearly labelled assumption, such as an assumed price or quantity, and carry on. Later parts can then be checked against your own value instead of being left blank.

resources.title: Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration: Study Guide (Physics 1 1.2)
resources.description: Build displacement, average and instantaneous velocity, and acceleration from first principles with algebra and graphs only, including signs, tangent slopes and limiting cases.
prerequisites: Choosing an axis and using + and − signs for direction in one dimension (Topic 1.1)
Finding the slope of a straight line from two points
learningObjectives: Describe a change in position as a displacement Δx = x − x₀ and tell it apart from distance travelled
Calculate average velocity and average acceleration from initial and final values over a time interval
Estimate an instantaneous velocity from shrinking time intervals or from the slope of a tangent line on a position–time graph
Decide whether an object is speeding up or slowing down from the signs of v_x and a_x
resources.calculatorNote: Algebra only; no calculus is used anywhere in this course. Where gravity appears we use g = 9.8 m/s², the value on the course equation table
keyPoints: Displacement is the change in position, Δx = x − x₀. It has a sign; distance travelled does not.
Average velocity is v_avg = Δx / Δt. Average acceleration is a_avg = Δv_x / Δt.
Instantaneous velocity is the average velocity over a very short interval: the slope of the tangent line on a position–time graph.
Same signs for v_x and a_x means speeding up; opposite signs means slowing down. A negative a_x does not by itself mean slowing down.
Always state your axis first, for example "+x to the right". Every sign in the answer depends on it.

faqs.question: Is speed the same as velocity?
faqs.answer: No. In one dimension, velocity v_x has a sign that shows direction; speed is its size, |v_x|, and is never negative. Average speed (distance ÷ time) can differ a lot from the size of the average velocity (displacement ÷ time).

faqs.question: Does this course use calculus for instantaneous velocity?
faqs.answer: No. This is the algebra-based course. You find instantaneous velocity by taking average velocities over smaller and smaller intervals, or by drawing a tangent line on a graph and measuring its slope.

resources.title: Representing Motion: Study Guide (Physics 1 1.3)
resources.description: Describe one-dimensional motion with motion diagrams, graphs, equations and words, link graphs by slopes and areas, and use the three constant-acceleration equations, including free fall.
prerequisites: Displacement, average velocity and average acceleration with signs (Topic 1.2)
Finding the slope of a line and the area of a rectangle, triangle or trapezium
learningObjectives: Move between a narrative, a motion diagram, position–time, velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs, and equations for the same motion
Find velocity and acceleration from tangent slopes, and displacement and change in velocity from areas under graphs
Choose and use the three constant-acceleration equations in any single dimension, including vertical free fall
Derive a symbolic result from the kinematic equations and use it to compare two situations
Describe and sketch graphs for motion with changing acceleration without calculating with it
resources.calculatorNote: Algebra only; no calculus. We use g = 9.8 m/s² to match the rest of this unit. Exam questions that need a number for g use 10 m/s², and 9.8 or 9.81 m/s² is also accepted
keyPoints: One motion can be shown five ways: words, a motion diagram, graphs, equations and data tables. Each should tell the same story.
Slope of x–t is velocity; slope of v_x–t is acceleration. Area under v_x–t is displacement; area under a_x–t is change in velocity.
The three kinematic equations work only when acceleration is constant. Pick the one that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor need.
Near Earth's surface, free-fall acceleration is constant and downward, about 9.8 m/s². With +y up, a_y = −g.
If acceleration changes, describe and sketch the motion, but do not use the constant-acceleration equations.

faqs.question: Which value of g should I use?
faqs.answer: Exam questions that need a number use g = 10 m/s², and 9.8 m/s² or 9.81 m/s² is not penalised. This guide uses 9.8 m/s² to match the course equation table and the rest of the unit.

faqs.question: Do I need calculus to find areas under curves?
faqs.answer: No. In this course the graphs you calculate with are made of straight lines, so the areas are rectangles, triangles and trapeziums. For curved graphs you only describe or estimate.

resources.title: Reference Frames and Relative Motion: Study Guide (Physics 1 1.4)
resources.description: Describe motion from different observers' points of view: reference frames, relative velocity along one line, converting positions between frames, and why acceleration is frame-independent.
prerequisites: Using + and − signs for direction along one axis (Topics 1.1 and 1.2)
Reading slopes of position–time and velocity–time graphs (Topic 1.3)
learningObjectives: Say which observer a measurement belongs to and describe that observer's reference frame
Combine the velocity of an object and the velocity of an observer along one line to find the velocity that observer measures
Convert positions and displacements measured in one frame into those measured in another
Explain, with an algebraic argument or a graph, why all inertial observers measure the same acceleration
Sketch how a velocity–time graph changes when the same motion is viewed from a moving frame
resources.calculatorNote: Algebra only; no calculus is used anywhere in this course. Where gravity appears we use g = 9.8 m/s², the value on the course equation table
keyPoints: Every position, velocity and displacement is measured by some observer. Name the observer, then the axis.
Write v_AB for the velocity of A relative to B. Then v_AC = v_AB + v_BC, and v_BA = −v_AB.
In this course, relative velocities are combined along one line only, using signs.
Observers in different inertial frames disagree about position and velocity, but they measure the same acceleration.
Assume every frame is inertial (not accelerating) unless a question says otherwise.

faqs.question: Is one reference frame the 'true' one?
faqs.answer: No. Any inertial frame is equally valid. The ground is often the easiest to use, but a passenger's measurements are just as correct in the passenger's own frame.

faqs.question: Do I need to add relative velocities at an angle, such as a boat crossing a river?
faqs.answer: Not in this course. Relative-velocity questions stay on one straight line, so you add and subtract signed numbers. Topic 1.5 uses vectors in two dimensions for other kinds of motion.

resources.title: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions: Study Guide (Physics 1 1.5)
resources.description: Resolve vectors into perpendicular components with trigonometry, add them, and analyse two-dimensional and projectile motion as two separate one-dimensional problems linked by time.
prerequisites: Using signs for direction and the constant-acceleration equations in one dimension (Topics 1.1–1.3)
Right-angled triangle trigonometry: sine, cosine, tangent and Pythagoras' theorem
learningObjectives: Split a vector into two perpendicular components using a stated coordinate system and sine, cosine or tangent
Rebuild a vector's size and direction from its components, checking the quadrant from a sketch
Add vectors such as successive displacements by adding their components
Treat motion in a plane as two one-dimensional motions that share the same time
Analyse projectiles with zero horizontal acceleration and constant downward vertical acceleration g
Predict how flight time and range change when launch speed, angle or height change, and plan a launch experiment
resources.calculatorNote: Algebra and trigonometry only; no calculus. Set your calculator to degrees. We use g = 9.8 m/s², the value on the course equation table; exam items that need a number for g use 10 m/s², and correct use of 9.8 m/s² is also accepted
keyPoints: Any vector can be replaced by two perpendicular components. With θ measured from the +x axis, A_x = A cos θ and A_y = A sin θ.
Size and direction come back from A = √(A_x² + A_y²) and tan θ = A_y / A_x, but always sketch the vector to pick the right quadrant.
Add vectors by adding their x-components and their y-components separately. Never add the magnitudes.
Motion in two dimensions is two one-dimensional motions, one along each axis. The only thing they share is the time.
A projectile has a_x = 0 and a_y = −g (with +y up), so its horizontal velocity never changes and its vertical velocity changes by 9.8 m/s every second.

faqs.question: Is the speed of a projectile zero at the top of its path?
faqs.answer: No. Only the vertical component is zero there. The horizontal component is the same as at launch, so the speed at the top equals v_x0, and the acceleration is still g downward.

faqs.question: Do I need to add velocities from moving frames at an angle, like a boat crossing a river?
faqs.answer: Not in this course. Combining an object's velocity with a moving observer's velocity is kept to one dimension (Topic 1.4). In this topic you add components of vectors that describe one object, such as successive displacements.

faqs.question: Does a heavier ball land sooner?
faqs.answer: No, when air resistance is negligible, which the course assumes unless told otherwise. Mass does not appear in any projectile equation.

resources.title: Systems and Center of Mass: Study Guide (Physics 1 2.1)
resources.description: Choose a system, decide when it can be treated as one object, and locate its center of mass by symmetry or with the weighted-average equation for up to five particles.
prerequisites: Choosing a positive direction and an origin (Topic 1.1)
Reading positions on x and y axes in two dimensions (Topic 1.5)
learningObjectives: Choose a system, draw its boundary, and sort interactions into internal ones and external ones
Decide when a system of many parts can be modelled as a single object, and when its internal structure matters
Recognise when energy or mass crosses a system boundary, and explain how parts of a system can move differently from the whole
Locate a center of mass on a line of symmetry without calculation
Calculate the center of mass of up to five particles in one or two dimensions, or of a symmetric object plus particles
resources.calculatorNote: Algebra only; no calculus. Positions in metres and masses in kilograms; answers to 2 significant figures unless the data justify more
keyPoints: A system is whatever you choose to study. Everything else is the environment. Interactions inside the boundary are internal; interactions across it are external.
If the parts and their interactions do not matter for the question, the whole system can be treated as one object located at its center of mass.
For a symmetric mass distribution, the center of mass lies on every line of symmetry.
x_cm = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂ + …) ÷ (m₁ + m₂ + …), and the same for y_cm. It is a mass-weighted average position.
The center of mass is always closer to the heavier part, and it does not have to be inside any material.

faqs.question: Is the center of mass the same as the center of gravity?
faqs.answer: Near Earth's surface, where g is the same across the object, they are at the same point. This course uses the term center of mass.

faqs.question: How many particles will I be asked to handle?
faqs.answer: The course expects calculations for up to five particles arranged in two dimensions, or for objects that are highly symmetric. Larger or irregular systems are described in words.

resources.title: Forces and Free-Body Diagrams: Study Guide (Physics 1 2.2)
resources.description: Treat every force as an interaction between two objects, tell contact forces from long-range ones, and draw free-body diagrams that follow the course conventions and lead straight to equations.
prerequisites: Choosing a system and locating its center of mass (Topic 2.1)
Resolving a vector into perpendicular components with sine and cosine (Topic 1.5)
learningObjectives: Describe any force as an interaction, naming the object that exerts it and the object it acts on
Explain why an object or system cannot exert a net force on itself
Tell contact forces from long-range forces, and explain that contact forces come from electric forces between atoms
Draw a free-body diagram for a chosen object or system, using the course conventions for arrows
Choose axes with one axis along the acceleration, including tilted axes on a ramp, and write each force in components
resources.calculatorNote: Algebra and trigonometry only; no calculus. Set your calculator to degrees. We use g = 9.8 m/s² (equivalently 9.8 N/kg), the value on the course equation table
keyPoints: A force is one object pushing or pulling on another. Every force has an object that exerts it, so name it: "force on the block by the floor".
Forces are vectors, measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²). An object or system cannot exert a net force on itself.
Contact forces (normal, friction, tension) are the large-scale result of electric forces between atoms. Gravity acts without contact.
A free-body diagram shows only the forces exerted on the chosen system by its environment, as straight arrows starting on a dot.
Draw whole forces on the diagram, never components. Do the components separately, with one axis along the acceleration.

faqs.question: Should I draw the velocity or the net force on a free-body diagram?
faqs.answer: Neither. A free-body diagram shows only the individual forces exerted on the system by other objects. Velocity, acceleration and the net force are not forces exerted by anything, so they do not belong on it.

faqs.question: Do I have to draw arrows to scale?
faqs.answer: Make the relative lengths sensible: a bigger force gets a longer arrow, and forces that balance get equal lengths. Exact scale drawing is not needed unless a question asks for it.

learningObjectives: Recall F_(A on B) = −F_(B on A) and the five features of a third-law pair

keyPoints: To find a partner force, swap the objects: 'A on B' becomes 'B on A'.
Paired forces act on different objects, so they never cancel.

resources.author: marlbridge-academic-team

resources.title: Newton's Third Law: Study Guide (Physics 1 2.3)
resources.description: Every force is one half of an interaction. Learn to find third-law force pairs, explain why internal forces leave the centre of mass alone, and reason about tension in strings and ropes.
prerequisites: Describing a force as an interaction and drawing free-body diagrams (Topic 2.2)
Choosing a system and locating its centre of mass (Topic 2.1)
learningObjectives: Name the third-law partner of any force by swapping the two objects in its label
Explain why the two forces in a third-law pair never cancel each other, using free-body diagrams of both objects
Use the idea that internal forces cannot change the motion of a system's centre of mass
Describe tension as the pull that neighbouring pieces of a string exert on each other, and say when it is the same everywhere
Predict how the sizes of paired forces compare when the two objects differ in mass, speed or size
resources.calculatorNote: Algebra only; no calculus is used anywhere in this course. Where gravity appears we use g = 9.8 m/s², the value on the course equation table
keyPoints: Forces come in pairs: if A pushes or pulls on B, then B pushes or pulls on A. F_(A on B) = −F_(B on A).
The two forces in a pair are equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type, and act at the same time on different objects.
Because they act on different objects, the two forces in a pair never appear on the same free-body diagram and never cancel each other.
Forces between parts of a system are internal. They cannot change the motion of the system's centre of mass.
An ideal string has negligible mass and does not stretch. Its tension is the same all along it. A heavy rope or chain can have different tensions at different points.

faqs.question: If the forces in a pair are equal and opposite, how does anything ever move?
faqs.answer: The two forces act on different objects. To decide how one object moves, you add only the forces exerted on that object. Its partner force acts on something else and does not appear in the sum.

faqs.question: Are the weight of a book and the normal force on it a third-law pair?
faqs.answer: No. Both act on the book, and they are different types of force. The partner of Earth's pull on the book is the book's pull on Earth. The partner of the table's push on the book is the book's push on the table.

resources.title: Newton's First Law: Study Guide (Physics 1 2.4)
resources.description: When does velocity stay constant? Net force as a vector sum, translational equilibrium, Newton's first law, forces balanced in one direction only, and inertial reference frames.
prerequisites: Drawing free-body diagrams and naming third-law pairs (Topics 2.2 and 2.3)
Resolving vectors into components (Topic 1.5)
Knowing what makes a reference frame inertial (Topic 1.4)
learningObjectives: Find the net force on a system by adding force vectors, using components along two axes
State the condition for translational equilibrium and write ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 from a free-body diagram
Use Newton's first law to link zero net force with constant velocity, including motion at constant speed
Explain how forces can balance along one axis but not the other, and predict which velocity component changes

resources.calculatorNote: Algebra and trigonometry only; no calculus is used anywhere in this course. Where gravity appears we use g = 9.8 m/s², the value on the course equation table
keyPoints: The net force is the vector sum of all the forces exerted on a system: ΣF.
Translational equilibrium means ΣF = 0. In two dimensions, ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.
Newton's first law: if the net force on a system is zero, its velocity stays constant. At rest stays at rest; moving keeps the same speed and direction.
Equilibrium does not mean at rest. A car cruising at a steady speed on a straight road is in equilibrium.
Forces can balance along one axis and not the other. Only the velocity component along the unbalanced direction changes.
An inertial frame is one in which the first law is observed to hold.

faqs.question: Does a moving object need a force to keep it moving?
faqs.answer: No. With zero net force, a moving object keeps moving at constant velocity. Everyday objects slow down because friction or air resistance acts on them, and that is a force.

faqs.question: If an object's velocity is constant, must the net force be zero?
faqs.answer: Yes. The first law says zero net force gives constant velocity, and Topic 2.5 shows that any non-zero net force would change the velocity. So constant velocity and zero net force always go together.

keyPoints: If the net external force on a system is not zero, the forces are unbalanced and the system’s velocity changes.
Newton’s second law: a = ΣF / m. The acceleration points in the same direction as the net force.
For a fixed mass, a is proportional to ΣF. For a fixed net force, a is inversely proportional to m.
Only external forces count. Forces between parts of the system cancel and cannot change the motion of its centre of mass.
ma is not a force. Never draw it on a free-body diagram.

faqs.question: Is F = ma the same as a = ΣF / m?
faqs.answer: They are the same law rearranged. Writing a = ΣF / m is safer, because it reminds you that the net force is the cause and the acceleration is the result, and that F means the vector sum of all external forces.

faqs.question: Does the net force point in the direction the object is moving?
faqs.answer: Not always. The net force points in the direction of the acceleration. A car braking while moving east has a net force pointing west.

Apparent weight is the normal force. It differs from mg whenever the system accelerates, and is zero in free fall.

faqs.question: Is weight the same as mass?
faqs.answer: No. Mass (kg) measures how much an object resists changes in motion. Weight (N) is the gravitational force on it, mg. A 2.0 kg object has a weight of 19.6 N on Earth but only about 3.2 N on the Moon; its mass is 2.0 kg in both places.

faqs.question: Are astronauts in orbit weightless because there is no gravity?
faqs.answer: No. At the height of a low orbit, a few hundred kilometres up, Earth’s field is still about 90% of its surface value. Astronauts feel weightless because gravity is the only force on them, so nothing pushes back on them: their apparent weight is zero.

faqs.question: Does friction always point backwards, against the motion?
faqs.answer: No. Friction opposes sliding between the two surfaces, not motion in general. When you walk, static friction on your foot points forwards, in the direction you move.

faqs.question: Why is it harder to start a heavy box moving than to keep it moving?
faqs.answer: Because the maximum static friction (μ_s F_n) is usually larger than kinetic friction (μ_k F_n) for the same surfaces. Once the box slides, the friction force drops.

Hooke's law: F_s = −kΔx. The size is k|Δx|; the minus sign means the force points opposite to the stretch or compression.

faqs.question: What does the minus sign in F_s = −kΔx mean?
faqs.answer: It shows direction only. If the spring is stretched in the +x direction, it pulls in the −x direction, and the other way round. For the size of the force, use k|Δx|.

faqs.question: Is a larger k a stiffer or a softer spring?
faqs.answer: Stiffer. A larger k means more force for each metre of stretch, so the same force stretches it less.

faqs.question: Is centripetal force a new kind of force to add to my free-body diagram?
faqs.answer: No. Draw only real forces such as weight, normal, tension and friction. "Centripetal" just names the direction of their net force: towards the centre. Never add an extra arrow labelled F_c.

faqs.question: Why does a passenger feel thrown outward on a sharp turn?
faqs.answer: In the ground frame nothing pushes the passenger outward. Their body tends to keep moving in a straight line while the car turns underneath them, until the seat or door pushes them inward.

keyPoints: Translational kinetic energy is the energy an object has because its center of mass is moving: K = ½mv².
K is a scalar. It depends on speed, not direction, and it is never negative.
K is proportional to v², so doubling the speed makes K four times bigger. Doubling the mass only doubles K.
